name: tench
Tinca tinca
0.description: A thick-bodied freshwater fish with a smooth-looking body covered in very small scales, usually colored olive-green, bronze, or brownish gold. It has a blunt head, small eyes that can show a reddish iris, a short pair of barbels at the corners of the mouth, and dark fins that are notably rounded rather than pointed.
0.guidelines: Classify as tench when the fish is deep-bodied and olive or bronze colored, with tiny scales giving a slick matte appearance, small mouth barbels, and uniformly rounded dark fins. Distinguish it from carp and common carp, which usually have larger visible scales and longer barbels; from bream, which are more laterally compressed and silvery with longer anal fins; and from trout or perch, which have more pointed fins, clearer spotting or striping, and lack the tench's smooth bronze-olive, rounded-fin look.

name: goldfish
Carassius auratus
1.description: A small to medium ornamental carp with no barbels around the mouth. Goldfish vary from slim, torpedo-shaped fish to deep-bodied, egg-shaped, or nearly spherical fancy forms. Fins may be short or long and flowing; the dorsal fin usually begins around mid-back and ends before the tail, though some breeds lack it entirely. Eyes may be normal or strongly protruding in telescope-eye varieties, and some fish develop fleshy head growths (wen). Color is highly variable, commonly solid orange, gold, red, white, or black, or mixed/calico patterns.
1.guidelines: Classify as goldfish when the fish has the typical goldfish body plan and lacks mouth barbels, even if it is a fancy breed with a round body, double tail, telescope eyes, or head growth. Do not confuse with koi or common carp, which usually have visible barbels and a more carp-like head; with aquarium livebearers such as guppies or mollies, which are much smaller and slimmer; or with cichlids/parrot cichlids, which have different head and fin shapes. Include both common and fancy ornamental varieties of goldfish.

name: great white shark
Carcharodon carcharias
2.description: A large, heavy-bodied shark with a dark gray to blue-gray back, bright white underside, and a sharply irregular boundary between the two that looks like uneven white splashes along the sides and around the gills. It has a thick, powerful, conical snout, large solid-black eyes, and broad triangular teeth with serrated edges. The body is robust with a tall dorsal fin and strong crescent-shaped tail.
2.guidelines: Classify as great white shark when the shark shows a robust body, blunt-conical snout, black button-like eyes, serrated triangular teeth, and especially the irregular jagged line between dark upper body and white belly. Do not confuse with mako sharks, which are slimmer with a more pointed snout and smoother color transition; tiger sharks, which have vertical stripes or blotches; bull sharks, which are stockier with a shorter blunter face and less dramatic countershading; or basking sharks and whale sharks, which have very different mouths and spotting patterns.

name: tiger shark
Galeocerdo cuvier
3.description: A large, heavy-bodied shark with a broad, blunt, somewhat rectangular snout, large dark eyes, a tall first dorsal fin, and a much smaller second dorsal fin set nearer the tail. The body is gray to brownish above and pale below, often showing dark vertical bars, stripes, or spots along the sides, especially in younger individuals.
3.guidelines: Classify as tiger shark when the shark has a stout body, very blunt head, and dark flank markings combined with a clearly smaller second dorsal fin. Distinguish it from requiem sharks such as sandbar or bull sharks, which are usually more uniformly colored and lack the characteristic side striping; from lemon sharks, which have two dorsal fins of more similar size; and from great white sharks, which have a more conical snout, crescent tail proportions, and no tiger-like side markings.

name: hammerhead shark
Sphyrnidae
4.description: A shark with a distinctive flattened, T-shaped or hammer-shaped head, with the eyes set far apart at the outer ends. The body is streamlined with a tall dorsal fin, a pointed snout profile across the hammer, and coloration typically gray, brownish-gray, or olive above with a pale underside.
4.guidelines: Classify as hammerhead shark when the broad hammer- or bonnet-like head is clearly visible; this head shape is the key defining feature. Do not confuse it with requiem sharks, tiger sharks, or great white sharks, which have conventional pointed snouts rather than a lateral head extension. Distinguish from sawfish and sawsharks by noting that hammerheads lack a long toothed rostrum. If the head is not visible, use caution and rely on the overall shark shape only when the hammer form is still evident from silhouette.

name: electric ray
Torpediniformes
5.description: A ray with a thick, fleshy, nearly circular or oval disc, small protruding eyes, and a short stout tail that clearly bears one or two dorsal fins and a distinct caudal fin. The body is smooth and soft-looking rather than angular, and coloration is often plain brown, gray, or tan, or marked with round spots, rosettes, or ocelli.
5.guidelines: Classify as electric ray when the animal has a rounded disc and a fish-like tail with obvious dorsal and tail fins. Do not confuse it with stingrays or eagle rays, which usually have a more diamond-shaped disc and a long whip-like tail lacking a strong caudal fin. It also differs from skates, which are typically more rhomboid, with a firmer-looking body and a less thick, cushion-like disc. The soft circular body and prominent dorsal/caudal fins are the key cues.

name: stingray
Myliobatiformes
6.description: A ray with a strongly flattened body forming a round, diamond-shaped, or kite-like disc, broad winglike pectoral fins, eyes on the upper surface, and a long slender tail that often bears one or more stinging spines. Color varies from plain gray, brown, or olive to boldly spotted or mottled patterns; some species are more angular and eagle-ray-like, while freshwater forms can look more circular.
6.guidelines: Classify as stingray when the animal has a flat disc-shaped body and a whip-like tail with a sting, usually resting on or gliding just above the bottom. Do not confuse with skates, which usually have thicker tails with small dorsal fins and no venomous sting, or with manta/devil rays, which have very broad triangular 'wings' and obvious forward-facing cephalic fins. Sharks have a clearly fish-like body rather than a flattened disc.

name: rooster
Gallus gallus domesticus
7.description: An adult male domestic chicken with an upright stance, large red comb and wattles, a pointed beak, and often long curved tail sickles and glossy hackle feathers. Plumage varies widely by breed and color, but the bird typically looks leaner and more ornamented than a hen, with a more prominent head crest and longer tail.
7.guidelines: Classify as rooster when the image shows a male chicken, usually identified by a conspicuous comb and wattles, long arched tail feathers, and showier plumage. Do not confuse with hens, which are usually smaller, duller, and lack the long sickle tail; or with wild junglefowl, which look similar but are not domestic barnyard chickens. Use the overall male chicken appearance rather than any single color pattern, since roosters occur in many breeds and colors.

name: hen
Gallus gallus domesticus
8.description: An adult female domestic chicken: a medium-sized farm bird with a rounded body, short bill, small to moderate red comb and wattles, and sturdy scaled legs. Plumage varies widely by breed and color pattern, including brown, white, black, red, buff, gray, mottled, or barred feathers, but the overall shape remains compact and chicken-like.
8.guidelines: Classify as hen when the bird is a domestic chicken and specifically female, typically lacking the long flowing tail feathers, large comb, and more upright, showy build of a rooster. Do not confuse with rooster/cock, which usually has larger wattles and comb, sickle tail feathers, and brighter ornamental plumage. Also distinguish from chicks, which are much smaller and fluffy, and from other poultry such as turkeys, guinea fowl, or ducks, which have clearly different body shape, head structure, and bill.

name: ostrich
Struthio camelus
9.description: A very large, flightless bird with an extremely long bare neck and long legs, a small head, large eyes, and a broad rounded body covered in loose feathers. Adult males are mostly black with prominent white wing and tail feathers; females and juveniles are grayish to brown with paler underparts. The bill is short and fairly flat, and the bird often appears tall, upright, and long-striding in open ground.
9.guidelines: Classify as ostrich when the bird is exceptionally tall and heavy-bodied, with a long mostly bare neck, long powerful legs, and a small head. Adult males usually show black-and-white plumage, while females and young are gray-brown. Distinguish it from emus and rheas: emus are shaggier, uniformly brown-gray, and darker-faced; rheas are smaller, grayer, and less strongly black-and-white in males. Also avoid confusing close-up heads with other ratites by checking the pinkish to pale bill, very large eye, and the overall ostrich body shape in wider views.

name: brambling
Fringilla montifringilla
10.description: A small finch with a stout conical bill, orange-buff breast and shoulders, black-and-white wings marked with a bold orange band, and a white belly that often shows dark mottling along the flanks. The rump and undertail are distinctly white. Its shape is finch-like but slightly longer-winged and longer-tailed than a European goldfinch.
10.guidelines: Classify as brambling when the bird shows the combination of orange breast/shoulders, black-and-white wing pattern with orange on the wing, and especially a white rump and white undertail. Do not confuse it with European goldfinch, which has a red face and bright yellow wing bar, or chaffinch, which lacks the brambling’s strong black-white-orange wing pattern and white rump. Winter birds may look duller, but the pale belly, orange tones, and white rump/undertail remain key cues.

name: American goldfinch
Spinus tristis
11.description: A small finch with a short conical bill and sharply contrasting black-and-white wings. Breeding males are bright lemon yellow with a black forehead and black wings and tail marked with bold white patches; females and nonbreeding birds are duller yellow-olive to buffy with darker wings and less black on the head. The body is compact and the bill is pale orange to horn-colored in many views.
11.guidelines: Classify this as an American goldfinch when the bird shows bright yellow or yellow-olive plumage combined with black wings bearing clear white bars or patches, often with a small black forehead cap in males. Do not confuse it with the European goldfinch, which has a striking red face and broader multicolored head pattern, or with yellow warblers and other small yellow songbirds, which have thinner pointed bills and lack the bold black-and-white finch wings. Pine siskins and lesser goldfinches are also similar; American goldfinches usually look cleaner yellow, with stronger white wing markings and a thicker seed-eating bill.

name: house finch
Haemorhous mexicanus
12.description: A small finch with a short conical bill and a fairly long, slightly notched tail. Males usually show rosy red to orange-red on the head, throat, and upper chest over a brown, streaked body. Females and juveniles are plain brownish-gray with heavy blurry streaking below, a rather plain face, and no strong facial pattern.
12.guidelines: Classify as house finch when the bird is a small streaky finch, often at feeders, with males showing red mostly on the head and breast and females looking plain-faced with blurred underpart streaks. Distinguish it from purple finch: purple finch males look richer raspberry-red over more of the body, and females show a stronger face pattern with a bold pale eyebrow and pale whisker stripe. Also separate it from Cassin's finch, which has a longer-looking head, crisper facial pattern, and males with red concentrated on the crown.

name: dark-eyed junco
Junco hyemalis
13.description: A small, round-bodied sparrow with a short pale pink bill, a dark eye, and a fairly long tail that often shows white outer feathers from below or in flight. Plumage varies by form, but most birds are gray to slate or brown above with a paler belly; many examples show a dark hood or head contrasting with a white or light gray underside.
13.guidelines: Classify as dark-eyed junco when the bird is a small sparrow-like songbird with a pink bill, clean pale belly, and obvious white outer tail feathers. Include the common color forms shown here, from slate-gray birds to brown-backed Oregon-type birds with darker hoods and buffy sides. Do not confuse with chickadees, which have a much smaller black bill and bold white cheek patches, or with towhees and other sparrows, which are larger, more heavily patterned, and usually lack the crisp white tail edges and plain pink bill.

name: indigo bunting
Passerina cyanea
14.description: A small seed-eating songbird with a short, thick conical bill. Breeding males are vivid all-over blue to blue-violet, often with slightly darker wings and tail; females and nonbreeding birds are plain warm brown. The body is slim and compact, with no bold wing bars.
14.guidelines: Classify as indigo bunting when the bird is a small bunting with a stout finch-like bill and, in males, mostly uniform bright blue plumage. Do not confuse with blue grosbeak, which is bulkier, has a much heavier bill, and shows two obvious chestnut wing bars. Also distinguish from lazuli bunting males, which have a rusty breast and white belly rather than solid blue overall.

name: American robin
Turdus migratorius
15.description: A medium-sized thrush with a yellow to orange-yellow bill, dark gray to blackish head and upperparts, a bold white eye ring or broken white arcs around the eye, warm orange to brick-red breast and belly, and a small white patch under the tail. Females are typically duller than males, and juveniles show a spotted breast.
15.guidelines: Classify as American robin when the bird shows the classic thrush shape, orange-red underparts, dark upperparts, yellow bill, and distinct white eye ring. Do not confuse it with the European robin, which is much smaller and has an orange face and breast but brown upperparts; with eastern bluebirds, which have blue upperparts and lack the strong white eye ring; or with varied thrushes, which have a dark breast band and orange eyebrow. Juveniles may look speckled, but still keep the robin shape and orange tones.

name: bulbul
Pycnonotidae
16.description: Medium-sized songbirds with a slim upright posture, fairly long tail, and a short to medium bill. Many have a dark cap or pointed crest, contrasting pale cheek or throat patches, and a bright vent or undertail area that may be red, yellow, or orange. Plumage is often brown, olive, gray, black, or white, with some species showing a red cheek patch or white head markings.
16.guidelines: Classify as bulbul when the bird has the typical bulbul shape: slender body, long tail, slightly raised stance, and often a crest or dark cap, frequently with colorful vent or face accents. Do not restrict to only red-vented or red-whiskered forms; the category includes several bulbul species. Distinguish from babblers by the usually cleaner, more upright silhouette and brighter vent/face markings; from shrikes by the lack of a heavy hooked bill; and from wagtails or flycatchers by the stouter body and bulbul-style crest, head pattern, and undertail coloring.

name: jay
17.description: A jay is a medium-sized corvid with a sturdy bill, fairly long tail, and often striking blue plumage. Many species show black-and-white facial or neck markings, pale underparts, and bold barred or spotted blue-and-black panels on the wings and tail. Some jays have a prominent crest, while others have a smoother, capped head; overall colors commonly combine bright blue, beige or gray, black, and white.
17.guidelines: Classify as jay when the bird has the typical corvid build and the characteristic colorful wing or tail patterning, often with blue barring, patches, or checkering. Include both crested and uncrested jays. Do not confuse with magpies, which usually have much longer tails and stronger black-and-white contrast, or with crows and ravens, which are larger and mostly plain black. Also distinguish from small blue songbirds such as bluebirds or buntings: jays are bulkier, have heavier bills, and show more complex wing markings.

name: Australian magpie
Gymnorhina tibicen
18.description: A medium-to-large black-and-white bird with a stout pale bill, dark eyes, and a strong upright stance. Most adults show a glossy black head, chest, wings, and tail with a white nape, shoulder patches, and underparts; the black areas often have a blue-green iridescent sheen. Plumage can vary somewhat by sex, age, and region, but the bold black-and-white pattern and heavy bill are consistent.
18.guidelines: Classify as Australian magpie when the bird is a robust, crow-like black-and-white songbird with a thick bill and relatively broad body. Key cues are the white nape/back of neck and white shoulder or back patches, not the very long wedge-shaped tail of the Eurasian magpie. Avoid confusing it with pied currawongs and butcherbirds, which are slimmer and differently patterned, and with the Eurasian magpie, which has a much longer tail and a whiter belly with different wing patterning.

name: chickadee
Poecile
19.description: Small, round-bodied songbird with a black cap and throat bib, bright white cheek patches, a short pointed bill, and soft gray to gray-brown upperparts. Underparts are pale whitish to buff, often with warmer buff on the flanks, and the tail is fairly long and narrow.
19.guidelines: Classify as chickadee when the bird shows the classic black cap, black throat, white cheeks, and compact gray body. Do not confuse it with titmice, which usually have a crest and lack the bold black bib, or nuthatches, which have a longer bill, shorter tail, and different posture. Also distinguish from similar small songbirds such as warblers or kinglets by the chickadee’s plain pattern, stout head, and strong black-and-white face.

name: white-throated dipper
Cinclus cinclus
20.description: A small, chunky, round-bodied river bird with a very short tail, long legs, and a straight pointed bill. It is typically dark brown to slate-brown above with a bold white throat and chest bib, often bordered below by rich chestnut on the breast and belly. It is usually seen standing low on rocks or in fast-flowing streams, sometimes bobbing or foraging at the water’s edge.
20.guidelines: Classify this as a white-throated dipper when the bird is a compact stream-dwelling passerine with a conspicuous white bib and short tail. Distinguish it from the American dipper, which is plainer slate-gray overall and lacks the strong white throat-and-chest patch. Also avoid confusion with wrens or small thrushes: those usually have longer tails, finer patterning, and are not so strongly associated with rushing water and waterside rocks.

name: bird of prey
21.description: A diurnal raptor with a hooked bill, strong feet and talons, and long broad wings adapted for soaring or gliding. Across the images, plumage varies widely from pale white to rufous, brown, and nearly black, and the tail may be forked, rounded, or square depending on the species. Most show the lean, predatory build typical of kites, hawks, and eagles.
21.guidelines: Classify images here when they show a raptorial bird such as a kite, hawk, or eagle: look for the sharply hooked beak, powerful grasping feet, and broad soaring wings. Do not confuse with vultures, which usually have heavier bodies, smaller heads relative to the body, and a more scavenger-like profile; falcons, which typically have more pointed wings and a compact, fast-flying shape; owls, which have round heads and forward-facing eyes; or gulls and other seabirds, which lack the heavy hooked bill and strong talons.

name: bald eagle
Haliaeetus leucocephalus
22.description: Large eagle with a dark brown body and wings, a bright white head and upper neck, and a white wedge-shaped tail in adults. It has a large, strongly hooked yellow beak, yellow eyes, broad rounded wings, and yellow legs that are feathered partway down. Immature birds are mostly dark brown with mottled white or pale brown patches on the body, and have darker beaks and eyes before acquiring the adult white head and tail.
22.guidelines: Classify as bald eagle when the bird shows the classic contrast of white head and tail against a dark brown body, plus a large yellow hooked bill. Juveniles can be identified by their heavy dark plumage with irregular white mottling and overall bulky eagle shape. Distinguish from golden eagle by the bald eagle's white adult head and tail, larger yellow bill, and lack of golden nape; from sea eagles such as white-tailed eagle by the cleaner white head and tail pattern and more sharply contrasting adult plumage; and from vultures or other large raptors by the fully feathered head, massive hooked bill, and broad eagle proportions.

name: vulture
23.description: A very large scavenging bird with a heavy body, broad wings, a relatively small bald or sparsely feathered head, a long neck, and a thick strongly hooked bill. Many show a pale or fluffy neck ruff, dark brown to black body plumage, and a hunched posture when perched. In flight, vultures appear long-winged and broad-winged, built for soaring rather than fast flapping.
23.guidelines: Classify as vulture when the bird has the classic scavenger build: bare head, hefty hooked bill, bulky body, and very broad soaring wings. Do not confuse it with eagles or hawks, which usually have fully feathered heads and a more powerful raptor look, or condors/corvids/turkeys seen at a distance. Distinguish from turkey vultures specifically if the category is broader: turkey vultures are one kind of vulture, but vultures overall also include paler-headed and heavier-billed Old World species. The bald head and carrion-feeding silhouette are the key cues.

name: great grey owl
Strix nebulosa
24.description: A very large, long-tailed owl with no ear tufts, a huge round facial disc marked by concentric gray rings, yellow eyes, and a small yellow beak partly hidden by facial feathers. Plumage is mostly gray to brown-gray with fine mottling and streaking, and there is typically a distinct dark patch or “bow tie” below the beak.
24.guidelines: Classify as great grey owl when the bird shows an oversized circular facial disc with concentric rings, yellow eyes, no ear tufts, and overall gray mottled plumage. Distinguish it from long-eared owl and other tufted owls by the complete lack of ear tufts; from barred owl by the more sharply defined circular face, yellow rather than dark eyes, and dark throat patch; and from other Strix owls by its especially large facial disc and very long tail.

name: fire salamander
Salamandra salamandra
25.description: A stout, heavy-bodied salamander with a cylindrical body, relatively short round tail, smooth moist glossy skin, and visible costal grooves along the sides. It has a broad rounded snout, large bulging black eyes, and two long prominent parotid glands behind the eyes. The body is deep black with bright yellow to orange markings in irregular spots, blotches, bands, or streaks across the head, back, limbs, and tail.
25.guidelines: Classify as fire salamander when the animal is a robust black salamander with conspicuous yellow or orange markings and large parotid glands behind the eyes. Do not confuse it with newts, which are usually slimmer, rougher-skinned in the terrestrial phase, and often have orange bellies rather than bold yellow-on-black dorsal markings. Distinguish it from alpine salamanders and other dark salamanders by the clear yellow/orange patterning; from mole salamanders such as tiger salamanders by its glossier skin, heavier build, and irregular blotchy pattern rather than neat bars or rows of spots.

name: smooth newt
Lissotriton vulgaris
26.description: A small, slender newt with an olive-brown to tan body, dark stripes on the head running through the eyes, and numerous dark spots on the throat, belly, sides, and tail. The belly is often orange or yellowish with black spotting. Breeding males show a wavy, undulating crest along the back and tail and often a bluish-white or silvery stripe on the tail; outside the breeding season the crest disappears, the skin looks smoother and more velvety, coloration becomes duller brown, and a faint pale stripe may run along the back.
26.guidelines: Classify as smooth newt when the animal is a small, slim European newt with eye stripes, a spotted underside, and in males a scalloped breeding crest plus a pale or silvery tail stripe. Distinguish it from palmate newt by the smoother, more developed crest and heavier spotting; from great crested newt by its much smaller size, finer build, and lack of the dark, warty, bulky appearance; and from salamanders by its more aquatic newt shape, laterally flattened tail, and spotted orange belly rather than bold yellow-and-black warning coloration.

name: red eft
Notophthalmus viridescens
27.description: A small juvenile newt with a slender body, bright orange to red-orange coloration, dry granular skin, a rounded tail without a fin, and distinct small red spots usually bordered by black rings along the back and sides.
27.guidelines: Classify as red eft only when the animal shows the terrestrial juvenile eastern newt form: vivid orange-red color, rough dry-looking skin, ringed red spots, and no paddlelike tail fin. Do not confuse it with adult eastern newts, which are more aquatic and have smoother skin and a finned tail, or with red salamanders and other orange salamanders, which are typically larger, smoother, and lack the characteristic black-ringed red spots.

name: spotted salamander
Ambystoma maculatum
28.description: A stout, smooth-skinned mole salamander with a dark black, bluish-black, brown, or slate-gray body and two fairly regular rows of round yellow to orange spots running from the head down the back and onto the tail. The head is broad and smooth, lacking large parotoid glands behind the eyes. The belly is plain pale gray to grayish and unmarked, and the tail is laterally compressed.
28.guidelines: Classify this as a spotted salamander when the animal is a dark, heavy-bodied salamander with conspicuous yellow or orange round spots arranged in paired rows along the back. Do not confuse it with tiger salamanders, which are usually more robustly blotched or striped rather than neatly spotted, or with slimy salamanders and other Plethodon species, which are slimmer and typically have small white flecks instead of large yellow spots. Also exclude newts, which often have rougher skin, smaller spots, and more obvious parotoid glands or different body proportions.

name: axolotl
Ambystoma mexicanum
29.description: A fully aquatic salamander with a broad flat head, small lidless eyes, a wide mouth, short legs with long toes, and a long finned tail. Its most distinctive feature is the three feathery external gill stalks on each side of the head. Common colors include pale pink or white with red gills, dark mottled brown, gray, or golden forms.
29.guidelines: Classify as axolotl when the animal is a stocky aquatic salamander with permanent external feathery gills and a tail fin running along the back and tail. Do not confuse it with mudpuppies (Necturus), which are usually darker, more uniformly salamander-like, and less commonly seen in the pale pet color morphs typical of axolotls. Also avoid confusing it with frog tadpoles, sirens, or larval newts/salamanders: axolotls have four legs, a broad head, obvious bushy side gills, and a characteristic aquarium-pet appearance.

name: American bullfrog
Lithobates catesbeianus
30.description: A very large, heavy-bodied frog with smooth to slightly warty olive green, brown, or mottled skin, a broad head, large eyes, and a conspicuously large tympanum behind each eye. It usually lacks the long dorsolateral folds seen in many other pond frogs, having instead a fold that curves around the eardrum. The hind legs are long and muscular, and the throat may be yellowish in males. It is typically seen floating low in water, sitting at pond edges, or resting on mud, rocks, or lily pads.
30.guidelines: Classify this as an American bullfrog when the frog is notably large and robust, with a big head, large round tympanum, and no dorsolateral ridges running down the back. Do not confuse it with green frogs or leopard frogs: green frogs are usually smaller and have clear dorsolateral folds ending midway down the back, while leopard frogs show distinct dark spots and lighter dorsolateral folds. Exclude tree frogs, which have toe pads and a smaller, more delicate build, and tailed frogs, which are squat stream frogs lacking the typical bullfrog shape.

name: tree frog
Hylidae
31.description: A small, slender frog adapted for climbing, usually bright green to yellow-green, sometimes with pale white, cream, or yellow striping on the side. It has smooth skin, long legs, large protruding eyes, and rounded adhesive toe pads for gripping leaves, stems, branches, and glass.
31.guidelines: Classify as tree frog when the frog has a lightweight climbing build and obvious toe pads, often resting on vegetation or vertical surfaces. Do not confuse it with pond frogs, bullfrogs, or toads, which are heavier-bodied, usually lack enlarged toe pads, and are more often brown, warty, or ground-dwelling. Also distinguish from poison dart frogs, which are smaller, more compact, and often boldly patterned rather than plain green.

name: loggerhead sea turtle
Caretta caretta
33.description: A large sea turtle with a broad, massive head, strong blunt beak, and a robust oval to heart-shaped shell. The carapace is usually reddish-brown to dark brown with five or more lateral scutes, while the underside is paler yellowish to cream. Flippers are large and paddle-shaped, and the head is noticeably bigger and squarer than in most other sea turtles.
33.guidelines: Classify as loggerhead sea turtle when the animal has a very large blocky head and stout jaws, plus a brownish shell with non-overlapping scutes. Distinguish it from green sea turtle, which has a smaller more rounded head and smoother-looking shell; hawksbill sea turtle, which has a narrow pointed beak and serrated overlapping shell scutes; leatherback sea turtle, which lacks hard shell scutes and has a ridged leathery back; and olive ridley/Kemp's ridley turtles, which are generally smaller and rounder-bodied with less massive heads.

name: leatherback sea turtle
Dermochelys coriacea
34.description: A very large sea turtle with a dark gray to black, leathery shell covered in small pale or white spots and marked by several prominent lengthwise ridges. Unlike hard-shelled sea turtles, the carapace is smooth and rubbery-looking rather than plated, and the body is broad with long front flippers.
34.guidelines: Classify as leatherback sea turtle when the turtle has a dark, leathery ridged back instead of a hard scuted shell. Key cues are the longitudinal ridges, white spotting, and massive streamlined body. Avoid confusion with green, loggerhead, hawksbill, olive ridley, and Kemp's ridley sea turtles, which have hard shells with distinct scutes; and with softshell turtles, which have flat soft shells and long snorkel-like noses and are usually freshwater turtles.

name: mud turtle
Kinosternon
35.description: A small aquatic turtle with a compact, oval, high-domed shell that is usually dark brown, olive, or black. The shell is smooth and plain-looking, and the body is similarly dark, sometimes with faint pale lines or spots on the head. It typically has short legs, a relatively small head, and a low, rounded profile suited to shallow muddy water.
35.guidelines: Classify as mud turtle when the turtle is small, dark-shelled, and plain, with a smooth oval carapace and no bright red, yellow, or ornate patterning. Do not confuse it with musk turtles, which often have stronger head stripes and a more peaked shell, or with painted turtles and sliders, which usually show brighter striping and more colorful shell margins. Exclude box turtles, which are more terrestrial and usually have bolder yellow or orange shell patterns and a more hinged, highly domed shell.

name: terrapin
36.description: A terrapin is a medium-sized freshwater or brackish-water turtle with an oval to rounded, moderately domed shell, usually dark brown, olive, or black with visible scute patterning. The shell often shows rings, lines, or mottled markings, and some kinds—especially diamondback terrapins—have embossed concentric scute patterns. The skin is commonly gray, olive, or dark, sometimes with pale striping or dense black spotting.
36.guidelines: Classify as terrapin when the animal is a small- to medium-sized aquatic or semi-aquatic turtle with a hard, patterned shell and non-flipper limbs. Do not confuse it with tortoises, which have stouter elephantine legs and a more strictly land-dwelling build; sea turtles, which have flattened bodies and flippers; or snapping turtles, which have a rougher body, very large head, and long serrated tail. Diamondback terrapins are a notable look-alike within this category and can be recognized by pale spotted skin and concentric shell markings, but images lacking those exact features may still be terrapins if they fit the broader terrapin body form.

name: box turtle
Terrapene
37.description: A small to medium terrestrial turtle with a high-domed, rounded shell and a hinged plastron that can close tightly like a box. The shell is usually dark brown to black with bold yellow, orange, or tan lines, spots, or radiating markings; the head and legs are often similarly patterned.
37.guidelines: Classify as a box turtle when the turtle has a strongly domed shell and a movable lower shell that allows it to shut itself in. Distinguish it from aquatic pond turtles and sliders, which are flatter, more streamlined, and usually lack a fully closing shell; from tortoises, which are bulkier with elephantine feet and no hinged box-like closure; and from wood turtles or painted turtles, which may have patterned shells but do not have the characteristic high dome plus hinged plastron of Terrapene.

name: western banded gecko
Coleonyx variegatus
38.description: A small, slender gecko with movable eyelids, a smooth velvety or suede-like skin texture, thin toes without adhesive pads, and a distinctly banded pattern. The body is usually pale pink, tan, cream, or gray with darker brown bands, blotches, or side markings, and the tail typically shows strong alternating light and dark rings.
38.guidelines: Classify this as a western banded gecko when the lizard has eyelids, narrow clawed toes lacking toe pads, smooth granular skin, and bold body bands or blotches with a ringed tail. Do not confuse it with house geckos or other pad-toed geckos, which have broad adhesive toe pads and usually lack obvious eyelids. It can also resemble leopard geckos, but western banded geckos are typically smaller and more slender, with cleaner crossbands and a narrower build.

name: green iguana
Iguana iguana
39.description: A large iguana with a heavy body, long banded tail, large round subtympanic scale below the ear, a prominent throat dewlap, and a tall row of spines running from the neck down the back and onto the tail. Usually bright green to olive, gray, or orange-brown, often with darker body and tail bands and coarse scaly skin.
39.guidelines: Classify as green iguana when the lizard shows the distinctive large circular scale below the ear together with the long dorsal crest and dewlap. Do not confuse it with rhinoceros iguanas or rock iguanas, which are bulkier, grayer, and lack the same large round subtympanic shield; marine iguanas, which are dark, blunt-snouted, and more heavily armored; or basilisks and other smaller arboreal lizards, which are slimmer and lack the iguana’s large jowl scale and robust crest.

name: green anole
Anolis carolinensis
40.description: A small, slender lizard with a long tail, smooth skin, and an elongated, somewhat flattened head. Usually bright green but often turns brown; the underside of the head is paler white or cream. Many images show a subtle pale eye ring and, in males, a pink throat fan (dewlap).
40.guidelines: Classify as green anole when the lizard is slim, small, long-tailed, and typically bright green or brown with a narrow head and smooth body. Do not confuse with geckos, which have broader toes and bulkier heads, or with iguanas and basilisks, which are much larger and more crested. Distinguish from other anoles by the overall plain green appearance, pale underside, and frequent pink dewlap rather than strong body striping, heavy patterning, or pronounced crests.

name: whiptail lizard
Teiinae
41.description: A slender, smooth-scaled teiid lizard with a narrow pointed head, very long tail, and long hind legs. The head is covered by large, smooth, symmetrical plates, with a distinct ear opening behind the head. The body usually shows bold longitudinal striping from neck to tail, though some members are spotted, checkered, or tiger-patterned. The back has finer granular-looking scales, the tail has larger ringed scales, the belly has smooth rectangular plate-like scales, and the fourth toe on the hind foot is notably long.
41.guidelines: Classify as whiptail lizard when the animal is a sleek, fast ground-running teiid with a very long whip-like tail, long toes, large head plates, and usually strong lengthwise stripes. Do not confuse with skinks, which are more glossy and cylindrical with smaller legs and less distinct head plating; with lacertid lizards, which lack the characteristic teiid belly plates and tail texture; or with iguanian/spiny lizards, which are bulkier and often have keeled or spiny scales. Exclude tegus and other larger robust teiids that lack the typical slender whiptail build.

name: agama
Agama
42.description: A medium-sized agamid lizard with a long tail, sturdy body, and rough, spiny-looking scales. Many individuals are dull brown, gray, or tan, but breeding males often show very bright colors, especially a red, orange, or yellow head with a vivid blue or blue-green body. They are often seen on rocks, walls, tree trunks, or bare ground.
42.guidelines: Classify as agama when the lizard has the typical agamid build: triangular head, rough scales, long tail, and often strong sexual color contrast with bright red/orange head and blue body in males. Do not confuse with iguanas, which are bulkier and usually have a dorsal crest and dewlap, or with anoles, which are slimmer, smoother, and often show toe pads. Also distinguish from skinks, which have shinier smoother scales and a more cylindrical body, and from bearded dragons, which are heavier-bodied with a broad spiky head and beard.

name: frilled lizard
Chlamydosaurus kingii
43.description: A medium-sized arboreal lizard with a very large circular neck frill, long tail, long limbs, and a triangular head. Usually gray, brown, olive, or reddish with mottled bark-like patterning that helps it blend into tree trunks. The expandable frill is normally folded around the neck and shoulders but can flare open dramatically, showing yellow, orange, pink, black, or cream patterning.
43.guidelines: Classify as frilled lizard only when the lizard has the distinctive oversized neck frill, whether folded or fully expanded. It is often seen clinging upright to tree trunks or standing bipedally with the frill spread. Do not confuse with bearded dragons or agamid lizards that have spiny beards or small throat flaps rather than a broad circular frill, or with basilisks and iguanas that may have crests but lack the neck ruff. The key cue is the unique umbrella-like frill attached around the neck.

name: alligator lizard
44.description: A long-bodied lizard with a relatively large triangular head, short but well-developed legs, a very long tail, and rough-looking keeled scales. Usually brown, gray, olive, or tan, often with darker crossbands, stripes, mottling, or barred sides; the body looks sturdier and more armored than a smooth skink.
44.guidelines: Classify as alligator lizard when the lizard has an elongated body, noticeably rough or ridged scales, short legs, and a long tail, often with banded or striped patterning. Do not confuse with skinks, which are usually shinier, smoother-scaled, and more cylindrical, or with whiptails/racerunners, which are slimmer, longer-legged, and typically have cleaner stripe patterns. Exclude salamanders or newts by checking for dry scaly skin, claws, and a reptilian head shape.

name: Gila monster
Heloderma suspectum
45.description: A large, heavy-bodied venomous lizard with short sturdy legs, a thick tail, and distinctive beaded skin formed by raised scales. Its coloration is black with pink, orange, peach, or yellowish markings arranged in bands, blotches, or chainlike patterns over the body and tail.
45.guidelines: Classify as a Gila monster when the lizard is stout and low-slung, with rough beadlike skin and bold black-and-pale banded or reticulated patterning, often with a thick fat-storing tail. Distinguish it from the Mexican beaded lizard by the Gila monster’s generally more banded, high-contrast pink/orange-and-black appearance and its typical Sonoran-desert look. Do not confuse it with monitors, skinks, or tegus, which have smoother-looking scales, longer limbs and tails, and lack the characteristic beaded skin.

name: green lizard
46.description: A slender lizard with a bright green body, narrow pointed head, long tapering tail, and relatively long legs. Most examples are smooth-scaled or finely textured and often perch on leaves, branches, walls, or other elevated surfaces; some show pale undersides, faint striping, or small crests or throat folds.
46.guidelines: Classify as green lizard when the animal is clearly a lizard and the overall appearance is predominantly vivid green with a slim body and very long tail. Do not confuse it with green snakes, which lack legs and have a more uniformly cylindrical body; geckos, which usually have broader toes and bulkier heads; iguanas, which are heavier-bodied with larger dorsal spines; or chameleons, which have turreted eyes and grasping feet. If multiple green lizard species are shown, use this broader label rather than a species-specific name such as European green lizard or green anole.

name: chameleon
Chamaeleonidae
47.description: A chameleon is a small to medium lizard with a laterally compressed body, a triangular head with often raised casque or horn-like ridges, bulging turreted eyes, grasping feet, and a long usually prehensile tail. Many are green, brown, yellow, or blue and may show bands, spots, or mottled patterning; body shape and ornamentation vary widely across species.
47.guidelines: Classify as a chameleon when the animal shows the distinctive turreted eyes, zygodactyl grasping feet, slow climbing posture on branches, and usually a curled prehensile tail. Do not confuse it with iguanas, anoles, or agamid lizards, which lack the independently movable bulging eyes and specialized grasping feet; horned lizards are flatter and spiny, and geckos lack the classic chameleon head shape and tail posture.

name: Komodo dragon
Varanus komodoensis
48.description: A very large, heavy-bodied monitor lizard with a long thick tail, stout legs, powerful claws, and a broad wedge-shaped head on a long neck. The skin is rough and pebbly with small scales, usually gray-brown, tan, or olive, sometimes with darker mottling. Adults look bulky and low-slung, often with a massive torso and heavy limbs; the long forked tongue is often visible when alert.
48.guidelines: Classify as Komodo dragon when the animal is a gigantic monitor lizard with a robust body, thick neck, broad head, and heavy limbs. Do not confuse it with other monitor lizards such as Asian water monitors, Nile monitors, or lace monitors, which are usually slimmer, more patterned, and less massively built. Juvenile Komodo dragons can be more slender, but the species still shows the broad head, sturdy proportions, and coarse gray-brown appearance rather than the brighter banding or spotting common in many other monitors.

name: Nile crocodile
Crocodylus niloticus
49.description: A large crocodile with a long, fairly narrow V-shaped snout, heavy armored scales, a broad muscular tail, and gray-brown to olive coloration. The teeth are often visible even when the mouth is closed, and the body is low, elongated, and usually seen basking on muddy banks or partly submerged in water.
49.guidelines: Classify as Nile crocodile when the animal is a true crocodile with a long pointed snout and exposed interlocking teeth. Do not confuse with alligators, which have a broader U-shaped snout and usually hide the lower teeth when the mouth is closed. Distinguish from gharials by the much broader snout and heavier body, and from dwarf or broad-snouted crocodilians by the Nile crocodile's larger, longer-headed, more elongated appearance.

name: American alligator
Alligator mississippiensis
50.description: A large, dark gray to black crocodilian with a broad, rounded U-shaped snout, heavy armored body, ridged back, and thick tail. It is usually seen partly submerged, with the eyes and nostrils high on the head; juveniles often show yellowish bands on a darker body.
50.guidelines: Classify as American alligator when the animal has a broad U-shaped snout and a robust body. Distinguish it from crocodiles, which usually have narrower V-shaped snouts and more visible lower teeth when the mouth is closed. Distinguish it from caimans by the alligator’s broader head and heavier build; juvenile alligators may resemble caimans but still keep the blunt, wide snout.

name: eastern wormsnake
Carphophis amoenus
52.description: A very small, slender snake with a smooth, glossy body, a dark brown to blackish back, and a distinctly pink to salmon-colored belly. The head is small and blunt with tiny eyes, and the tail is short and ends in a sharp spine-like tip.
52.guidelines: Classify as an eastern wormsnake when the snake is tiny, wormlike, smooth-scaled, and bicolored with a dark dorsum and pink underside. Distinguish it from earthsnakes and brown snakes, which are usually duller brown overall and lack the bright pink belly, and from blind snakes or threadsnakes, which are more uniformly colored and even more wormlike with less distinct head and tail contrast.

name: ring-necked snake
Diadophis punctatus
53.description: A small, slender snake with a smooth, dark gray to black or bluish back and a distinct yellow, orange, or reddish ring just behind the head. The belly is usually bright yellow, orange, or red, often with small dark spots, and the underside of the tail is especially vivid. The head is narrow and not much wider than the neck.
53.guidelines: Classify as ring-necked snake when the snake is thin, dark-backed, and shows a clear light-colored neck ring plus a bright belly or tail underside. Do not confuse it with red-bellied snakes, which usually lack a complete neck ring; crowned snakes, which have a darker head cap and different neck markings; worm snakes, which are more uniformly brown or pinkish and lack the bright neck ring; or garter/ribbon snakes, which have long longitudinal stripes instead of a plain dark back with a collar.

name: hognose snake
Heterodon
54.description: A stout-bodied snake with a distinctly upturned, shovel-like snout, broad head, and strongly keeled scales. Color and pattern vary widely: individuals may be tan, orange, gray, brown, olive, black, or nearly patternless, often with dark blotches, bands, or speckling. Many flatten the neck and body when threatened, giving a cobra-like or adder-like appearance.
54.guidelines: Classify as hognose snake when the snake shows the characteristic upturned snout, short broad head, and often a chunky body with variable blotched or banded pattern. Do not confuse with puff adders or sand vipers, which are true vipers with a heavier triangular head and lack the hognose's raised snout. Also distinguish from watersnakes, garter snakes, and juvenile racers: those may be blotched or dark, but they usually have a normal pointed snout rather than the obvious hog-like upturned nose.

name: rough green snake
Opheodrys aestivus
55.description: A very slender, vine-like snake with a long narrow body, bright leaf-green upperparts, and a pale yellow to cream underside. The head is slim with relatively large round eyes, and the body often appears slightly textured from keeled scales. It is commonly seen stretched along branches, twigs, or low vegetation.
55.guidelines: Classify this as a rough green snake when the snake is extremely thin, bright green, and elongated, with a narrow head, pale belly, and a lightly rough or ridged scale texture. Distinguish it from the smooth green snake, which is usually shorter-bodied, less arboreal-looking, and has smoother, less visibly keeled scales. Also avoid confusing it with green vine snakes (Ahaetulla), which usually have a much more pointed, elongated snout and a more distinctly triangular head, or green tree pythons and emerald tree boas, which are much thicker-bodied and heavily coiled.

name: kingsnake
Lampropeltis
56.description: A slender, smooth-scaled snake with a glossy body and a small, slightly distinct head. Typical patterning is bold and high-contrast: broad black-and-white, black-and-cream, or red, black, and pale bands or rings encircling the body; some individuals may show chainlike or striped pattern elements, but the class is most often recognized by crisp contrasting banding.
56.guidelines: Classify as kingsnake when the snake has smooth shiny scales and strong contrasting rings, bands, or chainlike markings, often in black with white or cream, or in red-black-pale triads. Do not confuse it with coral snakes: coral snakes are usually more uniformly ringed, with a distinctive red-yellow-black arrangement and a different head shape. Also distinguish from kraits and California mountain kingsnakes by context and pattern details; this class covers North American Lampropeltis-type kingsnakes broadly, including several banded and tricolored forms.

name: common garter snake
Thamnophis sirtalis
57.description: A slender, small- to medium-sized snake with a dark body and usually three light longitudinal stripes: one along the back and one on each side. The stripes are commonly yellow, cream, or greenish, and many individuals also show a checkered or chain-like pattern of darker blotches between the stripes. The head is narrow and not strongly distinct from the neck, with round pupils and smooth-looking scales.
57.guidelines: Classify as common garter snake when the snake is thin-bodied and shows the classic garter pattern of long light stripes on a darker background, often with checkering between them. Do not confuse it with ribbon snakes, which are even more slender with cleaner, sharper stripes and a noticeably longer tail, or with water snakes and rat snakes, which are heavier-bodied and usually lack the neat three-stripe garter pattern. Also distinguish it from the European grass snake, which typically has a pale collar behind the head rather than the longitudinal striped pattern seen here.

name: watersnake
Nerodia
58.description: A medium to large semiaquatic snake with a stout body, strongly keeled scales, and a banded to blotched brown, gray, reddish-brown, or black pattern. Many show dark crossbands near the neck that break into alternating blotches farther down the body; older individuals may look nearly uniform dark. Commonly seen swimming, basking, or resting on rocks, mud, branches, or vegetation at the edge of ponds, streams, marshes, and lakes.
58.guidelines: Classify as watersnake when the snake is a heavy-bodied, non-rattling semiaquatic snake with dark bands or blotches and keeled scales, usually in or beside freshwater. Distinguish it from cottonmouths by the narrower, less blocky head, lack of a bold facial mask, and overall banded/blotched Nerodia pattern; from garter snakes by the absence of clear longitudinal stripes; from queen snakes and ribbon snakes by their slimmer bodies and striped pattern; and from sea snakes or other marine snakes by the freshwater setting and typical brown-gray blotched appearance.

name: Asian vine snake
Ahaetulla nasuta
59.description: A very slender arboreal snake with a long, string-like body, an extremely elongated pointed head, and a narrow neck. Most individuals are bright green, though some can be brown or tan. The body is thin and whip-like, the snout projects forward, and the eyes are relatively large, giving the snake a sharp, streamlined profile suited to blending among vines and branches.
59.guidelines: Classify this as an Asian vine snake when the snake is exceptionally thin, vine-like, and has a distinctly long pointed snout. It is often green and stretched along twigs or leaves, sometimes holding the front of the body out rigidly. Do not confuse it with green tree snakes or rough green snakes, which are slender but usually have shorter, less pointed heads. It also differs from pit vipers, which are thicker-bodied with broader triangular heads, and from bronzeback tree snakes, which are slender but lack the extremely elongated snout typical of vine snakes.

name: night snake
Hypsiglena
60.description: A small, slender snake, typically gray, tan, or light brown with a series of darker brown or gray blotches or saddles along the back. The head is usually slightly wider than the neck, often showing a darker collar or neck blotches and a dark stripe through or behind the eye. The body is smooth-scaled and lightly built, with pattern intensity varying from bold blotches to faint spotting.
60.guidelines: Classify as a night snake when the snake is small and slender, pale gray-tan to brown, and marked with darker dorsal blotches plus a distinct dark marking on the head or neck. Do not confuse it with young gopher snakes or other Pituophis, which are usually larger, heavier-bodied, and more boldly patterned; with garter snakes, which usually have longitudinal stripes rather than blotches; or with leaf-nosed and other small desert snakes that have more specialized head shapes. Compared with rattlesnakes, night snakes lack a heavy triangular body build and rattle, and usually have a slimmer head and finer blotched pattern.

name: boa
Boidae
61.description: A boa is a heavy-bodied constricting snake with a thick, muscular body, a broad distinct head, and smooth patterned scales. Typical coloration ranges from tan, brown, gray, reddish, or cream with blotches or saddle-like markings, though some species are vivid green and arboreal. The body is stout rather than slender, and many individuals are shown coiled around branches or draped over a perch.
61.guidelines: Classify as boa when the snake has a robust constrictor build, a noticeably broad head, and classic boa-like blotched or saddle patterns, or the compact coiled arboreal look seen in tree boas. Do not confuse with pythons: pythons often show similar heavy bodies, but boas generally have a more typical boa head shape and lack the sharply heat-pit-heavy facial look common in many pythons. Do not confuse with anacondas, which are usually bulkier, more aquatic-looking, and have eyes and nostrils set higher on the head. Exclude slender colubrids and vine snakes, which have much thinner bodies and narrower heads.

name: African rock python
Python sebae
62.description: A very large, heavy-bodied python with a thick neck, broad triangular head, and tan to gray-brown ground color covered in large irregular dark-edged blotches and saddle-like markings. The head usually shows a dark stripe through the eye and a pale to brown spear-shaped marking on top.
62.guidelines: Classify as African rock python when the snake is a massive, muscular python with bold irregular brown blotches and a broad python head. Distinguish it from Burmese and Indian pythons by its usually higher-contrast, more broken blotched pattern and strong dark facial stripe; from boa constrictors by the less saddle-banded body and more python-like head pattern; and from vipers or rattlesnakes by the much longer body, smoother overall python form, and lack of a rattle.

name: Indian cobra
Naja naja
63.description: A medium to large cobra with an expandable hood, usually shown rearing up with the forebody raised. Color varies from pale tan and brown to gray or nearly black, with a lighter underside. The hood is often marked with a distinctive paired circular or spectacle-like pattern on the back, though markings can vary, and the body is smooth-scaled and fairly slender.
63.guidelines: Classify as Indian cobra when the snake shows a true cobra hood and especially the classic 'spectacle' mark on the back of the hood, together with the variable tan-to-black body colors typical of this species. Distinguish it from monocled cobra, which usually has a single round hood spot rather than paired spectacles; from king cobra, which is larger, longer-headed, and lacks the typical spectacle mark; and from non-cobra snakes that may flatten the neck slightly but do not form the broad, rounded hood of a cobra.

name: green mamba
64.description: A very long, slender arboreal snake with a narrow, elongated body, smooth scales, and a distinct coffin-shaped head. The overall coloration is usually bright leaf green to yellow-green, sometimes with paler underparts and darker edging between some scales. The eyes are relatively large, and the body is much thinner and more vine-like than that of heavier green snakes.
64.guidelines: Classify as green mamba when the snake is extremely slender, uniformly green, and has the characteristic long coffin-shaped mamba head. Do not confuse with green tree python or emerald tree boa, which are much thicker-bodied and usually rest in tight coils. Distinguish from vine snakes, which have an even more exaggerated pointed snout, and from green pit vipers, which are shorter, stouter, and have a broader triangular head with a clear neck. Avoid using this label for non-mamba green colubrids that lack the long, sleek body and mamba head shape.

name: sea snake
Hydrophiinae
65.description: A highly elongate marine snake with a laterally flattened, paddle-like tail used for swimming. The body is smooth and cylindrical to slightly compressed, and may be plain olive, brown, gray, or yellowish, or strongly banded in black and white. Many have a small head and a long, tapering body adapted to life in the sea.
65.guidelines: Classify as sea snake when the animal is clearly a marine snake with a distinct oar-shaped flattened tail, often seen swimming over reefs or sandy bottoms. This category includes both banded sea kraits and other true sea snakes, so color can vary from boldly ringed black-and-white to nearly plain. Do not confuse with eels, which lack scales and a paddle-tail snake shape, or with terrestrial snakes, which usually have a round pointed tail rather than a flattened swimming tail. Banding alone is not enough: the key cue is the marine snake body with the compressed paddle tail.

name: Saharan horned viper
Cerastes cerastes
66.description: A short, stout desert viper with a broad triangular head, strongly keeled scales, and distinctive horn-like scales projecting above the eyes. Usually pale sandy, tan, gray, or reddish with darker blotches or bands that camouflage it against sand and rocks. Often seen partly buried in sand or tightly coiled; unlike a rattlesnake, it has no tail rattle.
66.guidelines: Classify as Saharan horned viper when the snake shows clear supraocular horns, a compact heavy-bodied viper shape, and sandy desert camouflage. Do not confuse it with sidewinders or other rattlesnakes, which may have eye ridges but usually have a tail rattle and a different head/scalation. Also distinguish it from other Cerastes by using the classic horned appearance and robust desert-viper look; if the horns are absent or reduced, identification is less certain.

name: western diamondback rattlesnake
Crotalus atrox
67.description: A heavy-bodied rattlesnake with a broad triangular head, a distinct rattle at the tail tip, and a row of dark diamond-shaped blotches outlined in pale scales along the back. Color varies from gray and tan to brown, with strongly keeled scales and bold black-and-white tail bands just before the rattle.
67.guidelines: Classify this as a western diamondback rattlesnake when the snake is stout, shows clear dorsal diamonds, and usually has crisp black-and-white rings near the tail before the rattle. Do not confuse it with the eastern diamondback rattlesnake, which is bulkier and usually has larger cream-bordered diamonds on a more yellow-brown body, or with other rattlesnakes such as prairie or timber rattlesnakes, which tend to have blotches or chevrons rather than neat diamond rows and often lack the strongly banded tail pattern.

name: sidewinder
Crotalus cerastes
68.description: A small, pale desert rattlesnake with a short, stout body, strongly keeled scales, and a distinct rattle at the tail tip. It is usually sandy tan, gray, or light brown with darker blotches or crossbands that help it blend into sand and gravel. The head is broad and triangular, and the most distinctive feature is the pair of raised horn-like scales above the eyes.
68.guidelines: Classify as sidewinder when the snake is a pale desert rattlesnake with supraocular 'horns' and a rattling tail, often seen on sand or in a tight coil. Distinguish it from other rattlesnakes by the obvious eye horns and typically lighter sandy coloration. Do not confuse it with horned lizards, which have legs and a flattened body, or with other horned vipers from Africa or the Middle East, which have similar eye horns but are not rattlesnakes and lack the characteristic rattle.

name: trilobite
Trilobita
69.description: An oval to elongated extinct arthropod with a raised central axial lobe and two flatter side lobes running lengthwise, giving the body a distinctive three-lobed form. The body is also divided crosswise into three main parts: a head shield, a segmented thorax, and a tail shield. Many specimens show ribbed or ring-like thoracic segments, a broad semicircular head, and small faceted eyes on the sides of the head. Fossils may appear as dark or light stone impressions, reliefs, partial specimens, or fully preserved enrolled/curling forms; some images may show sculpted models reproducing the same anatomy.
69.guidelines: Classify as trilobite when the object shows the classic fossil arthropod body plan: three longitudinal lobes plus the three transverse regions of head, segmented thorax, and tail. Include both real fossils and accurate physical models. Do not confuse with horseshoe crabs or isopods, which lack the clear trilobite-style axial lobe and distinct pygidium/thoracic fossil segmentation; or with ammonites and other shelled fossils, which are spiral or shell-based rather than segmented arthropods. Also exclude generic rock textures or other arthropod fossils that do not show the characteristic trilobite outline and segmented exoskeleton.

name: harvestman
Opiliones
70.description: A small arachnid with an oval, single-looking body and extremely long, very thin legs. The body is usually tan, brown, orange-brown, or gray, sometimes with a darker saddle or banded pattern. Unlike true spiders, the body appears broadly joined rather than split into two distinct sections.
70.guidelines: Classify as a harvestman when the animal has a compact oval body with no narrow waist and very long threadlike legs. Common look-alikes are cellar spiders (Pholcidae), which are true spiders with two clearly separated body segments and are often seen hanging in messy webs, and crane flies, which have wings and insect body shape. Do not require one exact species such as Phalangium opilio unless species-level markings are consistently visible; this category is best recognized as harvestman broadly.

name: scorpion
Scorpiones
71.description: A scorpion is a small to medium-sized arachnid with eight legs, large pincer-like pedipalps at the front, and a long segmented tail that curves upward and ends in a bulbous stinger. The body is armored and flattened to slightly robust, usually tan, yellow, brown, or black, with clearly segmented abdomen and clawed front appendages.
71.guidelines: Classify as scorpion when the animal has both prominent pincers and a long jointed tail ending in a stinger. Do not confuse it with pseudoscorpions, which have pincers but no long tail, or with spiders, whip scorpions, and insects, which lack the scorpion’s distinctive combination of two large claws and an arched stinging tail.

name: black and yellow garden spider
Argiope aurantia
72.description: A large orb-weaver spider with a long oval abdomen patterned in bold black and yellow, often with pale or silvery areas near the front of the body. The legs are long, slender, and banded dark and light, and the spider is commonly seen hanging head-down in the center of a web that often includes a prominent white zigzag silk decoration.
72.guidelines: Classify as black and yellow garden spider when the spider shows the distinctive black-and-yellow abdomen, silvery cephalothorax, banded legs, and typical Argiope posture in an orb web, often with a zigzag stabilimentum. Do not confuse it with the cross orb-weaver (Araneus diadematus), which is usually browner or orange and has a white cross on the abdomen, or with yellow garden spiders in other Argiope species, which may have different striping or a more strongly lobed abdomen.

name: barn spider
Araneus cavaticus
73.description: A medium to large orb-weaver spider with a rounded, bulbous abdomen and long banded legs. It is typically brown, tan, or yellow-brown, often with lighter pale markings on the abdomen and a somewhat glossy, mottled appearance.
73.guidelines: Classify as a barn spider when the spider has the classic orb-weaver build: a large round abdomen, relatively small cephalothorax, and long spiny legs, usually in brown and yellowish tones. Do not confuse it with widow spiders, which have smoother, shinier bodies and more slender legs, or with cross orb-weavers and other Araneus species that often show a clearer white cross or sharper abdominal patterning. Use the overall orb-weaver shape plus the brown-yellow coloration and mottled rounded abdomen as the main cues.

name: cross orb-weaver
Araneus diadematus
74.description: Orb-weaving spider with a rounded, bulbous abdomen marked by a distinctive pale cross or row of white spots on the back. Color varies from tan and orange-brown to dark brown or gray, and the legs are stout, hairy, and distinctly banded.
74.guidelines: Classify as cross orb-weaver when the spider is sitting in an orb web and shows the characteristic white cross-like dorsal marking on a large rounded abdomen. Do not confuse it with other orb-weavers such as spotted orb-weavers or barn spiders, which may have similar body shape and web-building behavior but usually lack the clear cross pattern. The cross of pale spots, banded legs, and overall robust orb-weaver build are the key cues.

name: tarantula
Theraphosidae
76.description: A large, stout-bodied, very hairy spider with thick legs, a broad cephalothorax, and a rounded abdomen. Color varies widely by species—black, brown, tan, reddish, or boldly banded—but the overall look is heavy, fuzzy, and robust rather than slender or glossy.
76.guidelines: Classify as tarantula when the spider is large and densely hairy, with thick legs and a bulky body. Do not confuse it with wolf spiders, huntsman spiders, or trapdoor spiders: wolf spiders are usually less bulky and less shaggy, huntsman spiders have flatter bodies with longer laterally spread legs, and trapdoor spiders are typically darker, glossier, and less obviously hairy. Tarantulas often look plush or fuzzy and are much more robust than most other spiders.

name: wolf spider
Lycosidae
77.description: A robust ground-hunting spider with a low body, long strong legs, and prominent forward-facing eyes. Usually brown, gray, tan, or yellow-brown, often with longitudinal stripes on the cephalothorax and abdomen; many show two dark bands or a pale median stripe. Females are often seen carrying a round egg sac attached to the spinnerets or spiderlings on the back.
77.guidelines: Classify as wolf spider when the spider has the typical stout runner build, conspicuous large eyes, and brown or gray striped camouflage pattern, often on soil, leaf litter, rock, or walls rather than in an orb web. Distinguish from grass spiders and funnel weavers by the lack of long projecting spinnerets; from nursery web and fishing spiders by the more compact, stockier body and eye arrangement; from huntsman spiders by legs that are less laterigrade (not strongly crab-like sideways); and from jumping spiders by the much longer legs and lower, less compact body.

name: tick
Ixodida
78.description: A tick is a small parasitic arachnid with a compact, flattened to swollen oval body, eight legs, and a tiny head region projecting from the front. It is usually brown, reddish brown, gray, or black, sometimes with pale mottling or a patterned shield; unfed ticks look flat, while fed ticks become round and enlarged.
78.guidelines: Classify as a tick when the animal has 8 legs, a seed-like oval body, and the mouthparts attached at the front, often seen clinging to skin, fur, or vegetation. Do not confuse with spiders, which usually have a more clearly separated body and longer legs, or with mites, which are typically much smaller and less obviously tick-shaped. Also distinguish from insects such as beetles or bed bugs, which have 6 legs and antennae.

name: centipede
Chilopoda
79.description: A centipede is a long, flattened, segmented arthropod with one pair of legs on each visible body segment. It has a distinct head with long antennae, prominent venom claws just behind the head, and an elongated final pair of legs that often looks longer, thicker, or more spread apart than the others.
79.guidelines: Classify as a centipede when the animal has a flattened body, one leg pair per segment, visible forcipules near the head, and a distinctive last leg pair. Do not confuse with millipedes, which are more cylindrical, coil tightly, and have two leg pairs on most body segments; or caterpillars and larvae, which have soft bodies and lack the centipede’s many long jointed legs and venom claws. House centipedes are still centipedes despite their extremely long legs.

name: black grouse
Lyrurus tetrix
80.description: A medium-sized grouse with strong sexual dimorphism. Males are glossy bluish-black with a red comb above the eye, obvious white wing bars or wing spots, and a bright white undertail that often shows strongly in display; the tail is lyre-shaped with outward-curving outer feathers. Females are smaller and cryptically patterned gray-brown to brown, heavily mottled, with subtler white in the wings and tail.
80.guidelines: Classify as black grouse when the bird shows the male’s black plumage plus white wing patches and white undertail, often with a lyre-shaped tail and red eyebrow, or the female’s mottled brown grouse form in the same open moorland/lekking context. Distinguish it from capercaillie, which is much bulkier, darker, and lacks the black grouse male’s distinct white undertail and lyre tail; from ptarmigan, which are paler and seasonally much whiter; and from pheasants or domestic fowl, which have different body shape, longer tails, and lack the characteristic grouse display posture.

name: ptarmigan
Lagopus
81.description: A stout, short-billed grouse with a rounded body, short tail, and heavily feathered legs and feet. Plumage changes seasonally: mostly white in winter for snow camouflage, and mottled gray, brown, black, or chestnut in warmer seasons for camouflage among rocks, tundra, and grass. Males often show bright red combs above the eyes.
81.guidelines: Classify as ptarmigan when the bird is a ground-dwelling grouse with feathered feet and strong seasonal plumage shift, especially white winter plumage and red eye combs in males. Distinguish it from other grouse such as prairie chicken, sage-grouse, or pheasant by the smaller, chunkier build, arctic/alpine habitat, and fully feathered feet. Distinguish it from white birds like pigeons or doves by its short bill, gamebird shape, and mottled brown summer plumage.

name: ruffed grouse
Bonasa umbellus
82.description: A medium-sized forest grouse with a small crest or tufted head, mottled brown to gray plumage, barred flanks, and a broad tail that often shows a distinct dark subterminal band when fanned. Individuals occur in gray and reddish-brown color morphs, helping them blend with bark, leaf litter, and understory vegetation; males often show the crest and dark neck ruffs more strongly.
82.guidelines: Classify as ruffed grouse when the bird is a chunky woodland grouse with a slight crest, cryptic barred plumage, and especially a broad fan-shaped tail with a dark terminal band. Expect both gray and red morphs. Distinguish it from spruce grouse by the ruffed grouse's obvious tail band and stronger head crest; from ptarmigan by the lack of white winter plumage and feathered snow-adapted look; and from ring-necked pheasant or true partridges by its shorter tail, heavier grouse build, and forest camouflage pattern.

name: greater prairie chicken
Tympanuchus cupido
83.description: A stocky, ground-dwelling grouse with heavy brown, buff, and whitish horizontal barring across the body, a short tail, and rounded wings. Males in display show elongated dark neck feathers (pinnae) held upright and bright orange inflatable neck air sacs on the sides of the throat.
83.guidelines: Classify as greater prairie chicken when the bird is a barred prairie grouse with obvious male pinnae and orange throat sacs, or a plump, strongly barred female/immature in open grassland. Distinguish it from sharp-tailed grouse by the latter’s pointed tail, paler spotting, and purple rather than orange display sacs. Distinguish it from lesser prairie chicken by the greater prairie chicken’s heavier barring and typically shorter, less exaggerated pinnae; avoid using the broader 'prairie grouse' when the classic greater prairie chicken display features are visible.

name: Indian peafowl
Pavo cristatus
84.description: Large pheasant with an iridescent cobalt-blue head, neck, and breast, a small upright crest, and a metallic green-bronze back. Males are especially distinctive for their enormous ornamental train of elongated upper tail coverts covered with round blue-green eyespots, often fanned in display; the true tail is shorter and supports the train. Females are browner and less ornate, but the species still shows the characteristic peafowl shape, crest, and long tail area.
84.guidelines: Classify as Indian peafowl when the bird shows the familiar peacock/peahen form: bright blue neck, crest, and often the male's long eyespotted train. Distinguish from green peafowl by the Indian peafowl male's deeper cobalt-blue neck and more obvious fan of separate eyespotted feathers; green peafowl is generally greener overall with a different scaled neck pattern. Distinguish from turkeys, pheasants, and guineafowl by the peafowl's tall crest, blue head and neck, and especially the male's very long ornamental train with many eyespots.

name: California quail
Callipepla californica
85.description: A small, plump ground bird with a short tail, rounded body, and small head. Adults typically show a forward-curving teardrop-shaped topknot plume. Males have a bluish-gray breast and belly, a black face and throat bordered in white, chestnut crown, and bold scaling on the flanks; females are browner and duller but keep the compact shape and topknot. Overall coloration is cryptic brown, gray, and buff with patterned spotting and pale facial stripes.
85.guidelines: Classify as California quail when the bird is a stocky quail with a distinct drooping head plume and, in males, a black-and-white face pattern with scaled flanks. Do not confuse with Gambel's quail, which has a more extensive black belly patch and richer rufous crown/sides, or with bobwhite and other quail that lack the long curved topknot. Females and juveniles are browner, but the compact body, short tail, ground-dwelling posture, and characteristic plume remain key cues.

name: red-legged partridge
Alectoris rufa
86.description: A plump, ground-dwelling gamebird with a rounded body, short neck, small head, and sturdy bare red legs. Adults are mostly gray-brown above with a pale gray to buff breast, bold chestnut-and-black barred flanks, a white throat, and a strong black border or mask pattern around the face and upper neck. The bill is red, and the overall plumage is cryptic but neatly patterned rather than plain.
86.guidelines: Classify as red-legged partridge when the bird shows red bill and legs, a white throat enclosed by a bold black facial/neck pattern, and strongly barred flanks. Do not confuse with gray partridge, which lacks the red bill/legs and bold black-and-white face, or with quail, which are smaller and shorter-bodied with different head patterns. It is also similar to chukar; red-legged partridge is typically warmer brown overall and identified by the classic white throat with black border plus red bill and legs.

name: African grey parrot
Psittacus erithacus
87.description: A medium-sized parrot with mostly gray plumage, a pale whitish face and forehead, pale yellow eyes, a black curved bill, and body feathers edged in lighter gray that create a scalloped pattern. The lower belly and area around the eyes are paler gray to whitish, and the short tail and undertail are bright red.
87.guidelines: Classify as African grey parrot when the bird is predominantly gray with fine scalloped feather edging, a pale face, black bill, and a vivid red tail. Do not confuse it with the Timneh parrot, which is darker overall with a maroon tail and horn-colored upper bill, or with cockatoos and other parrots that may have pale faces but lack the uniform gray body and bright red tail.

name: macaw
88.description: A large, long-tailed parrot with a heavy, strongly curved bill, bare pale facial skin often marked by fine dark feather lines, and very bright plumage. Macaws are commonly red, blue, yellow, green, or combinations of these colors, with long pointed wings and an especially long tapering tail.
88.guidelines: Classify as macaw when the bird is a large parrot with vivid tropical colors, a massive hooked beak, bare patterned facial patch, and a very long tail. Do not confuse it with amazons or other parrots, which are usually shorter-tailed and stockier, or cockatoos, which typically have crests and less vividly multicolored plumage. Parakeets and conures are smaller and more slender, and toucans have oversized straight bills rather than a hooked parrot bill.

name: sulphur-crested cockatoo
Cacatua galerita
