89.description: A large white cockatoo with a prominent forward-curving yellow crest, mostly white plumage, a dark hooked bill that can look grey from powder, and yellow wash on the underside of the wings and tail and sometimes around the head and neck. Males and females look very similar; females typically have red-brown irises while males have very dark brown irises.
89.guidelines: Classify as sulphur-crested cockatoo when the bird is a mostly white cockatoo with a distinct yellow crest and dark bill. Do not confuse it with the umbrella cockatoo, which is white-crested rather than yellow-crested, or with the salmon-crested cockatoo / Major Mitchell's cockatoo, which show pink tones. White parrots without a raised cockatoo crest or with different crest colors should not be included.

name: rainbow lorikeet
Trichoglossus moluccanus
90.description: A brightly colored parrot with a blue to violet head, orange-red bill, green wings and back, a yellow-green collar on the nape, and a vivid breast that is orange to red with darker blue barring. The belly is deep blue to purple, the iris and beak of the adult are orange to red, and the legs are grayish. Its plumage combines many bright colors, giving it a rainbow-like appearance.
90.guidelines: Classify as a rainbow lorikeet when the bird shows the classic combination of a blue head, green upperparts, yellow-green neck band, orange-red chest, and blue belly. Do not confuse it with scaly-breasted lorikeet, which is mostly green with yellow scalloping and lacks the strong blue head and red-orange breast, or with musk lorikeet, which is greener overall with a red forehead and less extensive blue. Exclude other parrots and lories that may be colorful but do not have this distinctive blue-head plus orange breast and green wings pattern.

name: coucal
Centropus
91.description: A large, long-tailed cuckoo with a broad, graduated tail, reddish to red-brown eyes, a heavy downcurved bill, and a strong foot with a long straight hind claw. Many show dark glossy black or blackish head and body with rich chestnut or rufous wings, though some species are browner or have paler throat and underparts.
91.guidelines: Classify as coucal when the bird has the distinctive combination of a bulky cuckoo shape, very long broad tail, red eye, stout curved bill, and strong feet, often with chestnut wings contrasting with a darker body. Distinguish it from pheasants and rails by the slimmer arboreal bird shape and cuckoo-like bill, from drongos by its much heavier body, broader tail, and chestnut wings, and from other cuckoos by its larger size, stronger legs, and typical red eye.

name: bee-eater
Meropidae
92.description: A slender, brightly colored bird with a long, slightly downcurved bill, a dark eye-stripe running from the bill through the eye, and a relatively long tail. Many individuals show elongated central tail feathers projecting beyond the rest of the tail. Plumage is vivid and often combines green, blue, yellow, chestnut, or rufous tones.
92.guidelines: Classify as bee-eater when the bird has the classic slim shape, long pointed bill, bold black eye-mask, and bright multicolored plumage, often with tail streamers. Do not confuse with kingfishers, which are usually stockier with larger heads and shorter tails; rollers, which have heavier bills and broader bodies; or swallows and drongos, which may have long tails but lack the bee-eater’s curved bill and colorful patterning.

name: hornbill
93.description: A hornbill is a large, long-necked bird with a very heavy, elongated, often downward-curving bill, usually topped by a prominent casque or helmet. Many are black, white, or cream with strong contrasts, long tails, and bare facial or throat skin; some species have vivid red, blue, yellow, or orange on the bill and face.
93.guidelines: Classify as hornbill when the bird has a massive bill with a casque and the characteristic sturdy hornbill shape. This category includes both tree hornbills and ground hornbills, so plumage and color can vary widely. Do not confuse with toucans, which have broad, flattened, brightly colored bills but lack a hornbill casque and are New World birds; or with ibises, storks, and similar long-billed birds, which have slimmer bills and no helmet-like bill structure.

name: hummingbird
Trochilidae
94.description: A very small, compact bird with a relatively large head, tiny feet, a long slender bill, and narrow pointed wings. It often appears hovering in place or darting near flowers and feeders. Plumage varies by species from dull gray or green to brilliant iridescent green, blue, purple, or red, but the overall body shape stays short-bodied and streamlined.
94.guidelines: Classify as hummingbird when the bird is tiny, has a long thin bill, and especially when it shows the characteristic hovering posture with rapidly blurred wings. Do not confuse with sunbirds, honeyeaters, or nectar-feeding moths: sunbirds and honeyeaters usually perch more like songbirds and have less specialized hovering form, while moths have antennae, six legs, and insect wings rather than feathers. Also distinguish from swifts and swallows, which have short bills and different wing and body proportions.

name: rufous-tailed jacamar
Galbula ruficauda
95.description: A slender jacamar with a long, straight, needle-like bill, very short legs, and a long narrow tail. The upperparts are metallic green to bronze-green, often with golden glossing; the underparts are rich rufous to chestnut. Most birds shown have a distinct white throat patch or chest spot that contrasts with the darker face and colorful body.
95.guidelines: Classify as rufous-tailed jacamar when the bird shows the classic jacamar shape: long straight bill, short legs, upright perch posture, and especially a long slim tail, together with green iridescent upperparts and rufous underparts. Distinguish it from kingfishers, which are stockier, larger-headed, and usually have broader bills and shorter tails; from hummingbirds, which are much smaller with much shorter tails and different body proportions; and from other jacamars by the combination of white throat patch, coppery-rufous belly, and long rufous tail.

name: toucan
Ramphastidae
96.description: A tropical perching bird with a disproportionately large, deep bill that is often brightly colored in yellow, orange, red, green, or black. Most examples have mainly black plumage with bold white or yellow throat and face patches, a compact body, short neck, and medium-length tail. The bill is the defining feature: long, lightweight-looking, and strongly curved or slightly arched.
96.guidelines: Classify as toucan when the bird shows the classic oversized colorful bill and bold black-and-contrasting body pattern typical of toucans. This category includes multiple toucan species, so bill and throat colors may vary. Do not confuse with hornbills, which usually have a casque on top of the bill and a different head shape, or with smaller aracaris and toucanets, which are typically slimmer or greener. The key cue is a large Neotropical bird with an enormous colorful bill and striking high-contrast plumage.

name: drake
97.description: An adult male duck. Typically shown as a waterfowl with a broad, flat bill, compact body, short legs set far back, and webbed feet; plumage is often more vivid or contrasting than in females, with examples ranging from iridescent green-headed mallards to boldly patterned wood ducks and other male ducks.
97.guidelines: Classify as drake when the image shows a male duck of any duck species, usually identifiable by male plumage and overall duck shape. Do not restrict to mallards: other male ducks such as wood ducks, mandarin ducks, pintails, and domestic ducks also fit. Exclude female ducks (hens), geese, swans, and other waterbirds. Male ducks are distinguished from female ducks mainly by brighter or more ornate plumage, but the key category is the sex-and-type combination: a duck that is clearly male.

name: red-breasted merganser
Mergus serrator
98.description: A slim, long-bodied diving duck with a narrow red-orange bill, shaggy double crest, and a long, low profile on the water. Breeding males show a dark green-black head, white neck collar, rusty-brown breast, pale sides, and black-and-white patterned flanks and back. Females and nonbreeding birds are grayer overall, with a warm brown head, messy crest, pale throat, and a sharper contrast between the brown head and lighter gray body.
98.guidelines: Classify as red-breasted merganser when the bird is a slender merganser with a thin serrated bill and obvious shaggy crest. Males differ from common merganser/goosander by the rusty breast and spiky crest rather than a clean white body and smoother head. Females differ from common merganser females by the thinner bill, shaggier crest, and less crisply defined white chin; they differ from hooded merganser by lacking the bold fan-shaped head patch and by having a longer, slimmer bill and body.

name: goose
99.description: A goose is a medium-to-large waterfowl with a long neck, stout body, relatively long wings, and a broad, flat bill. Plumage varies widely by species and domestic form, commonly showing combinations of gray, brown, black, or white, often with contrasting head or neck markings. Geese are usually heavier-bodied and longer-necked than ducks, but less elongated and less elegant than swans.
99.guidelines: Classify as goose when the bird has the typical goose build: a robust body, noticeably long neck, and duck-like bill, whether wild, domestic, adult, or gosling. Do not confuse with swans, which are usually larger, all-white or mostly white, with proportionally longer, more graceful necks; or with ducks, which are generally smaller, shorter-necked, and more compact. Include different goose species and domestic geese, even when coloration differs greatly, but exclude swans and other waterfowl that lack the characteristic goose proportions.

name: black swan
Cygnus atratus
100.description: A large swan with mostly black plumage, a long curved neck, and a bright red bill with a pale or white tip. The body often shows curled wing feathers, and juveniles are grayer or browner than adults.
100.guidelines: Classify as black swan when the bird is a swan-shaped waterfowl with predominantly black plumage and a red bill, usually with a white tip. Do not confuse it with mute swan or whooper swan, which are white, or with geese and ducks, which have shorter necks and different body shape. Juveniles can look gray-brown, but they still have the same overall swan form and dark coloration rather than white adult plumage.

name: tusker
101.description: An elephant distinguished by exceptionally long, thick, visually prominent tusks. The tusks typically reach at least to the tip of the trunk, are heavy at the base, and often curve forward and downward. The animal is usually an adult male with a massive body, long trunk, large head, and gray to brown wrinkled skin.
101.guidelines: Classify as tusker only when the elephant’s tusks are unusually large and dominant relative to the head and trunk, not merely present. The key cue is tusks with substantial basal thickness and length reaching trunk-tip level or beyond. Do not use this label for tuskless elephants, females, juveniles, or ordinary tusked elephants with short or modest tusks. It can include either African or Asian elephants if the defining oversized tusks are present; distinguish from general elephant categories by the exceptional size and visual prominence of the tusks.

name: koala
Phascolarctos cinereus
105.description: A stocky, tailless arboreal marsupial with dense gray to gray-brown fur, a pale or white chest, large round fluffy ears, and a broad black leathery nose. It has a compact body, short head, and strong limbs with grasping paws for climbing, and is usually seen perched in or hugging tree branches.
105.guidelines: Classify as koala when the animal shows the classic gray fluffy body, white chest, very large fuzzy ears, and prominent oval black nose, usually in a tree. Do not confuse with wombats, which are ground-dwelling, broader-bodied, and have smaller ears; possums, which are smaller, slimmer, and have long tails; or bears/teddy-bear depictions, which lack the koala’s distinctive nose, ear shape, and arboreal posture.

name: common wombat
Vombatus ursinus
106.description: A stout, low-slung marsupial with a broad flattened head, a large bare bear-like nose, tiny eyes, short rounded ears, and powerful short legs. It has a compact barrel-shaped body, almost no visible tail, and dense coarse fur that is usually gray, brown, or tan.
106.guidelines: Classify as common wombat when the animal is a heavy, ground-dwelling marsupial with a broad naked nose, squat body, and very short legs. Do not confuse it with wallabies or kangaroos, which have long tails and longer hind legs; koalas, which have fluffier ears and climb trees; or Tasmanian devils, which are darker, more dog-like, and often show a longer snout and contrasting chest markings. The bare nose and chunky tailless build are key cues.

name: jellyfish
107.description: A jellyfish typically has a soft, gelatinous, translucent bell or umbrella-shaped body that may be clear, white, blue, orange, pink, or patterned with spots or radial markings. Tentacles and frilled oral arms hang from the bell margin or underside, ranging from short and sparse to very long, trailing filaments.
107.guidelines: Classify as jellyfish when the animal shows a floating gelatinous bell with dangling tentacles or oral arms. Include forms with rounded saucer-like bells, deeper dome-shaped bells, or long-tentacled drifting bodies. Do not confuse with octopuses or squid, which have solid heads, visible eyes, and muscular arms; sea anemones, which are attached and lack a free-swimming bell; or comb jellies, which are more oval and usually lack the distinct umbrella bell and marginal tentacles typical of jellyfish.

name: sea anemone
108.description: A sea anemone is a soft-bodied marine invertebrate with a round central oral disc surrounded by many fleshy, smooth, water-filled tentacles. The tentacles may be short and bulb-tipped or long and tapering, and the body is usually attached to rock, coral, sand, or another surface rather than floating freely.
108.guidelines: Classify as sea anemone when the animal has a single attached polyp body with a central mouth and a ring of flexible tentacles. Do not confuse it with corals, which usually form hard stony colonies; jellyfish, which are free-swimming; sea urchins, which have rigid spines; or tube anemones and feather duster worms, whose tentacles are typically much finer and more plume-like.

name: maze coral
Platygyra
109.description: A massive stony coral that usually forms a rounded boulder, dome, or hemisphere. Its surface is covered with long, winding, maze-like valleys and parallel ridges, creating an intricate labyrinth pattern. The grooves are open and continuous rather than broken into separate cups, and the ridge edges are finely serrated by visible septa, giving them a comb-like texture. Color is often green, yellow-green, tan, brown, gray, or bluish.
109.guidelines: Classify as maze coral when the colony has a brain-like but distinctly labyrinthine surface: long meandering channels, mostly parallel ridge walls, and fine tooth-like septa along the ridges. Do not confuse it with other brain corals that have shorter, more enclosed grooves or more clearly separated circular corallites, nor with honeycomb or star corals whose surfaces are divided into many small polygonal cups. The key cue is an open maze pattern spread across a rounded massive colony.

name: flatworm
Platyhelminthes
110.description: A soft-bodied worm with a very thin, dorsoventrally flattened body, usually shaped like a leaf, ribbon, or oval sheet. It often has broad, ruffled or wavy margins and glides smoothly over surfaces. Individuals may be plain brown or vividly patterned with stripes, spots, or bright contrasting edge bands.
110.guidelines: Classify as a flatworm when the animal appears extremely flat and unsegmented, with a smooth leaf-like or ribbon-like body and often undulating edges. Do not confuse it with nudibranchs or sea slugs, which usually have a thicker body, visible rhinophores or gill structures, and a distinct back; or with leeches, earthworms, and other annelids, which are cylindrical or visibly segmented. Also exclude sea cucumbers and other soft marine invertebrates that are bulkier and not paper-thin.

name: Caenorhabditis elegans
Caenorhabditis elegans
111.description: A tiny transparent roundworm with a smooth, thread-like cylindrical body, gently curved posture, and tapered ends. It is slender and unsegmented, usually whitish in brightfield and often shown with fluorescently labeled internal tissues or cells.
111.guidelines: Classify as Caenorhabditis elegans when the image shows a small translucent laboratory nematode with a simple, even-width body and pointed head and tail. Do not confuse it with thicker parasitic roundworms, segmented worms, flatworms, or insect larvae. C. elegans is much smaller, smoother, and more transparent than most parasitic nematodes, and it lacks visible segmentation, legs, or a flattened body.

name: conch shell
112.description: A conch shell is a large marine gastropod shell with a heavy, thick, spiral form, a pointed spire, and a broad body whorl ending in a wide opening. Many are cream, tan, pink, orange, or white, often with smooth glossy surfaces or ridges, knobs, flared lips, or short spines depending on the kind.
112.guidelines: Classify as conch shell when the image shows a substantial spiral sea-snail shell with a large aperture and robust, often decorative form. This category includes varied common conch-like shells rather than one single species. Do not confuse it with bivalves such as clams, scallops, or oysters, which have two hinged shells, or with nautilus shells, which are flat and planispiral. It can also resemble whelks or other sea-snail shells; conch shells are typically larger, heavier, and have a broader opening and more prominent outer lip.

name: snail
113.description: A soft-bodied mollusk with a single coiled shell, a broad muscular foot, and a distinct head bearing tentacles. The shell is typically rounded or spiral and may be smooth, banded, striped, pale, or dark brown. The body is moist and flexible, extending from the shell as the animal crawls on surfaces such as leaves, soil, rocks, wood, or walls.
113.guidelines: Classify as snail when the animal has an obvious external spiral shell carried on its back and a soft body that extends from it. Do not confuse it with slugs, which lack an external shell, or with limpets and abalones, which have non-spiral shell shapes. Also distinguish snails from hermit crabs, whose borrowed shells contain visible crab legs and claws rather than a smooth mollusk body with tentacles.

name: slug
114.description: A slug is a soft-bodied, shell-less gastropod with an elongated, moist body, a broad creeping foot, and two pairs of retractable tentacles on the head. It is usually brown, gray, black, yellow, orange, or mottled, and may appear smooth, wrinkled, or slightly ridged. Terrestrial slugs are commonly seen on soil, rocks, leaves, bark, logs, mushrooms, and garden surfaces.
114.guidelines: Classify as slug when the animal is a shell-less, moist-bodied gastropod with tentacles and a smooth gliding posture. Do not confuse with snails, which carry an external shell; with caterpillars or worms, which lack the slug’s head tentacles and broad muscular foot; or with land planarians and leeches, which are flatter or more segmented-looking and do not show the typical slug head and mantle.

name: nudibranch
Nudibranchia
115.description: A soft-bodied marine gastropod with an elongated or flattened slug-like body, no external shell, and a distinct pair of head tentacles called rhinophores that look like small horns. Many are brightly colored or boldly patterned, and some have frilly gills, finger-like cerata, or ruffled body edges.
115.guidelines: Classify as nudibranch when the animal is a shell-less sea slug with a visible pair of rhinophores on the head. Shapes vary widely, from smooth and oval to highly frilled or covered in cerata, but the horn-like rhinophores are a key cue. Do not confuse with sea hares or other sea slugs that are bulkier, more plain-bodied, or have different head structures; avoid flatworms, which can be similarly colorful and flat but lack rhinophores and typical nudibranch body anatomy.

name: chiton
Polyplacophora
116.description: An oval, low-domed marine mollusk with a back divided into 8 overlapping shell plates arranged in a row like tiles or armor. A thick girdle or belt surrounds the plates and may be smooth, granular, scaly, bristly, or hairy. Colors vary from gray, brown, olive, black, red, or mottled; in some species the plates are partly hidden by the girdle. The underside is broad and muscular, often orange, yellow, or pale, giving an opened animal a sole-like appearance.
116.guidelines: Classify as chiton when the animal has a flattened oval body with exactly 8 dorsal plates and a surrounding girdle. The clearest cue is the row of 8 articulated valves, even if they are partly obscured. Do not confuse with limpets or abalones, which have a single shell, or with barnacles and other encrusting animals, which lack the 8-plated armored back. Also distinguish from trilobite-like fossils or segmented arthropods: chitons are soft-bodied mollusks attached to rocks, usually seen on shorelines or tide pools, with a continuous girdle around the plates.

name: chambered nautilus
Nautilus pompilius
117.description: A marine cephalopod with a smooth, tightly coiled spiral shell that is nearly symmetrical around the center. The outer shell is creamy white to pale beige with bold brown or orange-brown zebra- or tiger-like stripes. Cut or broken shells reveal many internal chambers arranged in a precise spiral.
117.guidelines: Classify as chambered nautilus when the image shows the distinctive striped, smooth, planispiral shell or the living animal emerging from it with many slender tentacles. Do not confuse it with ammonites, which are usually fossils seen in rock and often have ribbed or mineralized shells, or with snails and other gastropods, whose shells are asymmetrical rather than evenly coiled around the center. The clean white-and-brown striped shell and visible internal chambers are the key cues.

name: Dungeness crab
Metacarcinus magister
118.description: A large crab with a broad oval carapace that is noticeably wider than long, usually smooth to finely granular and dark brown to purplish above. The legs and outer claw surfaces are darker, while the undersides and inner limbs are much paler. The claws are stout and show a conspicuous light to white patch on the fingers and tips.
118.guidelines: Classify as Dungeness crab when the crab has a wide rounded-oval shell, dark brown or purple upper body, and heavy claws with distinct pale or white-tipped fingers. Distinguish it from blue crabs by the lack of bright blue legs and swimming-paddle rear legs, from red rock crabs by its smoother broader carapace and paler claw fingers, and from king or spider crabs by its much flatter, more compact body and shorter legs.

name: rock crab
Cancer irroratus
119.description: A medium-sized crab with a broad oval carapace, usually brown to reddish or purplish, marked with many small dense spots. The shell and claws are generally similar in color, and the claw tips are not black. The claws are fairly smooth rather than strongly serrated, and the side margin from the eye region to the widest part of the carapace shows 9 teeth.
119.guidelines: Classify as rock crab when the crab has a spotted brown-red carapace, smooth-looking claws with no black tips, and the typical broad Cancer crab shape with 9 lateral teeth. Distinguish it from Dungeness crab and other Cancer crabs by the dense speckling and lack of black claw tips; distinguish it from red rock crab by the absence of black-tipped claws and less strongly rough or serrated claws; distinguish it from shore crabs such as European green crab by the broader heavier body and different side-tooth pattern.

name: fiddler crab
120.description: A small shore crab with one greatly enlarged claw in the male and one much smaller feeding claw, long stalked eyes held above the head, and a broad trapezoidal to boxy carapace. Body color varies from pale sand, white, and yellow to orange, red, blue, or dark brown, often matching mudflat or mangrove habitats. The oversized claw is smooth-looking rather than hairy, and the crab is often seen at the entrance of a burrow on wet mud or sand.
120.guidelines: Classify as fiddler crab when the crab shows the classic asymmetry: one oversized claw and one normal small claw, plus raised eyestalks and a compact mudflat crab body. Do not confuse with ghost crabs, which are larger, more square-bodied, fast-running beach crabs with two similar claws; or with shore/mangrove crabs and sesarmid crabs, which usually have two claws of similar size. Females lack the giant claw, so use the eyestalks, small burrow-dwelling mudflat setting, and overall fiddler-crab shape; however, avoid labeling ordinary small crabs as fiddler crabs unless the body form and context fit clearly.

name: red king crab
Paralithodes camtschaticus
121.description: A very large spiny crab with a broad, somewhat heart-shaped carapace, long thick legs, and massive front claws. The shell is rough and heavily armored with sharp conical spikes across the carapace, legs, and claws. It is usually reddish to orange-red, including in cooked specimens, and the top of the shell often shows a central hexagonal pattern of six prominent spines.
121.guidelines: Classify as red king crab when the crab is huge, red to orange, and strongly covered in stout spikes over most of the body and legs. Distinguish it from spider crabs and Japanese spider crabs, which have much thinner, longer legs and a less bulky, more delicate body; from snow crabs, which are smoother, less heavily armored, and more slender-legged; and from horseshoe crabs, which have a smooth domed shell and tail spine rather than crab claws and walking legs.

name: American lobster
Homarus americanus
122.description: A large true lobster with a heavy armored body, long antennae, and two oversized front claws, typically one broader crusher claw and one narrower cutter claw. Live animals are usually dark bluish green to brown with orange-red spines and joints, a spiny rostrum forming a crown-like ridge on the nose, and orange to reddish lining on the inner edges of the claws. Cooked specimens appear bright red.
122.guidelines: Classify as American lobster when the animal has the classic Homarus lobster form with very large unequal claws, a dark blue-green to brown shell when alive, orange-red spines on the carapace and claw joints, and a distinctly spiny rostrum. Do not confuse it with spiny lobsters or rock lobsters, which lack the huge front claws, or with crayfish, which are much smaller and slimmer. It can resemble the European lobster, but American lobster is typically darker and often shows stronger orange-red spines and inner claw coloration.

name: spiny lobster
Palinuridae
123.description: A large marine crustacean with a hard segmented body, very long thick antennae, and a spiny, thorny carapace. It lacks the oversized front claws of true lobsters. Usually reddish, brown, orange, or mottled, often with stripes, spots, or pale banding on the legs and tail.
123.guidelines: Classify as spiny lobster when the animal has extremely long whip-like antennae, a heavily armored spiny shell, and no enlarged pincers on the first pair of legs. Do not confuse with true lobsters, which have one large crushing claw and one large cutting claw, or with crayfish, which are smaller freshwater animals with obvious front claws. Slipper lobsters are flatter and broader, with shovel-like antennae rather than long spiny ones.

name: crayfish
124.description: A small freshwater crustacean with a segmented, smooth to lightly textured shell, a long narrow tail, very long antennae, and a pair of prominent front claws. Crayfish typically have a compact lobster-like body, walking legs beneath the thorax, and colors ranging from brown, olive, and gray to red, blue, or white depending on species and molt state.
124.guidelines: Classify as crayfish when the animal is a small lobster-like freshwater crustacean with long antennae and large pincers. Do not confuse it with true lobsters, which are usually larger marine animals with a heavier body, or with shrimp/prawns, which have a slimmer body and no oversized front claws. Crabs have a wide flattened body and tucked tail, unlike the elongated body and obvious tail of a crayfish.

name: hermit crab
Paguroidea
125.description: A small to medium decapod crustacean with a soft, curved abdomen tucked into a borrowed spiral shell. It typically shows long antennae, prominent stalked eyes, and several jointed legs, with one pair of claws often larger or more robust. Shells may be plain or overgrown with algae, anemones, or other marine life.
125.guidelines: Classify as hermit crab when the animal is a crab-like crustacean visibly occupying and carrying a borrowed gastropod shell. Distinguish it from true crabs, whose broad abdomen is tucked under a rigid body rather than hidden in a portable shell, and from snails, which have a fleshy mollusk body without jointed legs or claws. Do not confuse it with shell-dwelling snails or empty shells; visible stalked eyes, antennae, claws, and walking legs are key cues.

name: isopod
Isopoda
126.description: Crustaceans with a flattened, segmented body made of seven main trunk segments, one pair of long segmented antennae, seven pairs of similar legs, and a rear pleotelson bearing short tail appendages (uropods). They range from marine forms to terrestrial woodlice and pill bugs, and are typically oval, armored, and clearly divided into overlapping plates.
126.guidelines: Classify as isopod when the animal has the classic many-plated body, one obvious pair of antennae, and seven pairs of legs. Include both marine isopods and terrestrial woodlice/pill bugs. Do not confuse with insects, which have only six legs, or millipedes and centipedes, which have many more segments and legs. Distinguish from amphipods by the isopod's broader, flatter, more symmetrical body rather than a laterally compressed, shrimp-like form.

name: white stork
Ciconia ciconia
127.description: A large long-legged stork with a mostly pure white body, black flight feathers and wing edges, a long straight pointed bill, and long slender legs. Adults typically have a bright red bill and red legs; juveniles are duller with darker brownish or blackish bill and legs. The face shows a dark bare-skin stripe linking the eye to the base of the bill, and a dark patch of bare skin is visible at the base of the lower mandible. In flight, the neck is held fully extended straight forward.
127.guidelines: Classify as white stork when the bird is a large white stork with sharply contrasting black wings, a long straight red or dark juvenile bill, and red or dark juvenile legs, often seen standing in fields or on large stick nests on roofs, poles, or platforms. Distinguish it from herons, egrets, and cranes by its heavier stork build, straight extended neck in flight, and black-on-white wing pattern. Separate it from ibis and spoonbills by the lack of a curved or spatulate bill. Distinguish it from painted stork and other storks by the plain white body, black flight feathers, and absence of pink tertials, patterned wings, or yellow bill.

name: black stork
Ciconia nigra
128.description: A large long-legged stork with mostly black plumage showing a green and purple metallic sheen, especially on the neck and wings, and sharply contrasting white underparts forming a white belly patch. Adults have bare red skin around the eye, a long red bill, and red legs; juveniles are duller brownish-black or grayish with an olive or gray bill and legs and little to no gloss. In flight it shows broad wings with splayed fingered tips and holds the neck fully extended straight.
128.guidelines: Classify as black stork when the bird is a dark stork with glossy black upperparts, a crisp white belly/underbody, and red bill and legs in adults. Do not confuse with white stork, which is mostly white with black only on the wings, or with ibises, which are smaller, more uniformly dark, and have distinctly downcurved bills. Also distinguish from herons and cranes by the heavy stork build, straight extended neck in flight, and the strong black-and-white underbody contrast.

name: roseate spoonbill
Platalea ajaja
129.description: A large wading bird with very long legs, a long flat bill that widens into a spoon-shaped tip, and predominantly pink plumage. Adults are pale pink to deep rosy with brighter magenta patches on the wings and shoulders, often with a whitish neck and head and a bare yellow-green to orange facial skin area. It is usually seen wading in shallow water, perched, or flying with broad pink wings.
129.guidelines: Classify as roseate spoonbill when the bird has the distinctive spoon-shaped bill and pink body plumage. Do not confuse it with ibises, which may also be pinkish but have a slender downcurved bill rather than a flattened spatulate bill. It also differs from flamingos, which have much longer necks and legs and a thick sharply bent bill, and from white spoonbills, which share the bill shape but are mostly white rather than pink.

name: flamingo
Phoenicopteridae
130.description: A tall, long-legged wading bird with a very long S-curved neck, small head, and a thick downcurved bill. Plumage ranges from very pale pink to vivid salmon or red, often with brighter orange-pink on the wings; the legs are long and pink, and the bill is pale with a contrasting black tip or black lower portion.
130.guidelines: Classify as flamingo when the bird has the distinctive combination of extremely long legs, a long curved neck, and a heavy sharply bent bill, usually with pink plumage. Do not confuse with cranes, storks, or herons, which have straight pointed bills; ibises, which are smaller and darker with thin decurved bills; or spoonbills, which have flattened spoon-shaped bills. Pink color can vary widely from nearly white to deep red, so body shape and bill shape are the key cues.

name: little blue heron
Egretta caerulea
131.description: A small to medium heron with a slim build, long legs, a long pointed bill, and overall dark slate-blue to blue-gray plumage. Adults are usually uniformly dusky blue with a purplish or maroon tint on the head and neck, especially in breeding condition, and may show wispy head or back plumes. The bill is two-toned, often pale bluish-gray at the base with a darker tip. It is usually seen wading in shallow wetlands, marshes, pond edges, or perching low near water.
131.guidelines: Classify as little blue heron when the bird is a relatively slender dark blue heron with mostly uniform slate-blue body color and no strong white underparts. Do not confuse it with tricolored heron, which typically has a whiter belly and more contrasting white throat stripe; reddish egret, which is shaggier with a pinker-based bill and a more ragged look; great blue heron, which is much larger, heavier-billed, and has a bolder facial pattern; or white-faced heron and other gray herons, which look paler gray and less uniformly dark. Ignore pose or breeding plumes, and focus on the compact heron shape, dark blue overall coloration, and slender two-toned bill.

name: great egret
Ardea alba
132.description: A large white egret with a long S-curved neck, long yellow to yellow-orange daggerlike bill, and long black legs and feet. In breeding season it may show delicate lacy back plumes, a somewhat darker bill, and paler or greenish lores. The body is entirely white and the bird is slimmer and longer-necked than stockier white herons.
132.guidelines: Classify as great egret when the bird is a large all-white egret with a yellow bill and black legs/feet. Distinguish it from snowy egret by the snowy egret’s black bill and bright yellow feet; from cattle egret by its shorter neck, shorter thicker bill, and buff breeding patches; and from intermediate egret by its smaller size, shorter neck, and gape line that ends near the eye rather than extending well behind it. Do not confuse with the white morph of great blue heron ('great white heron'), which is bulkier with heavier proportions and different head pattern.

name: bittern
Botaurinae
133.description: A stocky marsh heron with a brownish to buff body heavily marked by vertical streaks or stripes, especially on the neck and breast. It has a thick neck that blends smoothly into the head, a long pointed bill, yellowish to greenish legs, and plumage patterned to camouflage among reeds and grasses.
133.guidelines: Classify as bittern when the bird is a cryptically patterned, reed-dwelling heron with strong vertical streaking and a hunched, thick-necked profile. Bitterns are often seen standing upright in marsh vegetation with the bill angled upward. Distinguish them from egrets and typical herons, which are usually plainer gray, white, or blue and have a clearer head-neck transition; from rails, which are smaller, shorter-necked, and shorter-billed; and from juvenile night herons, which may be streaked but are bulkier, shorter-necked, and less reed-camouflaged.

name: limpkin
Aramus guarauna
135.description: A medium-large wading bird with a long neck, long legs, and a long slightly downcurved bill. Plumage is overall dark brown to olive-brown, heavily marked with bold white spots and streaks on the neck, breast, back, and wing coverts, giving a striped-speckled look. The head and neck are finely streaked, and the bird often appears lanky and rail-like when walking in marshes or shallow water.
135.guidelines: Classify as limpkin when the bird is a brown marsh wader with dense white spotting/streaking and a long gently decurved bill. Distinguish it from ibises, which are usually more uniformly colored and have longer, more strongly curved bills; from juvenile night herons and bitterns, which are stockier with shorter thicker bills; and from curlews, which are slimmer shorebirds with longer, more strongly curved bills and less bold white spotting. Do not rely on habitat alone; the combination of brown plumage, prominent white markings, and the distinctive slightly curved bill is key.

name: purple swamphen
Porphyrio
136.description: A large rail-like marsh bird with a deep blue to purple body, often with greenish or turquoise iridescence on the back and wings. It has a thick bright red bill with a frontal shield, long pinkish-red legs and toes, and often shows white undertail coverts when walking or flicking the tail. Body shape is robust, with a short tail, rounded wings, and a tendency to forage among reeds, marsh grass, and shallow water.
136.guidelines: Classify as purple swamphen when the bird is a large, vividly blue-purple swamphen with a heavy red bill and shield and very long reddish legs. Do not confuse it with the smaller purple gallinule, which is more slender, has a finer bill, and typically shows yellowish legs and a more delicate build. Do not confuse it with coots or moorhens/gallinules, which are darker, less richly blue-purple, and usually lack the massive red bill and shield combination. Exclude takahe if the bird is extremely heavy-bodied, short-legged, and obviously flightless-looking with a much bulkier bill and more terrestrial posture.

name: American coot
Fulica americana
137.description: A dark, stocky waterbird with a rounded body, black to slate-gray plumage, a short tail, and a short thick white bill often marked with a dark tip ring. Adults typically show a white frontal shield with a small reddish-brown patch near the top, red eyes, and long greenish-yellow legs with large lobed toes rather than fully webbed feet.
137.guidelines: Classify as American coot when the bird is a dark gray-black rail-like swimmer with a bright white bill and frontal shield, red eye, and conspicuously lobed greenish feet. Do not confuse it with moorhens or gallinules, which usually have a red bill or red frontal shield and often a white flank stripe; or with ducks, which have broader bills and webbed feet. Eurasian coot is very similar, but American coot usually shows the reddish-brown spot on the frontal shield and is the intended category here.

name: kori bustard
Ardeotis kori
138.description: A very large, long-legged African bustard with a long neck, small head, and heavy horizontal body. Plumage is mostly buff, gray-brown, and finely barred or mottled above, with paler underparts and bold black-and-white patches on the folded wing. The head and neck are usually pale gray to buff with a slight shaggy crest or raised crown feathers; breeding or displaying males can show an inflated white neck, darker chest markings, and striking black-and-white contrast.
138.guidelines: Classify as kori bustard when the bird is a very large terrestrial bustard with a long pale neck, mottled sandy-brown body, and distinct black-and-white wing or flank patterning. Displaying males often look especially distinctive with puffed white neck feathers and a dark crest. Do not confuse it with ostriches, which are much taller with much longer bare legs and necks, or with cranes and secretarybirds, which are slimmer, longer-winged, and differently patterned. Compared with smaller bustards, the kori bustard is bulkier, heavier-bodied, longer-necked, and less finely patterned overall.

name: ruddy turnstone
Arenaria interpres
139.description: A small, stocky shorebird with a short, slightly upturned, chisel-like bill, bright orange legs, and bold black-and-white markings on the head and neck. In breeding plumage it typically shows rich chestnut upperparts mixed with black and white; in nonbreeding or juvenile plumage it looks browner and duller but retains the compact build and orange legs.
139.guidelines: Classify as ruddy turnstone when the bird is a compact beach or rocky-shore wader with orange legs, a short wedge-shaped bill, and a striking piebald or chestnut-black-white pattern, often foraging by flipping stones or seaweed. Distinguish it from sandpipers and stints, which are slimmer, longer-billed, and usually lack the bold head pattern and bright orange legs. Separate it from red knot and sanderling by the turnstone’s stockier shape, shorter bill, and stronger black-white facial and breast markings; separate it from black turnstone by the latter’s much darker overall plumage.

name: dunlin
Calidris alpina
140.description: A small, fairly plump shorebird with a medium-length bill that droops slightly toward the tip and black legs. Nonbreeding birds are mostly gray-brown above and pale below, while breeding birds show richer rufous on the back and a dark, often black belly patch. The bird is compact, short-necked, and typically seen feeding in shallow water or on mudflats.
140.guidelines: Classify as dunlin when the bird is a small sandpiper with black legs and a distinctly decurved bill. In breeding plumage, the black belly patch and reddish back are strong clues; in nonbreeding plumage, look for the plain gray-brown upperparts, white underparts, and the same drooping bill. Distinguish it from sanderling by the sanderling's straighter, shorter bill and paler, rounder look; from western, least, semipalmated, and other small Calidris sandpipers by dunlin's longer drooping bill and bulkier body; and from curlew sandpiper by curlew sandpiper's longer legs, longer bill, and more elongated shape.

name: common redshank
Tringa totanus
141.description: A medium-sized wader with bright orange-red to red legs and a fairly straight bill that is dark toward the tip and red or orange-red at the base. Plumage is generally brownish to gray-brown above, with a finely streaked or mottled breast and sides, paler underparts, a faint whitish supercilium in front of the eye, and a pale eye-ring. In many views it looks slim, long-legged, and often stands in shallow water, mud, or on posts.
141.guidelines: Classify this as common redshank when the bird shows the combination of clearly red legs, a mostly straight medium-length bill with a reddish base and dark tip, and brown-gray shorebird plumage with light streaking on the breast. Distinguish it from greenshank by the latter's greenish legs and slightly upturned bill; from yellowlegs by their yellow legs and different North American appearance; from spotted redshank by its longer bill, darker breeding plumage, and overall lankier look; and from sandpipers such as dunlin or Ruff by their shorter legs, different bill shapes, and lack of the classic red-leg/red-bill-base combination.

name: dowitcher
Limnodromus
142.description: A medium-sized, chunky shorebird with a fairly long, straight, stout bill, typically about twice the head length. It has a compact body, relatively short legs, and mottled brown, gray, buff, or rusty plumage depending on season. In all plumages, dowitchers often show a pale eyebrow and darker line through the eye, with finely patterned upperparts and a plain to barred underbody.
142.guidelines: Classify as a dowitcher when the bird is a stocky sandpiper with a long, straight sewing-needle-like bill and a compact posture, usually feeding by probing in shallow water or mud. Do not confuse it with snipes, which usually have bolder head stripes and a more cryptic, crouched look; with stilt sandpipers or yellowlegs, which are slimmer and longer-legged; or with godwits, which are larger and longer-bodied, often with slightly upturned bills. If the image does not clearly separate short-billed from long-billed dowitcher, use the broader category dowitcher.

name: Eurasian oystercatcher
Haematopus ostralegus
143.description: A large, stocky shorebird with a long, straight, stout orange-red bill, pink to reddish-pink legs, and a black head, neck, and upper breast. The upperparts are mostly black to very dark brown, while the underparts and a broad wing or flank patch are white, creating a sharp black-and-white pattern. In flight it shows white underwings and bold contrasting wing markings.
143.guidelines: Classify as Eurasian oystercatcher when the bird has the classic black hood, white belly, heavy orange-red bill, and pink legs. Do not confuse it with the American oystercatcher, which is mostly dark brown-black with much less white on the body, or with avocets and stilts, which have much thinner legs and slimmer, differently shaped bills. The thick straight bill and strong black-and-white body contrast are the key cues.

name: pelican
Pelecanus
144.description: Large waterbird with a very long bill and prominent expandable throat pouch, long neck, heavy body, broad wings, and short webbed legs. Plumage varies by species from brown-gray to mostly white, but all share the oversized pouched bill and pelican silhouette.
144.guidelines: Classify as pelican when the bird has an unmistakably huge pouched bill and bulky body. Do not confuse with herons, storks, or cranes, which have long pointed bills but no throat pouch; cormorants and anhingas, which are slimmer with hooked or narrow bills; or boobies and gannets, which have long bills but lack the large pouch and heavy pelican build.

name: king penguin
Aptenodytes patagonicus
145.description: Large penguin with a black head, dark gray to gray-black back, clean white belly, bright orange-yellow patches on the sides of the upper chest and neck, and a long slender bill that is mostly black with orange along the lower mandible and base.
145.guidelines: Classify as king penguin when the bird shows a tall, sleek shape with vivid orange ear/neck patches and a long narrow bill. Distinguish it from emperor penguin by the king penguin’s slimmer build, longer bill, and stronger orange throat patches; emperors are bulkier with broader yellow areas and a shorter heavier bill. Distinguish it from gentoo, chinstrap, and Adélie penguins by the absence of a white head stripe or chin band and by its much larger size and orange neck coloration.

name: black-browed albatross
Thalassarche melanophris
146.description: A large seabird with a white head and underparts, dark grey to grey-black upperwings and back, and long narrow wings built for soaring. It has a strong pale yellow to orange bill with tubular nostrils, and a distinctive dark eyebrow-like mark over each eye.
146.guidelines: Classify as black-browed albatross when the bird shows the classic white head, dark upperparts, long slim wings, hooked yellow-orange bill, and especially the dark brow line. Distinguish it from other albatrosses such as the waved albatross (buffier head and neck, no sharp dark eyebrow), Laysan albatross (dark eye patch rather than a narrow brow, pinker bill), and royal or wandering albatrosses (much larger and paler overall, lacking the bold black brow). Avoid labeling gulls or shearwaters as this class: gulls have shorter bills without tubular nostrils, and shearwaters are smaller, slimmer, and less strikingly white-headed.

name: gray whale
Eschrichtius robustus
147.description: A large baleen whale with no dorsal fin, a mottled dark gray body that often looks dirty or scarred, and skin commonly covered with barnacles and whale lice. It has a long, somewhat narrow head with a slightly downcurved snout and low knuckles along the back near the tail.
147.guidelines: Classify as a gray whale when the whale lacks a true dorsal fin and shows a mottled, scarred, barnacle-covered gray body with a narrow, gently arched head. Distinguish it from humpback whales by the absence of long white pectoral fins and the different head shape; from right whales by the lack of callosities and the more slender, downcurved rostrum; and from fin, blue, or minke whales by the missing dorsal fin and rougher, patchier skin texture.

name: orca
Orcinus orca
148.description: Large black-and-white toothed whale with a robust body, blunt rounded head, no beak, and a tall upright triangular dorsal fin, especially tall and straight in adult males. It has a conspicuous white oval eye patch, white underside, and a gray saddle patch just behind the dorsal fin.
148.guidelines: Classify as orca when the animal shows the classic black-and-white pattern, blunt head, white eye patch, and tall triangular dorsal fin with a gray saddle patch behind it. Do not confuse it with dolphins or pilot whales, which are darker overall and lack the bold white eye patch and saddle patch; with sharks, which show a fin but no blow, tail flukes, or black-and-white body pattern; or with other whales, which usually have different dorsal fin shapes and lack the sharply contrasting orca markings.

name: dugong
Dugong dugon
149.description: A large, smooth-bodied marine mammal with a pale gray to pinkish-gray body, a rounded head, tiny eyes, and a broad downturned muzzle ending in thick fleshy lips used for grazing. It has short paddle-like foreflippers, no dorsal fin, and a whale-like tail fluke on an otherwise bulky, sealike body.
149.guidelines: Classify as dugong when the animal is a sirenian with a distinctly downturned snout and a fluked tail. Do not confuse it with a manatee: manatees have a broader, paddle-shaped tail and usually a less strongly downturned snout. Also avoid confusing it with dolphins, seals, or whales, which have more elongated faces, different flipper and tail shapes, or visible dorsal fins.

name: sea lion
150.description: A large pinniped with a smooth, streamlined body, visible external ear flaps, long front flippers, and the ability to prop its chest high off the ground on its foreflippers. The head has a broad, rounded, dog-like muzzle with prominent whiskers. Color is usually tan, brown, or dark brown, and individuals are often seen upright on rocks, docks, or pool edges as well as swimming.
150.guidelines: Classify as sea lion when the animal has clear ear flaps and a characteristic upright posture supported by large front flippers. Distinguish it from true seals, which lack external ears and usually lie flatter with smaller front flippers, and from fur seals, which tend to have a pointier snout, denser fluffy-looking fur, and proportionally larger eyes. Do not rely on water setting alone; the ear flaps, dog-like muzzle, and foreflipper-supported posture are the key cues.

name: Chihuahua
Canis lupus familiaris
151.description: A very small toy dog with a compact body, fine-boned legs, a short muzzle, large round eyes, and notably large upright ears. The coat may be short and smooth or long and soft, and comes in many colors and patterns.
151.guidelines: Classify as Chihuahua when the dog is tiny and delicate-looking with oversized erect ears and a distinctly toy-breed build. Do not confuse with Russian Toy or Miniature Pinscher, which are leggier and more slender; Papillon, which has a fuller silky coat and fringed butterfly-like ears; or Pomeranian, which has a much fluffier double coat and rounder body.

name: Japanese Chin
Canis lupus familiaris
152.description: A small toy dog with a rounded head, very short muzzle, large wide-set eyes, and a silky coat with feathering on the ears, legs, and plumed tail. The coat is typically white with black patches, though other markings occur, and the ears are long and pendant.
152.guidelines: Classify as Japanese Chin when the dog is toy-sized with a distinctly flat face, large prominent eyes, a fine silky coat, and a high plumed tail carried over the back. Distinguish it from the Pekingese by its leggier, lighter build and less profuse coat; from the Cavalier King Charles spaniel by its longer muzzle and less flattened face; and from Papillon-type dogs by its drop ears rather than erect butterfly-like ears.

name: Maltese
Canis lupus familiaris
153.description: A toy-sized companion dog with a compact body, drop ears, dark round eyes, and a black nose. The coat is typically pure white and either long, straight, and silky or trimmed short, while still appearing soft and fine-textured.
153.guidelines: Classify as Maltese when the dog is very small and predominantly white, with a fine silky coat, dark eyes, and a black nose. Do not confuse it with the Bichon Frise, which has a puffier curly coat; the Coton de Tuléar, which often has a cottony, slightly wavier coat and may show cream or tan shading; or small poodle mixes and Havanese, which usually have curlier, heavier, or more variably colored coats. A long, straight white coat and delicate toy-dog proportions are the key cues.

name: Pekingese
Canis lupus familiaris
154.description: A toy dog breed with a compact, low-set body, abundant long coat, and a broad flat face. It has a very short muzzle, large round eyes, drop ears hidden in heavy fur, and a plumed tail carried over the back. Common coat colors include fawn, cream, white, black, and mixed markings, often with a dark facial mask.
154.guidelines: Classify as Pekingese when the dog is very small, long-haired, and distinctly brachycephalic, with a flat face and short muzzle on a sturdy low body. Distinguish it from the Japanese Chin by the Pekingese’s heavier build and fuller coat, and from the Shih Tzu or Lhasa Apso by its shorter muzzle and flatter face. Avoid confusing it with Pomeranians or other toy spitz breeds, which have erect ears and a foxlike muzzle rather than a flat-faced expression.

name: Shih Tzu
Canis lupus familiaris
155.description: A small toy dog with a compact body, a rounded head, large dark eyes, a very short muzzle, and a flat-faced expression. The coat is long, dense, and often straight or slightly wavy, commonly groomed to hang around the face and body; many are black and white, gold and white, tan, or cream.
155.guidelines: Classify as Shih Tzu when the dog is toy-sized with a distinctly short muzzle, broad round face, and long flowing coat. Distinguish it from Lhasa apso by the Shih Tzu's flatter face and shorter muzzle; from Pekingese by its less extreme body shape and usually longer-legged, less heavy front; and from Maltese or Havanese by its brachycephalic face rather than a longer, narrower muzzle.

name: Blenheim Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
Canis lupus familiaris
156.description: A small toy spaniel with a silky chestnut-and-white coat, broad white blaze, long feathered ears, round dark eyes, and a compact, graceful body. The ears, legs, chest, and tail are usually well feathered.
156.guidelines: Classify as a Blenheim Cavalier King Charles Spaniel when the dog is a small spaniel with the classic chestnut-on-white Blenheim pattern and long silky ears. Do not confuse it with the tricolor Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, which has black in the coat, or with the larger King Charles Spaniel/English Toy Spaniel, which has a shorter muzzle and more domed head. Also distinguish it from cocker spaniels, which are larger, heavier, and longer-bodied.

name: Papillon
Canis lupus familiaris
157.description: A very small toy spaniel with a fine-boned body, long silky coat, plumed tail carried over the back, and especially large upright ears fringed with long hair that create a butterfly-like look. The coat is usually white with colored patches, often on the head and ears.
157.guidelines: Classify as Papillon when the dog is a tiny, elegant toy dog with prominent fringed ears and a light, silky coat. Distinguish it from the Phalène variety by the Papillon’s erect ears rather than dropped ears. It can resemble a long-haired Chihuahua or small mixed toy dog, but Papillons usually have larger more wing-like ear fringes, a more spaniel-like face, and a fuller plumed tail.

name: toy terrier
Canis lupus familiaris
158.description: A very small, fine-boned terrier-type dog with a slender body, short smooth coat, narrow muzzle, and large upright pointed ears. Common colors include black-and-tan, white with black or tan patches, or tricolor patterns.
158.guidelines: Classify as toy terrier when the dog is tiny but distinctly terrier-like: slim, long-legged for its size, smooth-coated, and alert with large erect ears. Do not confuse with Chihuahua, which usually has a rounder head, shorter muzzle, and more compact body; Miniature Pinscher, which is typically more uniformly black-and-tan or red and less white-marked; or Rat Terrier/Toy Fox Terrier, which are closely related but often slightly sturdier or more consistently patterned. Use the overall tiny terrier build, smooth coat, and upright ears as the key cues.

name: Rhodesian Ridgeback
Canis lupus familiaris
159.description: A large, athletic, deep-chested dog with a short, sleek wheaten to reddish-brown coat, a strong muscular build, drop ears, and a long tail. The breed’s defining feature is a narrow ridge of hair along the spine that grows in the opposite direction from the rest of the coat.
159.guidelines: Classify as Rhodesian Ridgeback when the dog is a lean but powerful hound-type breed with a solid wheaten/red coat and, ideally, the characteristic dorsal hair ridge. Do not confuse it with Vizsla, which is usually lighter, more slender, and lacks the ridge; Redbone Coonhound, which has a longer ear set and more hound-like proportions; or Black Mouth Cur/boxer mixes and other brown short-haired dogs, which may share coat color but lack the distinctive ridgeback silhouette and breed-typical head and body shape.

name: Afghan Hound
Canis lupus familiaris
160.description: A tall, elegant sighthound with a slender build, long legs, a narrow refined face, and a very long silky flowing coat. The ears are heavily feathered, the topknot is long, and the coat commonly appears in cream, gold, black, brindle, or mixed colors.
160.guidelines: Classify as Afghan Hound when the dog has the distinctive combination of a slim sighthound body and an exceptionally long, fine, silky coat with a narrow muzzle and long feathered ears. Do not confuse with Saluki, which is also slender but usually has a much shorter body coat with feathering mainly on the ears, tail, and legs; or with Borzoi, which has a longer Roman-nosed head and a wavy rather than curtain-like silky coat. Unlike shaggy herding breeds, the Afghan Hound has a clearly hound-like outline and refined, aristocratic proportions.

name: Basset Hound
Canis lupus familiaris
161.description: A scent hound with a long, low body, very short legs, a deep chest, heavy bone, long drooping ears, and loose, droopy facial skin and eyes. The coat is usually short and smooth, often tricolor or red-and-white.
161.guidelines: Classify as Basset Hound when the dog has the breed’s distinctive low-slung build, extra-long ears, and mournful drooping face. Avoid confusion with beagles and other hounds: beagles are taller-legged, lighter-built, and less wrinkled; bloodhounds are much larger, taller, and more heavily wrinkled; dachshunds have long bodies but much shorter ears and a different head shape.

name: beagle
Canis lupus familiaris
162.description: A small to medium hound with a compact, sturdy body, short smooth coat, and long drooping ears. Most are tricolor with a black saddle, tan or brown head and sides, and white chest, legs, tail tip, and facial blaze, though some are lemon-and-white or other hound color patterns. The muzzle is medium length, the eyes are large and expressive, and the tail is carried upright.
162.guidelines: Classify as beagle when the dog is a small scent hound with a short coat, long rounded drop ears, and typical hound markings, especially the common tricolor pattern. Do not confuse with basset hound, which is much lower to the ground with a heavier body, much longer ears, and looser skin; foxhound, which is taller, leggier, and less compact; or Harrier, which is larger and more athletic-looking. Puppies may look rounder, but the long drooping ears, compact hound build, and beagle coloration remain key cues.

name: bloodhound
Canis lupus familiaris
163.description: A large scent hound with very long, pendulous ears, loose wrinkled skin, a heavy muzzle, and deep-set droopy eyes. The coat is short and typically black-and-tan, liver-and-tan, or red, with a long body, strong legs, and an overall solemn expression.
163.guidelines: Classify as bloodhound when the dog has the breed’s distinctive loose facial skin, pronounced wrinkles, very long hanging ears, and heavy hound head. Do not confuse it with coonhounds, foxhounds, or ridgebacks, which are usually tighter-skinned, less wrinkled, and have shorter ears and a lighter head. Basset hounds also have long ears and loose skin, but they are much shorter-legged and lower to the ground.

name: Bluetick Coonhound
Canis lupus familiaris
164.description: A medium-to-large hound with a lean but muscular build, long drooping ears, and a short glossy coat mottled blue-gray by dense black ticking. Most have a dark head with tan markings on the face and legs, and many show black patches on the body. The muzzle is long, the expression is hound-like, and the tail is carried upright or gently curved.
164.guidelines: Classify as Bluetick Coonhound when the dog has the characteristic blue-ticked coat, long pendant ears, and coonhound proportions. Do not confuse it with the American English Coonhound or pointer-type dogs, which may also be ticked but are usually leggier and less heavy-eared; or with Beagles and other hounds, which are smaller and more compact. The key cues are the blue-speckled coat, black-and-tan hound head, and long low-hanging ears.

name: Black and Tan Coonhound
Canis lupus familiaris
165.description: A large, athletic scenthound with a lean but muscular build, a short glossy black coat, and distinct tan markings on the muzzle, chest, legs, and small spots above the eyes. It has a long, narrow head, long drooping ears, a deep chest, and a long tail.
165.guidelines: Classify as Black and Tan Coonhound when the dog is a black-and-tan hound with very long pendant ears, a sleek short coat, and a tall, leggy scenthound build. Do not confuse with the Dobermann, which is more square-built with a sharper wedge-shaped head and shorter ears; the Rottweiler, which is heavier, broader, and stockier; or the Dachshund, which is much lower to the ground with a long body and short legs. Compared with other coonhounds, this breed is specifically black with clear tan points rather than tricolored, redtick, bluetick, or lemon-and-white patterns.

name: Treeing Walker Coonhound
Canis lupus familiaris
166.description: Medium-to-large athletic scenthound with a lean, long-legged build, deep chest, narrow waist, and long drooping ears. The coat is short and smooth, most often tricolor: a white base with a black saddle or large black patches and tan markings on the head and face.
166.guidelines: Classify as Treeing Walker Coonhound when the dog has the classic tall, streamlined hound shape, long pendant ears, and a short tricolor coat with strong white, black, and tan patterning. Distinguish it from the beagle, which is smaller, shorter-legged, and more compact; from the American Foxhound, which is very similar but is often less distinctly saddle-marked and more variable in coloration; and from coonhound breeds such as the Bluetick Coonhound or Black and Tan Coonhound, which have different coat patterns.

name: English Foxhound
Canis lupus familiaris
167.description: A large, athletic scenthound with a sturdy but lean body, long legs, a deep chest, and a short smooth coat. Most are tricolor—black saddle, tan head or flanks, and white legs, chest, and tail tip—though some are mostly white with tan or black patches. It has long drooping ears, a fairly broad muzzle, and a straight tail carried level or upright.
167.guidelines: Classify as English Foxhound when the dog is a tall, substantial hound with a smooth short coat, long legs, and classic foxhound tricolor patterning. Distinguish it from the smaller Beagle by its much larger size, leggier build, and less compact body. Distinguish it from the American Foxhound by the English Foxhound’s heavier, sturdier build and shorter-coupled appearance; American Foxhounds usually look slimmer and more refined. Avoid confusing it with coonhounds, which often have longer ears, looser skin, and a heavier, more drooping expression.

name: Redbone Coonhound
Canis lupus familiaris
168.description: A medium-to-large hound with a short, smooth, solid red to deep reddish-brown coat, a lean muscular build, a long muzzle, and long drooping ears. The body is athletic and balanced, with a deep chest, long legs, and a hound-like expression.
168.guidelines: Classify as Redbone Coonhound when the dog is a sleek, solid red scenthound with no black saddle or strong tan-point patterning. Distinguish it from the Rhodesian Ridgeback by the Redbone’s longer drooping ears and lack of a back ridge, and from the Vizsla by its heavier hound head, longer ears, and more distinctly coonhound build. Also avoid confusion with Black and Tan Coonhound or other coonhounds, which usually show black-and-tan or tricolor markings rather than a uniform red coat.

name: Borzoi
Canis lupus familiaris
169.description: A very tall, slim sighthound with long legs, a deep narrow chest, a tucked waist, and a long, narrow head with a pointed muzzle. The coat is long, silky, and often slightly wavy or feathered, especially on the tail, legs, and neck. Common colors include white, cream, gold, red, gray, black, or mixed patches.
169.guidelines: Classify as borzoi when the dog has the classic elegant sighthound build: very tall and narrow-bodied, long refined head, and a long silky coat with feathering. Distinguish it from the greyhound and whippet, which are similarly slender but have short, smooth coats. Distinguish it from the rough collie or Afghan hound by the borzoi’s more extreme sighthound proportions, narrower head, and less heavily coated body than an Afghan hound.

name: Irish wolfhound
Canis lupus familiaris
170.description: A very large sighthound with an exceptionally tall, long-legged, muscular body, a deep chest, and a long narrow face. The coat is rough and shaggy rather than smooth, often gray, brindle, wheaten, cream, red, black, or white, with a bearded muzzle and small folded ears.
170.guidelines: Classify as Irish wolfhound when the dog is giant, lanky, and wolf-like, with a wiry coat and elongated head. Distinguish it from the Scottish Deerhound by the Irish wolfhound’s heavier, taller build and broader frame; from Great Danes and other giant breeds by its rough coat instead of a short smooth coat; and from wolfdog- or borzoi-like dogs by its coarser shaggy fur, beard, and more rugged, muscular outline.

name: Italian Greyhound
Canis lupus familiaris
171.description: A very small sighthound with a slim, fine-boned body, deep narrow chest, tucked waist, long delicate legs, a thin tail, and a short smooth coat. The head is narrow with a long muzzle, and the ears are small and folded or rose-shaped. Common coat colors include gray, blue, fawn, black, cream, and white, often in solid or piebald patterns.
171.guidelines: Classify as Italian Greyhound when the dog is toy-sized yet clearly greyhound-shaped: elegant, very slender, long-legged, and short-haired. Distinguish it from the Whippet by its much smaller size and finer build, and from the Greyhound by being far smaller and more delicate overall. It can resemble Miniature Pinschers or Chihuahuas, but those breeds are less greyhound-like in body shape, with broader heads or different ear set and proportions.

name: Whippet
Canis lupus familiaris
172.description: A small to medium sighthound with a very slim, athletic build, deep chest, narrow waist, long fine legs, and a short smooth coat. The head is long and narrow with a tapered muzzle, small rose-shaped ears, and a long thin tail. Coat colors vary widely, including solid, brindle, parti-color, black, fawn, cream, blue, and white combinations.
172.guidelines: Classify as whippet when the dog is a lightly built sighthound of moderate size with a pronounced tuck-up, deep chest, and fine-boned legs. Distinguish it from the Greyhound by its smaller size and lighter, less towering frame; from the Italian Greyhound by its larger, sturdier build; and from lurchers or other mixed sighthounds by the consistent whippet proportions, short smooth coat, and refined but muscular outline.

name: Ibizan Hound
Canis lupus familiaris
173.description: A lean, tall sighthound with a very slender build, long legs, deep chest, narrow waist, and a long fine tail. It has a long wedge-shaped head, a flesh-colored or light nose, and very large upright pointed ears. The coat is usually short and smooth, most often white, red, or white-and-red, though some dogs may be wire-haired.
173.guidelines: Classify as Ibizan Hound when the dog is an elegant, fine-boned sighthound with especially large erect ears and the typical red-and-white or white coat. Distinguish it from the Pharaoh Hound, which is usually more uniformly tan or chestnut and less often patched white; from the Basenji, which is much smaller, more compact, and has a tightly curled tail; and from Whippets or Greyhounds, which have rose ears rather than large upright ears. Do not rely on pose alone—use the combination of sighthound body shape, huge erect ears, and light red/white coloration.

name: Norwegian Elkhound
Canis lupus familiaris
174.description: A medium-sized, sturdy spitz-type dog with a compact body, erect pointed ears, a tightly curled tail over the back, and a dense double coat. The coat is typically gray or silver-gray with darker shading on the muzzle, ears, and back, giving a wolfish appearance.
174.guidelines: Classify as Norwegian Elkhound when the dog shows the classic gray spitz build: compact frame, plush double coat, erect ears, and a strongly curled tail. Distinguish it from similar spitz breeds such as the Keeshond and Finnish Spitz by its heavier build and gray wolf-like coloring rather than a fuller mane or reddish coat; from the Norwegian Buhund by its lighter wheaten or black coloration; and from husky- or shepherd-type dogs by its shorter, more compact proportions and tightly curled tail.

name: otterhound
Canis lupus familiaris
175.description: A large, sturdy hound with a shaggy, rough, waterproof coat, a broad head, long drooping ears, and a bearded muzzle. The coat is typically wheaten, grizzle, black-and-tan, or mixed earth tones, giving a tousled, rustic appearance.
175.guidelines: Classify as otterhound when the dog is a large rough-coated hound with very long pendant ears, a shaggy face, and a substantial build. Distinguish it from Airedale terriers and other terriers by its heavier hound-like body and longer ears; from spinoni or doodle-type dogs by the classic hound head and coarse, untidy coat; and from briards or bearded collies by its shorter coat, heavier muzzle, and clearly drooping hound ears.

name: Saluki
Canis lupus familiaris
176.description: A very slender, long-legged sighthound with a narrow head, deep chest, tucked waist, and a smooth silky coat. Typical Salukis have long feathering on the ears, tail, and sometimes the backs of the legs, though some are smooth-coated. Colors vary widely, including cream, fawn, white, black and tan, tricolor, and grizzle.
176.guidelines: Classify as Saluki when the dog has the classic elegant sighthound build plus distinctive long, silky feathered ears and refined proportions. Do not confuse with Greyhound or Whippet, which are usually more muscular and have short, unfeathered ears and coats. Afghan Hound has a much longer, fuller coat over the whole body. Borzoi is larger with a longer, more arched back and a noticeably longer, narrower muzzle with a wavier coat.

name: Scottish Deerhound
Canis lupus familiaris
177.description: A very tall, long-legged sighthound with a lean body, deep chest, tucked waist, rough shaggy coat, and a long narrow head with a tapered muzzle. The coat is usually gray, blue-gray, brindle, or dark, giving a wiry, slightly unkempt appearance.
177.guidelines: Classify as Scottish Deerhound when the dog is giant and greyhound-like but clearly rough-coated, with a narrow head, long legs, and an overall lanky, elegant build. Distinguish it from the Irish Wolfhound by its generally lighter, more refined frame and longer, narrower head; from Greyhounds and other sighthounds by the shaggy wiry coat; and from large shaggy herding or hunting dogs by the pronounced sighthound silhouette with deep chest and tucked abdomen.

name: Weimaraner
Canis lupus familiaris
178.description: A medium-to-large sporting dog with a sleek, short silver-gray to mouse-gray coat, a lean athletic build, a deep chest, long legs, a narrow head, and long floppy ears. The eyes are typically light amber, gray, or blue-gray, giving the breed a distinctive pale-eyed look.
178.guidelines: Classify as Weimaraner when the dog has the characteristic solid gray/silver coat, slender athletic body, long drop ears, and pale eyes. Do not confuse it with a Labrador Retriever, which is stockier with a broader head and usually darker eyes; a Vizsla, which is similar in build but reddish-gold rather than gray; or a German Shorthaired Pointer, which typically has liver-and-white patterning instead of a solid gray coat.

name: Staffordshire Bull Terrier
Canis lupus familiaris
179.description: A compact, muscular, smooth-coated dog with a broad skull, pronounced cheeks, short muzzle, and strong jaw. It has a stocky but athletic build, a deep chest, sturdy legs, and a short coat that may be black, brindle, blue, fawn, red, or pied, often with white markings on the chest or face.
179.guidelines: Classify as Staffordshire Bull Terrier when the dog is medium-small, very muscular, and compact, with a broad head and short muzzle. Do not confuse it with the American Pit Bull Terrier or American Staffordshire Terrier, which are usually taller, leggier, and less compact; or the Bull Terrier, which has a distinctive egg-shaped head. Also distinguish from boxers and mastiff-type dogs by the Staffordshire Bull Terrier's lower height, shorter coat, and terrier-like compactness.

name: pit bull
Canis lupus familiaris
180.description: A medium-sized, very muscular dog with a short smooth coat, broad blocky head, strong jaws, deep chest, and a compact athletic build. The muzzle is medium length, the ears are often semi-pricked or folded, and the coat comes in many colors and patterns including solid, brindle, and white-marked forms.
180.guidelines: Classify as pit bull when the dog has the classic pit-bull-type build: muscular but agile body, broad head, short coat, and a medium-length muzzle. Do not confuse with boxer, which usually has a shorter squarer muzzle and more pronounced facial wrinkles; bull terrier, which has a distinctive egg-shaped head; American bulldog, which is typically heavier and bulkier; or mastiff-type dogs, which are larger with looser skin and droopier jowls. Use the overall pit-bull-type silhouette rather than coat color.

name: Bedlington Terrier
Canis lupus familiaris
181.description: A small, slender terrier with a distinctive lamb-like look: a curly or woolly coat, long narrow head, tasseled ears, and a noticeably arched back with a tucked-up waist. The coat is often pale blue-gray, sandy, liver, or white, and many dogs are shown in a clipped show trim that emphasizes the rounded topknot and slim legs.
181.guidelines: Classify as Bedlington Terrier when the dog has the characteristic lamb-like outline, narrow head, curly coat, and arched loin. Do not confuse it with poodles, which usually have a longer muzzle and more obviously stylized pom-pom grooming, or with other curly terriers such as the Kerry Blue Terrier or Soft-coated Wheaten Terrier, which lack the same pronounced arched back and sheep-like head and coat shape.

name: Border terrier
Canis lupus familiaris
182.description: A small, compact terrier with a sturdy body, relatively short muzzle, small V-shaped folded ears, and a dense rough or wiry coat. The coat is usually grizzle-and-tan, wheaten, red, or blue-and-tan, often with a slightly scruffy face and beard.
182.guidelines: Classify as Border terrier when the dog is a small rough-coated terrier with an otter-like head, short muzzle, folded ears, and a plain, workmanlike build. Distinguish it from Norfolk and Norwich terriers by its less plush coat and longer, narrower head; from Cairn terriers by its less shaggy, less round-faced appearance; and from mixed-breed small terriers by the consistent wiry coat, modest beard, and balanced, low-fuss terrier proportions.

name: Kerry Blue Terrier
Canis lupus familiaris
183.description: A medium-sized terrier with a compact, square build, a soft dense wavy to curly coat, and a distinctive long beard and facial furnishings. The coat is typically blue-gray, slate, or silver-gray, though some individuals appear very dark or nearly black, especially when clipped or in younger dogs. The legs are often groomed into fuller cylindrical columns, and the ears are small and folded forward.
183.guidelines: Classify as Kerry Blue Terrier when the dog shows the breed’s characteristic blue-gray curly coat, terrier outline, and prominent beard. Do not confuse it with the Bedlington Terrier, which has a lamb-like arched back and topknot; the Standard Schnauzer or Giant Schnauzer, which have a harsher wiry coat and more sharply defined schnauzer eyebrows; or curly-coated doodle-type dogs, which usually lack the classic terrier head, beard, and show-style outline.
