Distinguish it from gray foxes by the lack of a grizzled gray coat and black dorsal tail stripe; from kit foxes or fennec foxes by its less oversized ears and fuller red coat; and from coyotes, wolves, or dogs by its much smaller size, shorter muzzle, and more delicate fox-like build.

name: kit fox
Vulpes macrotis
278.description: A very small, slender fox with an exceptionally large-eared head, a narrow pointed muzzle, and a pale sandy, buff, or grayish-tan coat. The legs are relatively long and slim, the face is lightly marked, and the tail is bushy, usually with a darker tip. Overall it looks delicate, lightly built, and desert-colored.
278.guidelines: Classify as kit fox when the animal is a tiny pale fox with disproportionately huge upright ears and a fine-boned, slender build. Do not confuse it with the fennec fox, which has even larger ears and a creamier coat; the bat-eared fox, which has a shorter muzzle and darker face/legs; the swift fox, which is slightly stockier with smaller ears and often more gray on the back; or red and gray foxes, which are larger, darker, and less delicately built.

name: Arctic fox
Vulpes lagopus
279.description: A small fox with a compact body, short muzzle, pointed ears, and a very thick, fluffy coat. In these images it is mostly in the white winter morph, appearing white to creamy white, sometimes with light gray or darker shading on the face, ears, or back. It has a bushy tail, relatively short legs, and a rounded, fur-padded appearance adapted to cold climates.
279.guidelines: Classify as Arctic fox when the animal is a small fox with an extremely dense coat, small ears, and a short, compact face, often pure white or whitish in winter. Distinguish it from red foxes and other foxes by the shorter ears and muzzle, stockier body, and much fluffier coat. Distinguish it from domestic dogs or white wolves by its smaller size, more delicate fox-like face, and very bushy tail. Summer Arctic foxes may be brown or gray, but they still keep the compact proportions and small ears typical of the species.

name: gray fox
Urocyon cinereoargenteus
280.description: A small fox with a salt-and-pepper gray back, rusty to reddish sides, legs, and neck, a pale face and underparts, and a bushy tail marked by a distinct black stripe along the top and a dark tip. It has a slender muzzle, large pointed ears, and often shows a darker line along the back.
280.guidelines: Classify as gray fox when the animal shows the characteristic grizzled gray upper body combined with reddish flanks and a black-striped tail. Distinguish it from the red fox, which is usually brighter orange-red overall with black legs and a white tail tip, and from kit foxes or swift foxes, which are paler, sandier, and have proportionally larger ears. The black tail stripe and mixed gray-and-rufous coat are the key cues.

name: tabby cat
Felis catus
281.description: A domestic cat with the characteristic tabby coat pattern: a distinct dark "M" marking on the forehead, striped or swirled markings on the face and body, and often rings on the tail and legs. Coat colors vary widely, including brown, gray, silver, orange, and cream, and the fur may be short or long.
281.guidelines: Classify as tabby cat when the cat is a domestic cat showing the tabby pattern, especially the forehead "M" and striped, blotched, spotted, or ticked coat markings. Do not require one specific color or fur length. Distinguish from tiger cat by using tabby as the broader domestic-cat pattern category; reserve tiger cat only for clearly strongly striped tabbies if your label set separates them. Exclude solid-colored, pointed, calico, tortoiseshell, or bicolor cats unless the tabby pattern is clearly present.

name: tabby cat
Felis catus
282.description: A domestic cat with a tabby coat pattern, especially the striped form: a short-haired cat with narrow dark stripes on a gray, brown, or tan background, often with parallel lines along the sides, rings on the legs and tail, dark chest and neck bars, thin facial stripes, and a distinct M-shaped mark on the forehead.
282.guidelines: Classify domestic cats showing the characteristic tabby pattern, especially striped tabbies. Key cues are the forehead M, facial lines, leg and tail rings, and dark striping over a lighter coat. Do not confuse with wild cats such as tigers, servals, ocelots, or margays, which have very different body shape and markings. Also distinguish from non-tabby pet cats such as solid-color, bicolor, calico, or pointed cats. If the image is simply a domestic cat with tabby markings, it belongs here.

name: Persian cat
Felis catus
283.description: A long-haired cat breed with a very round head, short broad muzzle, small low-set ears, large round eyes, and a dense, full coat. The body looks compact and cobby, with a short neck, short legs, and a thick plumed tail. Many examples show the flat-faced (brachycephalic) look typical of Persians, and coats occur in many colors and patterns.
283.guidelines: Classify as Persian cat when the cat has the characteristic long, luxuriant coat plus a round, compact build and especially a short, flattened face with small ears and large round eyes. Distinguish from Himalayan cats by the absence of a required colorpoint pattern; Himalayans are Persian-type cats but specifically have Siamese-like points and blue eyes. Distinguish from Maine Coon and Norwegian Forest cats by their longer muzzles, larger ears, and less flat faces. Distinguish from British Longhair by the Persian's more extreme flat face and heavier coat.

name: Siamese cat
Felis catus
284.description: A slender short-haired domestic cat with a pale cream to fawn body and much darker colorpoint markings on the face, ears, legs, and tail. It typically has a wedge-shaped head, very large pointed ears, a long fine tail, and vivid blue eyes. The contrast between the light body and dark extremities is the defining visual trait.
284.guidelines: Classify as Siamese cat when the cat has the classic short-haired pointed coat pattern plus the lean, elegant Siamese build, large ears, and blue eyes. Do not confuse with Balinese, which has the same point coloration but long silky fur and a plumed tail; Himalayan, which is long-haired and cobby-faced; or Tonkinese/colorpoint shorthair types, which are often stockier or have less extreme Siamese head shape. Exclude non-pointed cats and long-haired pointed cats unless they clearly match a recognized Siamese appearance.

name: domestic cat
Felis catus
285.description: A small domestic feline with a compact, flexible body, triangular upright ears, prominent whiskers, and a long tail. Coat color, length, and pattern vary widely, including tabby, solid black, colorpoint, silver, and long-haired forms, but the overall appearance is that of a pet house cat rather than a wild cat.
285.guidelines: Classify as domestic cat when the animal is a typical pet cat of any coat pattern or breed-like appearance. Do not restrict this class to Egyptian Mau cats: the examples include many ordinary house cats. Distinguish it from wild cats such as leopard cats, ocelots, servals, or lynxes by the smaller pet-cat build, absence of strongly wild spotting/rosetting, lack of ear tufts, and typical home-cat proportions. Also exclude big cats and hairless cats unless the image still clearly shows an ordinary domestic cat.

name: cougar
Puma concolor
286.description: A large, slender wild cat with a uniform tawny to grayish-brown coat, pale underparts, a small rounded head, upright rounded ears often dark on the back, and a long thick tail usually tipped darker. The face commonly shows a pale muzzle with darker markings around the nose and mouth, and the body is long-legged and athletic without stripes, spots, or a mane in adults.
286.guidelines: Classify as cougar when the animal is a large plain-colored cat with a long tail and no rosettes or stripes. Distinguish it from lions by the lack of a mane and tail tuft, from leopards and jaguars by the absence of spots, from cheetahs by the lack of tear marks and spotted coat, and from bobcats or lynx by the much longer tail and more elongated body. Do not confuse dark-coated 'panthers' used colloquially for melanistic leopards or jaguars with this species.

name: lynx
Lynx
287.description: A medium-sized wild cat with a short bobbed tail, long legs, a broad face, and prominent black ear tufts. The coat is usually gray, tawny, or reddish-brown, often with faint to distinct spotting, and many individuals show a facial ruff and pale underside.
287.guidelines: Classify as lynx when the cat has the classic lynx shape: short tail, tall pointed ears with black tufts, long legs, and a broad ruffed face. Do not confuse with domestic cats or small wildcats, which usually lack strong ear tufts and the heavy ruff. Distinguish from cougar or other larger cats by the much shorter tail, and from foxes by the feline face, paws, and body shape.

name: leopard
Panthera pardus
288.description: A medium-to-large wild cat with a sleek, muscular body, relatively small head, and a golden to tawny coat covered in dark rosette-shaped spots. The rosettes are generally smaller and lighter-built than those of a jaguar and usually lack central dots. The tail is long, and the overall build is slimmer than a tiger or jaguar.
288.guidelines: Classify as leopard when the cat has a slender build and a tawny coat marked with many small rosettes, typically without spots inside the rosettes. Do not confuse it with jaguar, which is stockier, broader-headed, and usually has larger rosettes with central dots; cheetah, which has solid round spots and black tear marks on the face; or tiger, which has stripes instead of rosettes. Snow leopard is paler, fluffier, and has a very thick tail with larger diffuse rosettes.

name: snow leopard
Panthera uncia
289.description: A large pale gray to smoky-white big cat with a thick woolly coat covered in dark rosettes and spots, a relatively small rounded head, short rounded ears, large pale eyes, broad furry paws, and very large nostrils. Its tail is exceptionally long, thick, and bushy, nearly as long as the body.
289.guidelines: Classify as snow leopard when the cat shows a pale, heavily furred coat with dark open rosettes, a very thick extremely long tail, and broad furry feet adapted to cold mountain habitats. Distinguish it from the common leopard and jaguar by its much paler coat, denser fur, longer thicker tail, and less powerfully built body; from clouded leopard by the absence of huge cloud-shaped blotches; and from lynx or bobcat by the long tail and lack of ear tufts.

name: jaguar
Panthera onca
290.description: A large, powerfully built big cat with a stocky body, muscular legs, large paws, a broad square head, and a relatively short tail. The coat is usually golden yellow to tawny with large black rosettes, often containing one or more small black spots in the center; melanistic black individuals also occur.
290.guidelines: Classify as jaguar when the cat is robust and heavy-set, with a broad head, short tail, and large rosettes that usually contain central dots. Do not confuse with leopard: leopards are typically slimmer, with a smaller head, longer tail, and rosettes that usually lack central spots. Also avoid confusion with cheetah or other spotted cats, which lack the jaguar’s large rosettes and stocky build. Black panthers in this class are melanistic jaguars, not a separate species.

name: lion
Panthera leo
291.description: A very large tawny big cat with a broad face, short rounded ears, and a muscular body. Adult males usually have a prominent mane ranging from blond to dark brown or black around the head, neck, and chest; females usually lack a mane and appear sleeker. The coat is generally plain buff, sand, or golden-brown, sometimes with a pale underside and a dark tail tuft.
291.guidelines: Classify as lion when the animal has the characteristic lion build and plain tawny coat, especially a male mane or the broad-faced, mane-less lioness form. Distinguish from tigers by the lack of stripes, from leopards and jaguars by the lack of rosettes, and from cheetahs by the heavier build and absence of tear marks. Avoid confusing male lions with heavily furred domestic cats or other big cats; the mane, tail tuft, and uniform coat are key cues.

name: tiger
Panthera tigris
292.description: A very large, powerfully built cat with a rich orange to tawny coat marked by bold black vertical stripes. The underparts, cheeks, and areas around the eyes are usually white, and the face often shows strong black striping with a pink nose. Some images may show pale or white color variants, but the same dark stripe pattern and tiger body shape remain visible.
292.guidelines: Classify as tiger when the animal is a massive striped big cat with an orange (or occasionally white) coat and black vertical stripes over the body, neck, and face. Do not confuse it with leopards or jaguars, which have rosettes rather than stripes, or with cheetahs, which have spots and tear marks. Lions lack striping, and tabby domestic cats are much smaller and less powerfully built. The key cue is the tiger’s large, muscular body and bold dark stripes on a usually orange coat.

name: cheetah
Acinonyx jubatus
293.description: A slender, long-legged big cat with a small rounded head, deep chest, narrow waist, and short tawny coat covered in solid black spots. The most distinctive marking is the dark tear stripe running continuously from the inner corner of each eye down to the sides of the mouth. The tail is long and ringed near the tip.
293.guidelines: Classify as cheetah when the cat has a very slim build, small head, solid round spots, and clear black tear marks from eye to mouth. Distinguish it from leopard and jaguar, which are stockier and have rosette-shaped markings rather than solid spots; from serval, which has much larger ears and proportionally shorter body; and from cougar or lion cub, which lack the strong tear stripes and dense spotted adult coat.

name: brown bear
Ursus arctos
294.description: A very large, heavy-bodied bear with shaggy fur that ranges from pale blond and tan to medium brown and very dark brown. It has a broad head, small rounded ears, a relatively dished face, powerful limbs, and a noticeable shoulder hump; the coat is often grizzled or lighter on the head and back.
294.guidelines: Classify as brown bear when the animal is a bulky bear with a pronounced shoulder hump, broad concave face, and variable brown-to-blond coat. Do not confuse with the American black bear, which usually lacks the strong shoulder hump, has a straighter facial profile, and often appears sleeker with larger ears. Do not confuse with polar bear, which is white to cream and more long-necked, or with sloth bear, which has a much shaggier coat, longer muzzle, and pale chest mark.

name: American black bear
Ursus americanus
295.description: A medium to large bear with a compact, heavy body, rounded ears, a relatively straight facial profile, and glossy black fur in most individuals. The muzzle is usually tan to brown, and some animals show a small white chest patch. It has a shorter, less shaggy coat and less prominent shoulder hump than brown bears.
295.guidelines: Classify as American black bear when the bear is black or very dark brown with rounded ears, a lighter muzzle, and no strong shoulder hump. Distinguish it from brown/grizzly bears, which are bulkier with a pronounced shoulder hump, dish-shaped face, and longer claws; from Asiatic black bears, which more often show a bold crescent-shaped white chest mark and a shaggier look; and from sloth bears, which have a longer snout, shaggy coat, and pale muzzle.

name: polar bear
Ursus maritimus
296.description: A very large bear with dense white to creamy-white fur, a long neck, relatively small rounded ears, a narrow head, and a black nose. The body is heavy and muscular with broad paws adapted for walking on snow and swimming. It is usually seen on sea ice, snow, rocky Arctic shores, or in water.
296.guidelines: Classify as polar bear only when the animal shows the characteristic white or pale cream coat, elongated neck, small ears, and bear build. Do not confuse it with brown bears or grizzly bears, which are typically brown and bulkier-faced, or with American black bears, which are darker and smaller. It can resemble other white bears in zoos or overexposed photos, but the combination of Arctic setting, long neck, narrow head, and large paddle-like paws distinguishes the polar bear.

name: spectacled bear
Tremarctos ornatus
297.description: A medium-sized black bear with shaggy dark fur, a relatively short broad muzzle, and distinctive pale cream or whitish markings on the face, especially around the eyes and muzzle, often forming spectacle-like patterns. Many individuals also show a pale patch or crescent on the chest. The body is stocky, with rounded ears and long, pale claws.
297.guidelines: Classify as spectacled bear when the bear has dark fur plus clear pale facial markings around the eyes and muzzle, often with a light chest mark. Do not confuse with sloth bear, which typically has a much longer, shaggier coat, a longer narrower snout, and lacks the neat spectacle-like face pattern; sloth bears also often show a larger shaggy mane and a pale V-shaped chest patch. Also distinguish from American black bear, which usually lacks the pale eye rings and contrasting cream muzzle seen here.

name: mongoose
Herpestidae
298.description: A small to medium-sized, long-bodied carnivoran with a pointed muzzle, short legs, small rounded ears, and a moderately long, often bushy tail. Typical coloration is gray, sandy, brown, or grizzled, sometimes with faint stripes or bands depending on species. Mongooses are often shown alert on the ground or standing upright, and may appear confronting snakes.
298.guidelines: Classify as mongoose when the animal has an elongated body, pointed face, short legs, and a long tail, with the overall look of a small terrestrial predator. This category includes different mongoose species, so color and striping may vary. Do not confuse with meerkats only if treated separately; meerkats are a kind of mongoose but are especially slender and often stand upright in open habitats. Distinguish from mustelids such as weasels, ferrets, and otters by the mongoose’s shorter legs, less flexible-looking body, more pointed face, and typical dry-land setting. Distinguish from civets and genets by the lack of bold spots or ringed tails in most cases and the generally stockier, less catlike build.

name: meerkat
Suricata suricatta
299.description: A small, slender mongoose with a tan to gray-brown coat, pale underside, dark eye patches that look like "glasses," a pointed muzzle, small rounded ears, and a long thin tail often held low or slightly curved. It is frequently seen sitting or standing upright on its hind legs.
299.guidelines: Classify as meerkat when the animal shows the distinctive dark eye mask, slim body, pointed face, and sentinel-like upright stance. Distinguish it from prairie dogs, ground squirrels, and marmots, which are stockier, lack the dark eye patches, and have shorter, bushier tails. Distinguish it from mongooses more broadly by the strong black eye markings and the familiar upright posture common in meerkat images.

name: tiger beetle
Cicindelinae
300.description: A slender, long-legged predatory beetle, often with a metallic green, blue, bronze, or purplish sheen. It has a narrow body, large prominent eyes, long antennae, strong curved mandibles, and relatively long legs for fast running. The wing covers are usually smooth and shiny, sometimes marked with pale spots or wavy cream markings.
300.guidelines: Classify as tiger beetle when the insect has the classic fast-running ground-beetle shape plus very large bulging eyes, long legs, and sickle-like jaws, often with bright metallic coloration. Do not confuse it with other ground beetles (Carabidae), which are usually darker, less shiny, broader-bodied, and have smaller eyes and shorter legs. Also distinguish from jewel beetles and leaf beetles, which may be metallic but typically have a more compact body, shorter legs, and lack the oversized eyes and predatory jaws of tiger beetles.

name: ladybird beetle
Coccinellidae
301.description: A small, strongly domed, nearly hemispherical beetle with a smooth, shiny shell. Most are bright red, orange, or yellow with black spots, but some are black with red or orange marks, and spot number can vary widely. The head is short and partly hidden by the pronotum, which is often black, white, or patterned; legs and antennae are short.
301.guidelines: Classify as a ladybird beetle when the insect is a tiny round, highly convex beetle with glossy wing covers and typical red/orange/yellow-and-black warning coloration. This category includes multiple color forms and spot patterns, including spotless and dark forms. Avoid confusing it with leaf beetles or scarab beetles, which are usually more elongated, less hemispherical, and lack the classic short-faced, dome-backed ladybird shape. Also distinguish from true bugs and stink bug nymphs, which are flatter, show segmented bodies and long antennae, and do not have hard beetle wing covers.

name: ground beetle
Carabidae
302.description: A ground beetle is a usually dark, flattened to elongated beetle with a hard shell, long running legs, and threadlike antennae. The body is often black or brown, sometimes metallic green, blue, or bronze, and the wing covers commonly show lengthwise grooves or ridges.
302.guidelines: Classify as a ground beetle when the beetle has a low, elongated body built for running, prominent legs, and smooth or ridged elytra, often in dark or metallic colors. Do not confuse it with scarab or dung beetles, which are more rounded and stout; click beetles, which are narrower with pointed rear corners on the thorax; darkling beetles, which are often bulkier and less distinctly long-legged; or rove beetles, which have very short wing covers leaving much of the abdomen exposed.

name: longhorn beetle
Cerambycidae
303.description: Beetles with an elongated, cylindrical to somewhat flattened body and very long, threadlike antennae, often as long as or longer than the body. Most are brown, black, gray, or mottled, though some are brightly patterned with bands or spots. Legs are relatively long, and the pronotum may be smooth, spined, or rounded depending on the species.
303.guidelines: Classify as longhorn beetle when the insect is clearly a beetle with exceptionally long antennae arising near the eyes, usually combined with a narrow, elongate body. Do not confuse with weevils, which have a distinct snout; leaf-footed or assassin bugs, which are true bugs with a flatter body and different wing texture; or spider wasps and other wasps, which have a narrow waist and membranous wings rather than hard wing covers. Also distinguish from click beetles and ground beetles, which may be elongate but usually have much shorter antennae.

name: leaf beetle
Chrysomelidae
304.description: Small to medium-sized beetles with a compact oval to rounded body, smooth shiny wing covers, and relatively short antennae. They are often brightly colored or metallic—green, blue, red, orange, yellow, black, or patterned with spots and stripes—and are commonly seen sitting on leaves and stems.
304.guidelines: Classify this as a leaf beetle when the insect is a smooth, dome-like or oval beetle with short to moderate antennae and often vivid or metallic coloration. Do not confuse it with ladybugs, which are usually more strongly domed with very short clubbed antennae, or with longhorn beetles, which have much longer antennae and a more elongated body. Also distinguish it from scarab/jewel beetles, which are typically bulkier or more tapered and less associated with the typical small plant-feeding leaf-beetle form.

name: dung beetle
Scarabaeinae
305.description: A small to medium beetle with a stout, rounded body, a very hard shiny shell, and strong spade-like front legs adapted for digging and manipulating dung. It is usually black or dark brown, though some species can be metallic green, blue, or bronze.
305.guidelines: Classify as dung beetle when the beetle is robust, smooth-shelled, and often shown rolling, burying, or standing on dung, with broad digging forelegs. Do not confuse it with other scarab beetles such as rhinoceros beetles or flower chafers: rhinoceros beetles are larger and often have prominent horns, while flower chafers are typically seen on flowers and lack the typical dung-handling behavior and digging forelegs.

name: rhinoceros beetle
Dynastinae
306.description: A large, heavy-bodied scarab beetle with a smooth, hard, glossy shell and stout legs. Most individuals are dark brown, reddish brown, black, or olive to tan. Males typically have one or more prominent horns projecting from the head and/or thorax, sometimes long and curved; females are usually hornless or have much smaller horns. The body is oval, domed, and robust.
306.guidelines: Classify as rhinoceros beetle when the beetle is a bulky scarab with a strongly convex body and a distinct horn or paired horns, especially in males. Do not confuse it with stag beetles, which have large antler-like mandibles rather than horns growing from the head or thorax, or with longhorn beetles, which have very long antennae and a more elongated body. Also distinguish it from dung beetles and other scarabs that may be rounded and dark but lack the characteristic rhinoceros-like horn structure.

name: weevil
Curculionidae
307.description: A small beetle with a compact oval to pear-shaped body and a distinct elongated forward-projecting snout (rostrum). The antennae are usually elbowed and arise from the snout, and the body is often hard-shelled, rough, ridged, or scaly. Color varies widely from dull brown, gray, and black to metallic green or reddish tones.
307.guidelines: Classify as a weevil when the insect is a beetle with a clearly visible snout and elbowed antennae attached to that snout. Many species are tiny and rounded, while others are longer-bodied, but the rostrum is the key feature. Do not confuse with stink bugs, leaf-footed bugs, or other true bugs, which lack beetle wing covers and usually do not have elbowed antennae on a snout. Also distinguish from longhorn beetles and bark beetles: longhorn beetles have very long straight antennae but no true rostrum, and bark beetles are more cylindrical with little or no obvious snout.

name: fly
Diptera
308.description: A true fly: a small to medium insect with one visible pair of wings, large compound eyes, short antennae, and a compact or slender body. Appearance varies widely across the category, including metallic green or blue bottle flies, gray housefly-like forms, long-legged delicate flies, stout bee-mimicking hoverflies, and other predatory or nectar-feeding flies.
308.guidelines: Classify as fly when the insect is a member of Diptera, especially when it shows a single functional pair of wings and prominent eyes. This category includes many different fly types rather than one specific species. Do not confuse with bees or wasps, which have two pairs of wings and longer antennae; with moths or butterflies, which have scaled wings; or with mosquitoes and midges, which are much more slender with very long legs and a narrow body. Bee-mimicking hoverflies still count as flies if they have fly-like eyes, short antennae, and only one pair of wings.

name: bee
309.description: A bee is a small to medium flying insect with a stout or moderately slender body, six legs, two pairs of clear wings, and long segmented antennae. Many are hairy, especially on the thorax, and often show black, brown, yellow, orange, or metallic coloration. Forms vary from robust, fuzzy bumblebees to slimmer honey bees, shiny carpenter bees, and small solitary or cuckoo bees, but all share the typical bee shape and flower-visiting appearance.
309.guidelines: Classify as bee when the insect has the general bee body plan: elbowed-looking antennae, two wing pairs, and a pollen-feeding or flower-visiting form, often with visible body hair or pollen-carrying legs. Include honey bees, bumblebees, carpenter bees, cuckoo bees, and other true bees. Do not confuse with wasps, which are usually less hairy and have a narrower waist; hoverflies, which have only one pair of wings and very short antennae; or bee flies, which have a long proboscis and different fly head shape. Exclude close-ups where the animal is clearly a non-bee insect even if it resembles one in color.

name: ant
Formicidae
310.description: Small social hymenopteran insects with a distinctly narrow waist, elbowed antennae, and a body divided into head, thorax, and rounded abdomen. Typical forms are black, brown, red, or mixed-colored, with long legs and strong mandibles; some castes are wingless workers, while reproductive ants may be winged. Size and shape vary widely across species, from slender long-legged forms to more robust ants, but the pinched waist and elbowed antennae are consistent cues.
310.guidelines: Classify as ant when the insect has elbowed antennae and a clearly constricted waist with one or two nodes between thorax and abdomen. Include both wingless workers and winged reproductive ants. Do not confuse with termites, which have straight antennae, thicker waists, and two pairs of equal-length wings; with ant-mimicking spiders, which have eight legs and no true antennae; or with wasps such as velvet ants, which may resemble ants but usually have a different body texture, proportion, and wasp-like structure. Ant-like beetles and true bugs also lack the characteristic elbowed antennae plus nodal waist combination.

name: grasshopper
Caelifera
311.description: A grasshopper is a stout-bodied jumping insect with large hind legs, relatively short antennae, and narrow forewings folded along the back. It is commonly green, brown, tan, or gray, sometimes with striped or mottled camouflage, and lacks the strong leaflike body shape seen in katydids.
311.guidelines: Classify as grasshopper when the insect has enlarged hind legs for jumping, short to medium-length antennae, and a compact body that is not leaf-mimicking. Do not confuse it with katydids, which usually have very long threadlike antennae and often leaflike wings, or with crickets, which are generally flatter, darker, and also have longer antennae. Avoid using this label for cicadas or other insects with large transparent wings and no enlarged jumping legs.

name: cricket
Gryllidae
312.description: A cricket is a long-antennaed orthopteran insect with a compact, cylindrical to slightly humpbacked body, large hind legs adapted for jumping, and a head that is clearly visible from above. It is usually brown, black, tan, or green, sometimes with banding or pale markings, and its wings may lie flat over the back or be reduced. Unlike leaf-mimicking insects, the body is not broad or leaf-shaped.
312.guidelines: Classify as cricket when the insect has very long threadlike antennae, a stout non-leaflike body, and enlarged jumping hind legs. Distinguish it from katydids, which are usually more laterally flattened, greener, and often have broad leaf-shaped wings; and from grasshoppers, which have much shorter antennae and a more elongated visible body form. Do not rely on color alone, since crickets can be dark, tan, or green.

name: stick insect
Phasmatodea
313.description: A very slender, elongated insect that mimics a twig or small branch. The body is long, narrow, and usually straight or slightly segmented, with extremely thin legs and long antennae; coloration is typically brown, tan, or green to blend with stems and leaves. Some individuals show small leaf-like expansions or rough bark-like texture, but the overall look is sticklike and highly camouflaged.
313.guidelines: Classify as stick insect when the animal’s whole body is adapted to resemble a twig: long rod-like body, thin walking legs, and cryptic brown or green coloration. Do not confuse with mantises, which have a thicker body and enlarged raptorial front legs folded for grasping prey, or with katydids/grasshoppers, which usually have broader bodies, stronger hind legs for jumping, and more obvious wings. Also exclude leaf insects, which are wider and clearly leaf-shaped rather than stick-shaped.

name: cockroach
Blattodea
314.description: A cockroach is a flattened, oval-bodied insect with a glossy tan to dark brown exoskeleton, very long threadlike antennae, spiny legs, and a shieldlike pronotum covering the head. Adults may have long wings lying flat over the back, while nymphs are smaller and wingless. Many images show the typical indoor roach form seen crawling on floors, walls, drains, and other household surfaces.
314.guidelines: Classify as cockroach when the insect has a broad flattened body, long antennae, and fast-running spiny legs, often with the head partly hidden beneath the pronotum. Do not confuse with beetles, which usually have harder shell-like wing covers meeting in a straight seam and shorter antennae; crickets, which have enlarged hind legs for jumping; or true bugs, which are typically more angular or shield-shaped. Roaches are broader, flatter, and more oval than most similar household insects.

name: praying mantis
Mantodea
315.description: A slender predatory insect with a long narrow thorax, a triangular highly mobile head, large bulging eyes, and folded spiny forelegs held in a characteristic 'praying' pose. Usually green or brown and leaflike or sticklike in overall form, with an elongated abdomen and two pairs of wings in adults.
315.guidelines: Classify as praying mantis when the insect shows the distinctive raptorial front legs folded beneath the head and the elongated 'necklike' thorax. Do not confuse it with grasshoppers, katydids, or crickets, which have enlarged jumping hind legs rather than grasping forelegs; stick insects, which lack the triangular head and spined forelegs; or assassin bugs and other true bugs, which are flatter-bodied and do not have the mantis hunting posture.

name: cicada
Cicadoidea
316.description: A stout-bodied insect with a broad head, large widely spaced eyes, short antennae, and two pairs of long transparent membranous wings held rooflike over the body. Adults are usually green, brown, or black, often with bold vein patterns or mottling, while the immature stage is a wingless brown nymph with a thick body and strong digging forelegs; shed nymphal skins are common on bark, plants, and walls.
316.guidelines: Classify as cicada when the insect has a chunky body, very large eyes, and clear net-veined wings, or when it is a brown cicada nymph/exuvia with powerful shovel-like front legs. Do not confuse with grasshoppers or katydids, which have enlarged jumping hind legs and leathery forewings; leafhoppers or planthoppers, which are much smaller and more wedge-shaped; or dragonflies, which have much longer bodies and wings held out to the sides. Also exclude wasps and flies that may mimic cicadas but have very different body shape and wing structure.

name: leafhopper
Cicadellidae
317.description: Small, slender plant-feeding hopper with a wedge-shaped body, rooflike folded wings, and strong hind legs for jumping. Commonly green, yellow, tan, brown, or brightly patterned with stripes, spots, or netlike wing venation; often sits lengthwise along leaves or stems.
317.guidelines: Classify as a leafhopper when the insect is a tiny to small wedge-shaped hopper with wings held tentlike over the body and enlarged hind legs adapted for jumping. Do not confuse with planthoppers, which are often broader, fluffier, or carry more exaggerated head or wing shapes, or with treehoppers, which usually have a pronounced raised pronotum or thornlike hump. Leafhoppers are typically smoother, lower-profile, and more streamlined than those groups.

name: green lacewing
Chrysopidae
318.description: A delicate, slender insect usually pale green to yellow-green, sometimes tan, with very long threadlike antennae, large golden or coppery eyes, and two pairs of transparent wings covered in fine netlike veins. The wings are held rooflike over a narrow body, giving a soft, lacy appearance.
318.guidelines: Classify as green lacewing when the insect is slim-bodied with long antennae and clear, densely veined wings that look like lace, usually over a green body. Do not confuse it with damselflies, which have much longer bodies and different wing venation; caddisflies, which are hairier and duller-winged; mayflies, which usually have upright wings and long tail filaments; or antlions/owlflies, which tend to have stouter bodies or clubbed antennae. The golden eyes and fine lace-like wing network are key cues.

name: dragonfly
Anisoptera
319.description: A dragonfly is a slender-bodied flying insect with a long abdomen, a large rounded head dominated by very large compound eyes that touch or nearly touch, and two pairs of clear, net-veined wings held out flat or partly open at rest. Colors vary widely, including blue, green, red, brown, black, and metallic tones, often with banding or patches on the body or wings.
319.guidelines: Classify as dragonfly when the insect has a robust or elongated body, broad outstretched wings, and especially eyes that meet or almost meet on the head. The main confusion is with damselflies: damselflies usually have clearly separated eyes, a slimmer build, and typically hold wings folded together over the body at rest. Also avoid confusing dragonflies with other flying insects such as lacewings or mayflies, which lack the dragonfly’s huge eye-dominated head and characteristic wing shape and posture.

name: damselfly
Zygoptera
320.description: A slender, delicate odonate with a very thin elongated body, narrow abdomen, and two pairs of clear or lightly tinted wings. At rest, the wings are usually folded together over the back or held close above the body. Many are blue, green, black, or reddish with fine banding or colored tail segments. The head is broad, but the large eyes are distinctly separated on the sides rather than meeting.
320.guidelines: Classify as damselfly when the insect has a slim body, narrow wings, and clearly separated eyes. Most damselflies rest with wings closed or nearly closed above the abdomen. Do not confuse with dragonflies, which are stouter, have broader wings, and usually have eyes that touch or nearly touch; dragonflies also often rest with wings spread flat. Also avoid confusing them with mayflies or lacewings: damselflies have a long odonate body, strong thorax, and do not have the long tail filaments of mayflies.

name: red admiral
Vanessa atalanta
321.description: A medium-sized butterfly with very dark brown to black wings crossed by a bold red-orange band on each forewing and a broad red-orange border on the hindwings. The forewings also show distinct white spots near the tips. With wings closed, the underside is mottled brown and bark-like, helping it blend into surroundings.
321.guidelines: Classify as red admiral when the butterfly shows blackish wings with bright red-orange bands plus prominent white forewing tip spots. Do not confuse it with the white admiral, which has a white band instead of red-orange, or with tortoiseshell butterflies, which are overall orange with black patterning rather than mostly dark. Painted lady is also orange-brown and more finely mottled, lacking the clean dark ground color and strong red band of the red admiral.

name: ringlet
Aphantopus hyperantus
322.description: A small to medium brown butterfly with velvety dark brown to warm brown wings, usually showing several small pale-ringed black eyespots on the underside, especially on the hindwing. The upper side is often plainer and darker, sometimes with only faint or few visible spots.
322.guidelines: Classify as ringlet when the butterfly is uniformly brown and has multiple small circular eyespots with pale rings, most clearly visible on the underside of the wings. Distinguish it from meadow brown and gatekeeper, which usually show stronger orange patches and fewer prominent eyespots, and from wood-nymphs or other satyrs with larger or differently arranged eye markings. The combination of plain brown wings and a row of several neat ringed eyespots is the key cue.

name: monarch butterfly
Danaus plexippus
323.description: A large milkweed butterfly with bright orange wings crossed by bold black veins and bordered in black with rows of small white spots. The wings are broad and elongated, and the underside is similar but usually paler orange to tawny.
323.guidelines: Classify as monarch butterfly when the insect shows the classic orange-and-black veined pattern and lacks the black transverse line crossing the hindwing. The main confusion is the viceroy, which is smaller and has a distinct black band running across the hindwing. Also distinguish from queen butterflies, which are darker chestnut-brown with fewer heavy black veins and more extensive white spotting.

name: cabbage white
Pieris rapae
324.description: A small white butterfly with white to pale cream or pale yellow wings, usually showing one or two distinct black spots on each forewing. The forewing tips are often dusky to blackish, and the underside may appear yellowish or pale greenish.
324.guidelines: Classify as cabbage white when the butterfly is a mostly white or pale cream pierid with one or two black forewing spots and a dark forewing tip. Distinguish it from large white butterflies by its smaller size and less extensive black markings, and from orange-tip butterflies by the lack of orange forewing tips. Also avoid confusing it with sulfur butterflies, which are typically more uniformly yellow and lack the classic white-and-black cabbage white pattern.

name: cloudless sulphur
Phoebis sennae
325.description: A medium-to-large butterfly with broad, pointed wings that are usually bright lemon yellow to yellow-green. The upperside is often fairly plain, while the underside is paler yellow or greenish and may show a few small dark or silvery spots. The body is slender, and the overall look is clean, leaflike, and lightly marked rather than boldly patterned.
325.guidelines: Classify as cloudless sulphur when the butterfly is mostly solid yellow with little to no dark border and has elongated, pointed wings. Distinguish it from orange sulphur and clouded yellow butterflies, which usually show stronger black wing borders, and from brimstones, which have more angular, leaf-shaped wings. Avoid confusing worn white butterflies with this class: cloudless sulphurs remain distinctly yellow overall, often with only a few small discal spots underneath.

name: gossamer-winged butterfly
Lycaenidae
326.description: Small butterflies with rounded wings, often delicate and compact in shape. Many show shiny blue, violet, gray, or coppery upperwings, while the undersides are commonly pale gray or brown with fine stripes, spots, or eye-like markings. Some species have one or two short tail-like projections on the hindwings.
326.guidelines: Classify as gossamer-winged butterfly when the butterfly is a small lycaenid with a slender body, rounded wings, frequent blue or copper coloration, and often finely patterned undersides; some have tiny hindwing tails. Distinguish from skippers by the skippers' chunkier bodies, hooked antenna clubs, and more triangular wings. Distinguish from pierids and whites by their plainer white or yellow wings and lack of delicate tail/spot patterns. Distinguish from hairstreak look-alikes in other groups by the overall small lycaenid form and the characteristic blue/copper coloration or finely lined undersides typical of Lycaenidae.

name: sea star
Asteroidea
327.description: Marine echinoderm with a star-shaped body, usually five stout rays radiating symmetrically from a central disk, though some species have more. The body is firm rather than flexible, with a rough, granular, knobby, or slightly spiny surface, and colors vary widely from orange, red, purple, blue, tan, and mottled patterns.
327.guidelines: Classify as sea star when the animal has a broad star-like body with thick rays merging into a central disk and a textured upper surface. Do not confuse with brittle stars or basket stars, which have a small distinct disk and much thinner, snake-like arms; feather stars, which have many feathery branching arms; or sand dollars and sea urchins, which are disk-shaped or spherical rather than star-shaped.

name: sea urchin
Echinoidea
328.description: A marine echinoderm with a rounded, flattened, or slightly heart-shaped body covered in movable spines. It may appear as a dense prickly sphere, a low dome, or an empty rigid test with rows of small pores and a central opening. Color varies widely—black, purple, red, green, brown, white, or pink—and the spines can be short and velvety, stout and pencil-like, or very long and needle-thin.
328.guidelines: Classify as sea urchin when the animal has a rigid globular or disk-like test densely covered with radiating spines, or when the empty shell shows the characteristic urchin test pattern. Do not confuse with porcupinefish or pufferfish, which have eyes, fins, and a fish body; with chestnuts, burrs, or thistles, which are plant structures rather than radially symmetric animals; or with sea anemones, which have soft tentacles instead of stiff spines. Sand dollars and heart urchins are close relatives, but if the image shows the typical spiny urchin form or an obvious urchin test, it belongs here.

name: sea cucumber
Holothuroidea
329.description: Elongated, soft-bodied echinoderm with a flexible, shell-less body that is usually sausage-, cucumber-, or slug-shaped. It often has leathery or bumpy skin, sometimes with short spines, knobs, papillae, or tentacles at one end. Color varies widely from black and brown to red, orange, cream, or mottled patterns.
329.guidelines: Classify as sea cucumber when the animal is a thick, soft, tubular marine invertebrate lying on the seafloor or tide pools, often with a rough or warted surface and no obvious limbs or hard shell. Do not confuse with sea slugs/nudibranchs, which usually have a flatter body with distinct head structures and dorsal appendages; with sea hares, which show parapodia and head tentacles; or with worms, which are typically more clearly segmented and lack the leathery echinoderm appearance. Sea cucumbers are bulkier, more cucumber-like, and usually have a blunt, fleshy body texture.

name: rabbit
330.description: A small to medium lagomorph with a compact, rounded body, long upright ears, large dark eyes, short forelegs, stronger hind legs, and a short fluffy tail. Fur is typically brown, gray, tan, white, or mixed, often with a soft mottled coat and a pale underside.
330.guidelines: Classify as rabbit when the animal has the typical compact rabbit build, relatively short face, large ears, and short tail, whether wild or domestic. Do not restrict to cottontails only. Exclude Angora rabbits when the coat is extremely long and woolly over most of the body. Distinguish from hares and jackrabbits, which usually have a slimmer body, longer legs, and proportionally longer ears; and from pikas, which have very short ears and no obvious rabbit-like shape.

name: hare
Lepus
331.description: A hare is a rabbit-like mammal with a lean body, very long hind legs, and notably long ears, often with dark tips. It typically has a longer, narrower face and a rangier build than most rabbits. Fur is usually brown, tan, or gray with mottling, though some species turn white in winter.
331.guidelines: Classify as hare when the animal shows the typical Lepus shape: long ears, long powerful legs, a slim body, and a wild, open-country look. This category includes different hare species rather than one single species. Distinguish it from domestic rabbits and cottontails, which are usually stockier, shorter-eared, and shorter-legged. Exclude Angora rabbits and other fancy domestic breeds with unusually fluffy coats. Also avoid confusing hares with pikas, which have short ears and compact bodies.

name: Angora rabbit
Oryctolagus cuniculus domesticus
332.description: A small domestic rabbit with an extremely long, dense, woolly coat that makes the body look round and fluffy. The fur often covers much of the face and cheeks, with upright ears that may have noticeable tassels. Common colors include white, cream, gray, black, and broken patterns, but the defining feature is the abundant soft fiber rather than a specific color.
332.guidelines: Classify as an Angora rabbit when the rabbit has a conspicuously heavy wool coat over most of the body, often forming a puffball shape and facial furnishings. Do not confuse it with Lionhead rabbits, which usually have a mane concentrated around the head but much shorter body fur, or Jersey Wooly/American Fuzzy Lop rabbits, which are smaller specialty breeds and often have different ear carriage. Exclude long-haired cats or small fluffy dogs by checking for rabbit body shape, upright rabbit ears, and the compact lagomorph face.

name: Syrian hamster
Mesocricetus auratus
333.description: A small pet rodent with a compact, round body, short tail, blunt muzzle, small rounded ears, and prominent dark eyes. Its fur is soft and can be short or long, appearing in golden, cream, white, gray, brown, black, or patterned color forms; the underside is often lighter.
333.guidelines: Classify as Syrian hamster when the animal is a stout, round-bodied hamster with a very short tail and relatively broad head, often seen in common pet color morphs including golden and long-haired varieties. Distinguish it from dwarf hamsters, which are smaller and usually show a clearer dark dorsal stripe and a more compact, finer-featured look. Do not confuse it with mice, rats, or gerbils, which have much longer tails and more elongated bodies and faces.

name: porcupine
334.description: A stout, medium-to-large spiny mammal with a rounded body, short legs, a blunt snout, and a coat covered in long, rigid quills. The body is usually brown to blackish, often with white-tipped quills that create a striped or speckled look. Some species are ground-dwelling and heavily built, while others are more arboreal with longer tails, but all show prominent defensive quills as the defining feature.
334.guidelines: Classify as porcupine when the animal is a large rodent covered with long, obvious quills over the back and sides. Do not confuse it with a hedgehog: hedgehogs are much smaller, rounder, and have short, dense spines rather than long quills. Also distinguish from echidnas, which have a longer narrow snout, and from brushy-tailed or dark-furred mammals where the quills are not clearly visible. The key cue is a rodent-like body with conspicuous long quills.

name: fox squirrel
Sciurus niger
335.description: A large tree squirrel with a long bushy tail, a gray to grizzled gray-brown back, and a warm reddish, orange-brown, or buff underside and limbs. The ears are relatively small and usually lack long tufts, and the tail is often fuller and somewhat rusty-edged or mixed gray and orange.
335.guidelines: Classify as fox squirrel when the animal is a robust tree squirrel with a gray/grizzled upper body and noticeably reddish or orange underparts, often with a very bushy tail. Distinguish it from the eastern gray squirrel by the fox squirrel’s larger build, warmer orange-brown belly, and more reddish coloring overall; eastern gray squirrels are usually smaller and more uniformly gray with a white belly. Do not confuse it with red squirrels, which are much smaller and slimmer with shorter tails and stronger rufous coloration, often with ear tufts.

name: marmot
Marmota
336.description: A large, stocky ground squirrel with a chunky body, short sturdy limbs, small rounded ears, and a short bushy tail. Fur is typically brown, gray, tan, or blackish, often with paler or buff underparts and a frosted or grizzled look on the head and back.
336.guidelines: Classify as marmot when the animal is a heavy-bodied ground squirrel with a blunt face, short ears, and a thick, low-slung build, often seen on rocks, meadows, or near burrows. Do not confuse with prairie dogs, which are smaller, more uniformly tan, and usually have shorter tails; groundhogs, which are a single marmot species but typically darker brown and less alpine-looking; or beavers, which have broad flat tails and aquatic features. Squirrels and chipmunks are slimmer, have longer bushier tails, and appear more agile and tree-adapted.

name: North American beaver
Castor canadensis
337.description: A large, stocky semiaquatic rodent with a broad head, small rounded ears, dark eyes, dense brown fur, prominent orange incisors, and a wide, flat, paddle-shaped tail. It is often seen swimming low in the water with only the head and back visible, or sitting on muddy banks near ponds and streams.
337.guidelines: Classify as North American beaver when the animal shows the classic beaver build: chunky body, blunt snout, orange front teeth, and especially a broad flat tail. Do not confuse it with muskrat or nutria, which are smaller and have long, narrow, rat-like tails, or with otters, which have sleeker bodies, longer necks, and furred tails rather than a paddle tail.

name: guinea pig
Cavia porcellus
338.description: A small, compact rodent with a plump, barrel-shaped body, very short legs, a blunt face, small rounded ears, and no visible tail. The coat may be smooth, rough, or long, and comes in many colors and patterns including white, brown, black, tan, gray, and multicolored patches.
338.guidelines: Classify as guinea pig when the animal is a stocky, tailless cavy with a rounded body, short legs, and a short blunt muzzle. This category includes multiple coat types and color varieties. Do not confuse with hamsters, which are smaller with shorter faces and often visible cheek pouches; rats or mice, which have long visible tails and larger ears; rabbits, which have long ears and longer hind legs; or chinchillas, which have larger ears, denser plush fur, and a more upright, fluffy appearance.

name: chestnut horse
Equus ferus caballus
339.description: A horse with a red-based coat ranging from copper, gold, and rust to deep reddish brown or liver chestnut, always lacking cold black undertones. The mane and tail are usually the same reddish tone, but may be lighter golden or flaxen, or somewhat darker while still staying in the brown-burgundy range rather than true black. The legs match the body color unless covered by white markings, and the ears and eyelashes are brown or sorrel rather than black. Many individuals also show pink skin on facial markings, especially around the nose.
339.guidelines: Classify as chestnut horse when the horse has an overall red or reddish-brown coat with no black points: no black mane, no black tail, no black lower legs, and no black ear rims. This separates it from bay horses, which have a reddish body but clearly black mane, tail, and lower legs, and from black or dark brown horses, which lack the warm red cast. Distinguish it from palomino by checking that the body is red/chestnut rather than gold-cream, even if the mane is flaxen. Ignore white facial or leg markings, which can occur in chestnut horses.

name: plains zebra
Equus quagga
340.description: A horse-like African mammal with a short upright mane, long face, and a bold black-and-white striped coat covering the body, neck, and usually much of the legs. The stripe pattern is individual but typically broad and high-contrast, with a stocky to medium build and a tufted tail.
340.guidelines: Classify as plains zebra when the animal is a zebra with the typical broad body stripes of the common African savanna species. Do not confuse it with Grevy's zebra, which has much narrower, denser stripes, larger rounded ears, and a whiter belly, or with mountain zebra, which often has a visible dewlap and a more grid-like rump pattern. Exclude horses, donkeys, or okapis, which may have stripes only on parts of the body or lack the full zebra body pattern.

name: warthog
Phacochoerus africanus
343.description: A sturdy, pig-like African wild hog with a large wedge-shaped head, long curved tusks projecting upward from the snout, rough gray to brown skin, sparse bristly hair, and a coarse mane along the back. The face is broad and flattened with prominent wart-like pads, long pointed ears, thin legs, and a short tail often held upright when running.
343.guidelines: Classify as warthog when the animal shows the distinctive facial warts and large upward-curving tusks of an African wild pig. Do not confuse it with domestic pigs or wild boar, which usually have denser hair, less prominent facial pads, and different head shape. It can also resemble a babirusa, but babirusas have smoother bodies and extremely long tusks that curve back through the snout area rather than the heavy side tusks and warted face seen here.

name: hippopotamus
Hippopotamus amphibius
344.description: A very large semiaquatic mammal with a massive barrel-shaped body, short sturdy legs, and smooth to slightly wrinkled gray-brown skin that often looks shiny when wet. The head is broad and heavy, with small ears, raised eyes, and nostrils set high on the skull for surfacing in water. The mouth is extremely wide and can gape about 150–180 degrees, revealing large tusk-like canines and incisors.
344.guidelines: Classify as hippopotamus when the animal has a bulky hairless body, very short legs, and eyes, ears, and nostrils grouped on top of a broad head, often with most of the body submerged. Distinguish it from rhinoceroses by the lack of horns and from pigs or boars by its much larger size, smoother skin, and aquatic build. Distinguish it from pygmy hippopotamus by the common hippopotamus's much more massive body, broader squarer head, and more strongly top-set eyes and nostrils adapted for living in water.

name: ox
345.description: A large domesticated bovine used as a draft animal, typically shown yoked to plows, carts, or wagons. It has a heavy body, sturdy legs, a broad head, and usually short to medium horns that vary widely by breed; coat color ranges from white and gray to brown or black. Many examples show humped zebu-type cattle or similar working cattle in agricultural settings.
345.guidelines: Classify as ox when the animal is a working bovine used for pulling or plowing, especially when yoked or harnessed. Do not confuse with dairy or beef cattle shown simply grazing, which are not necessarily oxen. Also distinguish from water buffalo: buffalo usually have a bulkier body, broader muzzle, and thicker, more laterally sweeping crescent-shaped horns; oxen more often look like domestic cattle, including zebu-type cattle with a shoulder hump. The key cue is a draft bovine appearance, often in harness or farm work.

name: water buffalo
Bubalus bubalis
346.description: A large, heavy-bodied bovine with dark gray to black skin, sparse hair, and very large laterally spreading horns that curve outward and often upward in a broad crescent. The body is barrel-shaped with a thick neck, long face, and wide muzzle. It is frequently shown standing or wallowing in water, mud, marshes, or wet grassland.
346.guidelines: Classify as water buffalo when the animal is a dark, mostly hairless buffalo with broad crescent-shaped horns and a bulky build, especially in wet or muddy settings. Distinguish it from African buffalo, which usually has a massive horn boss across the forehead and shorter, heavier-curving horns; from gaur, which are taller, more muscular, and typically have pale 'stocking' lower legs; and from domestic cattle or oxen, which generally have slimmer bodies and different horn shapes.

name: American bison
Bison bison
347.description: Large, heavy-bodied wild bovine with a very prominent shoulder hump, oversized head, thick shaggy mane over the head, neck, and forequarters, short upward-curving dark horns, and a comparatively smoother, leaner hindquarters. Coat is usually dark brown to blackish, often with longer hair on the front half of the body.
347.guidelines: Classify as American bison when the animal shows the characteristic tall shoulder hump, massive shaggy front end, large head, and short curved horns. Distinguish it from domestic cattle and bulls, which usually lack the extreme hump and pronounced front-heavy build; from musk ox, which has much longer coat hair hanging low and a different horn shape; and from European bison (wisent), which is typically less hump-backed, less shaggy, and longer-legged with a less massive head.

name: ram
348.description: An adult male sheep, typically recognized by a heavy, muscular body, thick neck, and large curved or spiral horns that sweep outward, backward, or forward beside the head. Domestic rams often have dense woolly fleece and may show ear tags or farm markings, while wild rams usually have shorter, smoother coats and more massive horn curls; some wild forms also show a pale rump patch.
348.guidelines: Classify as ram when the animal is clearly a male sheep with the characteristic thick neck and prominent curved horns. This category includes both domestic and wild male sheep. Do not confuse it with ewes, which are usually smaller-headed, less thick-necked, and often hornless or less heavily horned. Distinguish rams from goats and billy goats by the sheep-like head, lack of a beard, heavier wool or sheep coat, and the usual downward-hanging tail rather than an upright goat tail. Also avoid labeling horned antelopes or ibex as rams: those animals tend to have slimmer faces, different horn shapes, and more goat-like body proportions.

name: bighorn sheep
Ovis canadensis
349.description: A stocky wild sheep with a muscular body, tan to brown coat, pale rump and muzzle, and very large curling horns. Adult males have massive horns that form thick full spirals, while females and young have shorter, slimmer, less curled horns. Often seen on rocky slopes, cliffs, and open mountain terrain.
349.guidelines: Classify as bighorn sheep when the animal has the characteristic heavy, tightly curved ram horns and a robust sheep-like build in rocky mountain habitat. Distinguish it from domestic sheep by its shorter coat and lack of woolliness, and from ibex or mountain goats by the horn shape: bighorn horns curl into broad spirals rather than rising as straighter backward scimitars or short black spikes. Also avoid confusion with antelope or deer, which have branched antlers or much slimmer, non-spiraled horns.

name: ibex
350.description: A wild mountain goat with a sturdy but fairly slim body, short tail, and very large ridged horns that sweep backward in a long arc. Males often have thicker, longer horns and a short beard. Coat color is usually tan, sandy, brown, or gray-brown, sometimes with paler underparts and darker leg markings.
350.guidelines: Classify as ibex when the animal is a goat-like wild caprid with especially long, backward-curving, heavily ridged horns and a mountain-adapted build. Do not confuse with domestic goats, which are more variable and usually less uniformly wild-looking; chamois or gazelles, which have much shorter, slimmer horns; or bighorn sheep, which have thicker horns that curl outward and forward rather than sweeping back in a long arc. If the images mix multiple ibex species, use the broader name ibex rather than a single species name.

name: hartebeest
Alcelaphus buselaphus
351.description: A large, long-faced African antelope with a slim body, long legs, and a noticeably elongated head. The coat is usually tan to reddish-brown, sometimes with darker markings on the face or upper legs. Both sexes have thick, ringed horns that rise upward and curve back in an S-shape or lyre shape.
351.guidelines: Classify as hartebeest when the animal has a very long narrow face and the distinctive high-set, doubly curved horns in both sexes. Do not confuse it with topi or tsessebe, which are stockier and often show stronger dark patches on the shoulders and legs, or with impala and gazelles, which have more slender, simpler horns and shorter faces. Wildebeest are heavier, shaggier, and have a broad head rather than the hartebeest’s long, refined profile.

name: impala
Aepyceros melampus
352.description: A slender, medium-sized antelope with a smooth reddish-tan to chestnut coat, pale underparts, and a white belly. It typically shows distinct black markings on the rump and tail, often with dark stripes on the rear thighs. Males have long, ridged, lyre-shaped horns; females are hornless.
352.guidelines: Classify as impala when the animal is a graceful, lightly built African antelope with a warm tan coat, white underside, and clear black rump/tail markings. Distinguish it from gazelles by the impala’s larger size, richer reddish coat, and the male’s heavier lyre-shaped horns. Distinguish it from springbok by the lack of a bold dark side stripe and dorsal crest, and from deer by the permanent antelope horns rather than branching antlers.

name: springbok
Antidorcas marsupialis
353.description: A small, very slender antelope with long thin legs, a tan to reddish-brown back, bright white underparts, and a bold dark brown side stripe separating the two. The face is pale with dark markings from the eyes toward the muzzle, and many individuals show a white rump area or erect dorsal skin fold. Both sexes may have narrow, black, slightly curved ringed horns.
353.guidelines: Classify as springbok when the animal has the sharp white belly, strong dark flank stripe, pale face with dark facial markings, and slender black ringed horns. Do not confuse it with Thomson's gazelle or Grant's gazelle: those are gazelles but typically lack the springbok's distinctive rump fold and have different facial and flank patterns. Also avoid impala, which is larger, more uniformly reddish, and lacks the bold side stripe and white facial pattern.

name: stoat
Mustela erminea
356.description: A very small, extremely slender mustelid with a long narrow body, short legs, small rounded ears, and a pointed face. Most images show a warm brown back, clean white or pale cream underside, and a relatively long tail with a distinct black tip; in winter some individuals may be nearly all white except for the black tail tip.
356.guidelines: Classify as stoat when the animal is tiny and very thin-bodied, with brown upperparts, white underparts, and especially a black-tipped tail. Do not confuse it with the least weasel, which is smaller and usually lacks the black tail tip, or with mink, martens, and ferrets, which are bulkier, darker, and proportionally less delicate.

name: American mink
Neogale vison
357.description: A small, long-bodied mustelid with short legs, a narrow head, small rounded ears, and a thick tail. The fur is usually dark brown to nearly black, sometimes with a lighter brown tone, and many individuals show a small white patch on the chin or throat. The face is plain and lacks a contrasting mask.
357.guidelines: Classify as American mink when the animal is a sleek, dark, semi-aquatic mustelid with a uniform face and no facial mask. Distinguish it from stoats and weasels by the darker overall coat, stockier build, and lack of a strongly contrasting white belly; from martens and fishers by the smaller ears, lower-slung body, and more uniform dark coat; and from European polecats or black-footed ferrets by the absence of a pale face with dark mask markings.

name: ferret
Mustela furo
358.description: A ferret is a small, long-bodied mustelid with short legs, a slender neck, a pointed muzzle, small rounded ears, and a fairly long tail. The coat is usually dark brown, sable, or blackish with paler underfur, and the face commonly shows a distinct dark mask around the eyes with a lighter forehead and muzzle.
358.guidelines: Classify as ferret when the animal has the typical elongated mustelid body plus a pale face with a dark eye mask, often in sable or dark brown pet-ferret coloration. Do not confuse with European polecat, which is usually wilder-looking, darker, and more uniformly brown; mink, which are sleeker, more uniformly dark, and usually lack the contrasting facial mask; stoats and weasels, which are slimmer with narrower heads and less masked faces; martens, which have bushier tails and often a pale throat bib; or skunks, which have bold white dorsal stripes rather than a facial mask.

name: domestic ferret
Mustela furo
359.description: A small, long-bodied mustelid with short legs, a slender neck, rounded ears, and a pointed muzzle. The coat is typically light cream, tan, sable, or mixed brown-and-white, often with a pale face and darker mask, legs, or tail. These images show pet ferrets in a range of common domestic color patterns.
359.guidelines: Classify as domestic ferret when the animal is a pet ferret with the typical elongated body, short legs, and pale-to-sable coat patterns common in captivity. Do not confuse it with the black-footed ferret, which is usually paler overall with a more distinct black facial mask and black feet, or with mink, martens, and polecats, which are generally darker, less variable in pet-like coloration, and less commonly seen in domestic indoor settings.

name: otter
Lutrinae
360.description: A sleek, semiaquatic mammal with an elongated body, thick neck, short legs, small rounded ears, dense fur, and prominent whiskers. Otters are usually brown to dark brown with a paler throat or face, and they are typically shown swimming, floating, or standing close to water.
360.guidelines: Classify as otter when the animal has a long streamlined body, broad whiskered muzzle, thick tapering tail, and is clearly adapted to life in water. Do not confuse with beavers, which have a wide flat tail and bulkier body; muskrats or nutria, which have smaller heads and rat-like tails; seals or sea lions, which lack visible legs and have flippers; or mink/weasels, which are slimmer, more snake-like, and usually have less broad faces.

name: striped skunk
Mephitis mephitis
361.description: A small, low-bodied mammal with black fur marked by bold white stripes or a broad white mantle running from the head down the back, and a very large, fluffy tail that is usually black mixed with white. The body is stocky with short legs, a pointed snout, and conspicuous contrasting black-and-white coloration.
361.guidelines: Classify as striped skunk when the animal shows the classic black body with distinct white dorsal stripes or a white back patch and an extremely bushy tail. Do not confuse it with other skunks such as hooded or spotted skunks: hooded skunks tend to have more extensive white over the back and tail, while spotted skunks are smaller and show broken stripes or spots rather than broad continuous stripes. Do not use the obsolete term polecat here; true polecats and ferrets have slimmer bodies, less bushy tails, and lack the bold skunk pattern.

name: European badger
Meles meles
362.description: A stocky, low-slung badger with a gray to grizzled body, short legs, and a pointed snout. The head is pale with two bold black stripes running from the nose past the eyes to the ears, creating the species’ most distinctive facial pattern.
362.guidelines: Classify as European badger when the animal has the classic white face with two strong black longitudinal stripes, a broad gray body, and a short tail. Do not confuse it with honey badger, which is black below with a broad pale mantle over the back, or American badger, which is flatter-bodied, sandier, and usually has a single central white facial stripe rather than two bold side stripes. Also exclude skunks and similar mammals that have prominent stripes on the back rather than mainly on the face.

name: orangutan
Pongo
365.description: A large great ape with very long, shaggy reddish-orange to brown hair, extremely long arms, and a dark gray to black bare face. Adults have a heavy body, broad chest, and grasping hands and feet; males may show large cheek pads and a throat sac. Infants are smaller, darker-faced, and cling closely to the mother. Orangutans are usually seen climbing, hanging, or sitting in trees or on the ground.
365.guidelines: Classify as orangutan when the ape has a distinctly reddish shaggy coat, very long arms, and a dark mostly hairless face. Do not confuse with chimpanzees, bonobos, or gorillas, which have darker shorter fur and different body proportions, or gibbons, which are much slimmer and smaller. Avoid naming it specifically as Bornean or Sumatran orangutan unless the image provides reliable species-level cues; for this category, the correct label is the broader orangutan.

name: gorilla
Gorilla gorilla
366.description: A very large, powerfully built ape with a broad chest, long muscular arms, and a dark gray to black coat. The face is mostly hairless and black, with a heavy brow ridge, wide flat nose, and small close-set eyes. Adult males are especially massive and often show a silver-gray saddle across the back.
366.guidelines: Classify as gorilla when the animal is a robust tailless great ape with very heavy build, dark fur, and a broad humanlike face. Do not confuse with chimpanzees or bonobos, which are smaller, slimmer, and have relatively larger ears and less bulky bodies, or with orangutans, which have reddish fur and much longer shaggy hair. Monkeys are excluded by their tails and generally narrower faces.

name: chimpanzee
Pan troglodytes
367.description: A large tailless ape with long arms, a compact muscular body, and dark brown to black fur over most of the body. The face, ears, hands, and feet are mostly bare and usually dark, with a flatter face, forward-facing eyes, and a pronounced brow ridge. Individuals may show lighter skin on the face when young and variable graying with age.
367.guidelines: Classify as a chimpanzee when the animal is a dark-furred great ape with relatively large ears, a bare dark face, and long arms but a slimmer, less heavy build than a gorilla. Distinguish it from bonobos by the chimpanzee’s usually stockier build, broader face, and less uniformly dark, more variable facial appearance; bonobos are typically more slender with longer legs and a finer face. Distinguish it from gorillas by its smaller size, less massive chest and shoulders, and lack of the gorilla’s broad nose and very robust build. Exclude monkeys by the absence of a tail.

name: white-handed gibbon
Hylobates lar
368.description: A small, tailless ape with an extremely slender body, very long arms, and a dark bare face framed by a pale ring of fur. Coat color is variable from cream or buff to brown or black, but the facial ring and long swinging limbs are consistent.
368.guidelines: Classify as white-handed gibbon when the animal is a tailless, long-armed gibbon with a black face encircled by pale fur. Do not confuse it with other monkeys, which usually have tails and shorter arms, or with siamangs, which are bulkier, typically darker overall, and lack the same crisp pale facial ring.

name: siamang
Symphalangus syndactylus
369.description: A large, black-furred gibbon with extremely long arms, a slender body, and a hairless dark face framed by shaggy fur. Adults often show a prominent inflatable throat sac used for calling, and many images show the partly fused toes characteristic of the species.
369.guidelines: Classify as siamang when the ape is a tailless, long-armed gibbon with uniformly black fur and a conspicuously large throat sac. Distinguish it from other gibbons, which are often buff, gray, or two-toned and usually lack such a prominent throat sac. Distinguish it from spider monkeys or other long-limbed monkeys by the absence of a tail and the ape-like face and posture.

name: guenon
Cercopithecini
370.description: A small to medium, slender Old World monkey with a long tail, narrow body, and a vividly patterned face. Typical guenons have a dark face framed by contrasting white cheek whiskers, brow bands, nose spots, or throat patches, with fur ranging from gray and olive to black, chestnut, yellow, or reddish tones.
370.guidelines: Classify as guenon when the monkey is lightly built, long-tailed, and especially shows a striking facial mask or contrasting facial markings. Do not confuse with macaques or baboons, which are heavier-bodied and usually have plainer faces, or with colobus monkeys, which are shaggier and more boldly black-and-white. Unlike mangabeys, guenons usually have more delicate proportions and more intricate face patterns.

name: patas monkey
Erythrocebus patas
371.description: A slim, tall Old World monkey with unusually long legs and a long tail, a reddish to chestnut back, pale underparts, and a pale gray-white face framed by darker markings. It often shows a dark nose and eye area, a white moustache-like muzzle, and a rusty crown.
371.guidelines: Classify as patas monkey when the monkey has a lanky, long-limbed build, reddish upperparts, and a pale face with dark facial markings. Distinguish it from vervet monkeys and grivets, which are grayer or greener and less red-backed; from red colobus, which are shaggier and more heavily built; and from macaques or baboons, which have shorter limb proportions and different facial structure. The very long legs and reddish coat are the key cues.

name: baboon
Papio
372.description: Large, robust Old World monkey with a long dog-like muzzle, close-set forward-facing eyes, and a hairless face. The body is heavy and dog-shaped, with strong limbs, a short tail, and often prominent cheek fur or a mane; coloration ranges from gray to olive, brown, or tan depending on the species and sex.
372.guidelines: Classify as baboon when the animal has a long projecting muzzle, sturdy ground-dwelling build, and a short tail. This category includes different baboon species, so coat color and mane size may vary. Distinguish it from mandrills and drills, which have brighter facial colors and more vividly colored rumps, and from macaques, which usually have shorter muzzles, rounder heads, and less elongated dog-like faces.

name: macaque
Macaca
373.description: Medium-sized Old World monkey with a sturdy body, round face, short muzzle, and prominent cheek pouches. Macaques usually have dense brown, gray, black, or tan fur, a relatively bare face that may be pink or red, and a tail that ranges from very short to fairly long depending on species.
373.guidelines: Classify as macaque when the animal has the typical Macaca build: robust body, rounded head, short snout, bare expressive face, and visible cheek-pouch area. This category includes different macaque species, so coat color and tail length can vary. Do not confuse with baboons, which have much longer dog-like muzzles, or langurs and colobus monkeys, which are slimmer and lack cheek pouches. Also distinguish from apes such as gibbons or orangutans, which have no tails and much longer arms relative to body size.

name: langur
374.description: A slender Old World monkey with a light to dark coat, very long limbs, and a long tail. It typically has a small narrow face, often dark or black, framed by paler fur, with a lean body adapted for climbing and sitting upright.
374.guidelines: Classify as langur when the monkey has a slim build, long legs, and a notably long tail, often with a dark face and pale or contrasting body fur. Do not confuse with macaques, which are stockier with shorter tails and broader faces; colobus monkeys, which are usually more boldly black-and-white with heavier mantle-like fur; or proboscis monkeys, which have a much larger nose and pot-bellied body.
