Do not confuse it with a sheet or bedsheet, which is thinner and flatter; a duvet cover, which is just the removable outer shell; or a blanket/throw, which is usually smaller, less structured, and often shown as a casual covering on a couch or chair. If the image centers on the padded decorative bed cover rather than the whole bed frame or pillows, this category fits.

name: race car
751.description: A motor vehicle built or modified for competitive racing. It is typically low-slung or otherwise performance-focused and often carries racing livery such as large numbers, sponsor logos, bright contrasting paint, aerodynamic parts, roll cages, slick tires, or other track-specific equipment.
751.guidelines: Classify as race car when the vehicle is clearly configured for motorsport use, whether it is an open-wheel formula car, prototype, touring car, stock car, drag car, rally-style car, or a road-car-based racer with numbers and sponsor markings. Do not confuse with ordinary sports cars, supercars, or tuned street cars: those may look fast but usually lack race numbers, sponsor decals, safety equipment, stripped interiors, or track-specific bodywork. Also exclude toy/model cars unless the image is clearly depicting a miniature rather than a real racing vehicle.

name: tennis racket
752.description: A tennis racket is a handheld sports implement with an oval or teardrop-shaped strung head attached to a narrow throat and a straight handle with a grip. It is typically lightweight, with an open string bed and a rigid frame made of wood, metal, graphite, or composite materials.
752.guidelines: Classify as a tennis racket only when the object is the racket used for tennis: a large oval strung head, relatively long handle, and proportions suited for striking a tennis ball. Include modern and wooden rackets, and rackets shown in use, close-up, or partially visible. Do not confuse with badminton rackets, which are slimmer, lighter, and have a smaller head; squash or racquetball rackets, which are usually shorter with different head shapes; or padel/paddle rackets, which have a solid perforated face instead of strings.

name: radiator
753.description: A radiator is a heat-exchange unit with many repeated metal fins, tubes, or sections to increase surface area. In homes it often appears as a freestanding or wall-mounted cast-iron or steel heater with vertical columns or ribbed panels connected to pipes. In vehicles it often appears as a flat rectangular metal core with a dense grid of thin fins, framed edges, and hose inlets/outlets.
753.guidelines: Classify both household heating radiators and vehicle cooling radiators here. Look for a metal structure built around repeated ribs, columns, or finned channels for dissipating heat. Do not confuse with decorative grilles or vents, which lack plumbing connections and heat-exchange cores; with space heaters, which usually include electrical housings or fans; or with generic heat exchangers such as condensers or intercoolers, which may look similar but are typically identified by different installation context and fittings rather than the classic radiator form.

name: radio receiver
754.description: An electronic device for receiving broadcast radio signals, usually shown as a boxy or built-in unit with a tuning display or dial, frequency scale, buttons or knobs, and often a speaker grille or audio controls. It may appear as a portable transistor radio, tabletop radio, car radio, stereo tuner, or other non-transmitting radio set.
754.guidelines: Classify as this category when the main object is a device used to receive AM/FM or similar radio broadcasts. Include portable radios, tabletop sets, car radios, boombox-style radios, and hi-fi tuners if their radio-tuning function is central. Do not confuse with walkie-talkies, CB radios, or ham radios used for two-way communication; those typically have push-to-talk microphones, handsets, keypads for channels, or obvious transceiver equipment. Also exclude speakers, tape decks, amplifiers, and other audio gear that lack a radio tuner or tuning display.

name: radio telescope
755.description: A large steerable parabolic dish antenna used for radio astronomy, typically with a broad bowl-shaped reflector, an open lattice or solid metal surface, and a receiver/feed structure suspended above the dish or mounted near its center. It is usually mounted on a substantial base or tower and often appears singly or in arrays.
755.guidelines: Classify as radio telescope when the image shows a large dish specifically built as an astronomical radio receiver. Key cues are the giant parabolic reflector, central feed support, and heavy observatory-style mounting. Do not confuse with smaller satellite dishes or VSAT antennas, which are usually compact communications equipment on buildings, poles, or homes. Also distinguish from radar antennas, which may have dish shapes but are commonly associated with military, airport, or weather installations and often differ in mounting or enclosed radomes. Large scientific dish arrays and fixed or steerable observatory reflectors belong here.

name: rain barrel
756.description: A rain barrel is a large outdoor water-collection container placed beneath a roof downspout to catch and store rainwater. It is usually a cylindrical plastic drum or barrel, but may also be made of wood, ceramic, or resin, often with a lid and a spigot near the bottom.
756.guidelines: Classify as a rain barrel when the image shows a barrel or tank specifically set up to collect runoff from a gutter or downspout, often beside a house. Common look-alikes include ordinary storage drums, trash cans, and planter barrels. Distinguish it by the connection to a downspout or water diverter, a lidded top for water capture, and often a faucet/spigot for dispensing stored water.

name: motorhome
757.description: A large road vehicle built or converted to include living quarters for travel and camping. It typically has a boxy or bus-like body with windows along the sides, a tall roof, and exterior compartments, and often shows features such as awnings, roof-mounted equipment, sleeping areas, kitchen space, and bathroom facilities.
757.guidelines: Classify as motorhome when the living space is integrated into a self-propelled vehicle. This includes bus-like Class A motorhomes, truck- or van-based Class C models with an over-cab section, and smaller camper-based motorhomes. Do not confuse with a travel trailer or caravan, which is towed and has no driving cab, or with an ordinary van, bus, or truck that lacks clear built-in residential features such as RV windows, vents, hookups, storage bays, or an over-cab sleeping area.

name: fishing reel
758.description: A fishing reel is a compact winding device mounted to a fishing rod, built around a spool that holds fishing line and a handle or crank used to retrieve it. Common forms include spinning, baitcasting, conventional, and fly reels, but all are characterized by a line spool and reel body attached near the rod handle, usually made of metal or composite materials.
758.guidelines: Classify as fishing reel when the image shows the reel component used on a fishing rod for storing and retrieving line. The key cue is a spool of fishing line within a reel housing, often with a crank handle, drag knob, bail arm, or round fly-reel frame. Do not confuse it with the fishing rod itself: the rod is the long flexible pole, while the reel is the smaller mounted mechanism near the grip. Also exclude unrelated reels such as film reels, hose reels, cable reels, or sewing bobbins, which lack rod-mounting hardware and sport-fishing features.

name: reflex camera
759.description: A reflex camera is a still camera with a prominent camera body and a large photographic lens mounted on the front, typically larger and deeper than a compact point-and-shoot. Common examples include SLR and DSLR cameras, often with a pentaprism hump on top, interchangeable lenses, manual controls, and a substantial hand grip; older versions may be boxier or twin-lens designs.
759.guidelines: Classify as reflex camera when the image shows an SLR/DSLR-style camera or another true reflex design, usually with a large lens and a substantial body rather than a slim compact form. Include vintage reflex models such as twin-lens reflex cameras. Do not confuse with point-and-shoot cameras, which are smaller and flatter with retractable lenses; rangefinder cameras, which lack the characteristic reflex body shape and prism hump; or camcorders, which are designed for video and have a side-handheld form.

name: refrigerator
760.description: A tall insulated household appliance for keeping food and drinks cold, typically a boxy cabinet with one or two front doors, smooth metal or plastic exterior panels, and an interior fitted with shelves, drawers, and door bins. Common forms include top-freezer, bottom-freezer, side-by-side, and compact models, usually in white, black, or stainless steel.
760.guidelines: Classify as refrigerator when the main object is a food-cooling cabinet with refrigerated interior storage. It may be shown closed from the outside or open with shelves, drawers, bottles, and other food items visible. Do not confuse with a freezer: freezers are often chest-shaped or consist mainly of frozen-storage compartments without the typical fresh-food door shelves and refrigerator layout. Also exclude cabinets, wardrobes, lockers, and vending machines, which may look similar externally but lack the characteristic refrigerated food-storage interior or appliance features such as door seals, crisper drawers, or ice/water dispensers.

name: remote control
761.description: A handheld electronic controller, typically long and narrow, with many labeled buttons arranged on the front face. Most are rectangular with rounded ends, sized to fit in one hand, and made of plastic in black, gray, white, or silver. Common features include a numeric keypad, directional pad, power button, and other small control keys; some have a small screen or sliding cover.
761.guidelines: Classify as remote control when the object is a handheld device used to operate another device at a distance, usually with a dense array of buttons on one side. Includes TV, stereo, media, universal, and similar remotes. Do not confuse with calculators, telephones, game controllers, or keyboards: calculators usually have a display and arithmetic layout; phones have a handset or dialing form; game controllers have grips, joysticks, or paired control sticks; keyboards are much larger with full key arrays.

name: restaurant
762.description: A place where food and drink are prepared and served to customers, typically shown as dining rooms with tables and chairs, place settings, menus, bars, serving counters, kitchens, or exterior storefronts and signs.
762.guidelines: Classify as restaurant when the image shows a commercial eating establishment or its dining/service spaces, including interiors, patios, kitchens, or recognizable storefronts. Do not confuse with a home dining room, banquet hall, cafeteria, bar, or food stall: restaurants usually have customer seating with table service or a dedicated dining area, restaurant signage/storefronts, menus or place settings, and visible food-service infrastructure.

name: revolver
763.description: A handgun with a short to long barrel and a rotating cylindrical chamber mounted behind the barrel. Typical examples have a metal frame, a visible multi-chamber cylinder, a pronounced grip, and either a modern double-action form or an older single-action “cowboy” style. Finishes are commonly blued, black, silver, or nickel, with wood, plastic, ivory-colored, or rubber grips.
763.guidelines: Classify as revolver when the firearm clearly has a rotating cylinder with multiple chambers. This is the key feature that separates it from semi-automatic pistols, which have a box magazine in the grip and a slide on top instead of a cylinder. It can be confused with old cap-and-ball handguns or toy revolvers, but true revolvers still show the characteristic cylinder-and-barrel layout. Do not require exactly six chambers: some revolvers hold five, seven, or more, so the cylinder matters more than the chamber count.

name: rifle
764.description: A rifle is a long-barreled shoulder firearm, typically with a straight stock, elongated fore-end, and a single barrel extending well beyond the receiver. It is usually held and fired from the shoulder and may appear in bolt-action, lever-action, pump-action, single-shot, or other manual forms; examples often show wooden or synthetic stocks, metal barrels, and sometimes iron sights or scopes.
764.guidelines: Classify as rifle when the object is a general long-barreled shoulder firearm. Include manual-action rifles and other non-assault-rifle long guns commonly recognized as rifles. Do not use this class for assault rifles or clearly automatic/semi-automatic military-style rifles; label those as assault rifle instead. Also avoid confusing rifles with shotguns: rifles usually have a slimmer barrel and rifle-style stock, while shotguns are often identified by shotgun receivers, smoothbore sporting forms, or double barrels. Exclude carbines only if they are clearly in the assault-rifle category; otherwise short rifles still count as rifles.

name: rocking chair
765.description: A chair mounted on two curved rockers so the whole seat and back can swing back and forth. It typically has a high back, a standard chair seat, and armrests, with the curved runners touching the floor instead of fixed legs; materials and styles vary widely from wooden porch rockers to wicker, upholstered, child-sized, and novelty forms.
765.guidelines: Classify as rocking chair only when the chair is built on curved runners for rocking motion. Do not confuse with a glider or swivel recliner, which may move but do not sit on two long curved rockers; with Adirondack or lounge chairs, which have fixed legs; or with benches, swings, and folding camp chairs. The defining cue is a chair-shaped seat mounted on a pair of curved bottom rails designed to rock.

name: rotisserie
766.description: A rotisserie is a cooking setup built around a horizontal rotating spit or multiple rotating spits that hold whole chickens, large cuts of meat, or other food in front of a heat source. It is typically seen as a metal oven, cabinet, or grill with rods, forks, and rows of evenly spaced turning items, often browned and glossy from roasting.
766.guidelines: Classify as rotisserie when the defining feature is the rotating spit-roasting apparatus or food mounted on a turning spit inside or over a heater. Do not confuse it with a standard oven, grill, smoker, or barbecue, which may roast meat but do not prominently use a rotating spit. Also exclude kebab or skewer setups unless they are clearly part of a rotisserie-style turning mechanism.

name: eraser
767.description: A small stationery item made of soft rubber or vinyl for removing pencil marks. It is usually a simple block, wedge, or rounded cap, often pink, white, or brightly colored, and may appear as a standalone block eraser, a novelty-shaped eraser, or an eraser attached to the end of a pencil.
767.guidelines: Classify as an eraser when the object’s primary function is rubbing out pencil writing. Include both separate block erasers and pencil-top or pencil-end erasers. Do not confuse with crayons, chalk, markers, or candy: erasers typically have a soft matte rubbery look, blunt edges, and are shown with pencils or pencil shavings. If the object is mainly a pencil with only a small eraser attached, it still belongs here when the eraser end is the visual focus.

name: rugby ball
768.description: An oval ball with a prolate-spheroid shape, pointed ends, and a stitched or paneled outer surface, typically leather or synthetic. It is usually white or patterned with colored panels, stripes, logos, or brand markings, and is the standard ball used in rugby.
768.guidelines: Classify as a rugby ball when the ball is oval with rounded pointed ends and the typical rugby-panel construction. Do not confuse it with an American football, which is usually darker brown, has more elongated sharp ends, and commonly shows prominent laces; or with an Australian rules football, which is also oval but is often bulkier and differently paneled. Ignore whether the ball appears in rugby play, since similar oval balls can appear in other sports or posed product shots.

name: ruler
769.description: A ruler is a straight measuring tool, usually a long narrow strip of plastic, wood, or metal, marked with evenly spaced units such as centimeters, millimeters, or inches along one or both edges. It is typically rigid and rectangular, though some examples may be slightly transparent or decorative.
769.guidelines: Classify as ruler when the object is primarily a straight, rigid measuring stick with printed measurement graduations. Include common school and drafting rulers made of plastic, wood, or metal. Do not confuse with tape measures or sewing tapes, which are flexible and coil or bend; meter sticks, which are much longer full-length measuring rods; or set squares and protractors, which are primarily triangular or curved angle-measuring tools rather than simple straight rulers.

name: sneaker
770.description: A low-top athletic shoe with a flexible rubber sole, lace-up closure, and an upper made from leather, mesh, knit, or synthetic panels. Typical examples have cushioned midsoles, textured tread, padded collars, and sporty branding or color accents; they may be designed for running, training, or everyday casual wear.
770.guidelines: Classify as sneaker when the shoe is a general athletic or casual sports shoe with a rubber sole and sporty construction. Include running-style and training-style sneakers. Do not confuse with dress shoes or loafers (harder, formal uppers), boots (higher ankle coverage), sandals (open construction), soccer or baseball cleats (studs/spikes), track spikes (very thin racing sole with forefoot spikes), or hiking boots/shoes (heavier, more rugged outdoor build). Basketball shoes are often higher-cut and bulkier around the ankle; skate shoes are usually flatter and wider with less pronounced cushioning.

name: safe
771.description: A safe is a strong, rigid lockable storage box or cabinet, usually made of thick metal. It is typically box-shaped with a heavy hinged door and a locking mechanism such as a key lock, combination dial, electronic keypad, handle, or locking bolts. Safes range from small home lockboxes to large freestanding or built-in vault-style cabinets.
771.guidelines: Classify as safe when the object is a heavy security container designed to protect valuables, documents, or money from theft or fire. Look for a thick metal body, reinforced door, and secure locking hardware. Do not confuse it with lockers, filing cabinets, wardrobes, or ordinary cabinets, which have thinner construction and are meant for general storage rather than security. Bank vault doors and vault rooms are related but much larger architectural structures; lockboxes and cash boxes are usually smaller and lighter than the safes shown here.

name: safety pin
772.description: A safety pin is a small metal fastening pin made from a single piece of wire bent into a loop with a coiled spring at one end and a pointed tip that snaps into a protective clasp at the other. It is usually silver-colored, though it may be painted, enlarged, or used decoratively.
772.guidelines: Classify as safety pin when the object has the characteristic spring coil, sharp pin shaft, and closed guard/clasp that covers the tip. Include ordinary, oversized, decorative, or jewelry-use examples as long as the basic safety-pin structure is present. Do not confuse with a straight pin or sewing pin, which lacks the clasp and spring coil; a brooch or kilt pin, which is decorative but typically has a different hinged catch; or a paper clip, which has no sharp point or locking clasp.

name: salt shaker
773.description: A small tabletop container for dispensing salt, typically with a perforated metal, plastic, or ceramic top. It is usually bottle-, vase-, or cylinder-shaped, made of glass, ceramic, metal, or plastic, and often filled with visible white salt crystals.
773.guidelines: Classify as a salt shaker when the object is a small salt dispenser with multiple holes in the top for shaking out salt. It may appear alone or as part of a salt-and-pepper set. Do not confuse it with a pepper shaker or pepper pot, which is often similar in shape but may have different hole patterns, labels, or darker contents. Exclude larger salt canisters, salt boxes, and grinders/mills, which dispense by pouring or grinding rather than shaking through a perforated lid.

name: sandal
774.description: An open shoe with most of the foot exposed, typically featuring a sole secured by one or more straps across the toes, instep, ankle, or heel. Sandals are usually open-toe and open-heel, and may be flat, platform, or heeled.
774.guidelines: Classify as sandal when the footwear is primarily open and held on by straps or a minimal upper, leaving the toes and much of the foot visible. Includes flat sandals, dress sandals, heeled sandals, slides, and children's strap sandals. Do not confuse with flip-flops or thongs, which are a narrower subtype defined by a Y-shaped toe post between the first two toes; use sandal only when the broader category is intended. Exclude pumps, loafers, and slippers, which have more enclosed uppers, and clogs or mules when the upper covers most of the forefoot rather than using open straps.

name: sarong
775.description: A sarong is a lightweight rectangular piece of fabric wrapped around the waist, hips, or body. It is usually worn as a tube skirt, tied at the side or front, or draped as a simple wrap, and commonly appears in bright colors, stripes, batik, floral prints, or other bold patterns.
775.guidelines: Classify as sarong when the garment is a single wrapped cloth rather than a tailored skirt or dress. Common look-alikes include lungi, pareo, and lavalava; these are very similar regional wrap garments, so use sarong for the broad wrapped-cloth style shown here. Do not confuse with a sari, which is much longer and draped over the shoulder, or with ordinary skirts, which are sewn garments with a fixed waistband and shape.

name: saxophone
776.description: A brass woodwind instrument with a long conical tube, a flared bell, a single-reed mouthpiece, and many pearl-topped keys along the body. Most examples show the common curved form with an S-like neck and downward bell, though some saxophones can be straighter, especially soprano models.
776.guidelines: Classify as saxophone when the instrument has a single-reed mouthpiece, dense keywork, and a wide flared bell, usually on a curved metal body. Do not confuse it with a clarinet or oboe, which are slimmer, usually straighter, and lack the large saxophone bell; or with brass instruments such as trumpets, tubas, and horns, which use cup mouthpieces rather than a reed. Straight soprano saxophones still count if they have saxophone-style keywork and bell shape.

name: scabbard
777.description: A scabbard is a protective sheath or holding pouch made to carry a bladed weapon such as a sword, dagger, knife, or bayonet. It is usually long and narrow, shaped to fit the blade, and may be made of leather, metal, wood, or synthetic materials, often with straps, fittings, or a belt attachment.
777.guidelines: Annotate as scabbard when the object is the sheath itself for a blade, or when an attached sheath clearly has the long, blade-matching form of a sword, dagger, knife, or bayonet cover. Do not confuse with a holster, which is shaped for a firearm rather than a blade. Also exclude the blade itself unless the sheath/scabbard is present and is the target object.

name: weighing scale
778.description: A device used to measure weight, shown in many forms including analog dial scales, digital electronic scales, platform scales, hanging scales, shop scales, bathroom scales, baby scales, and two-pan balance scales. It typically has a flat platform, tray, pan, or suspended hook for the item or person being weighed, together with a dial, pointer, numbered face, digital display, or balancing pans that indicate the measured weight.
778.guidelines: Classify as this category when the main object is a weighing device for measuring mass or weight, whether mechanical or electronic. Include bathroom scales, kitchen and market scales, industrial platform scales, hanging scales, infant scales, and equal-arm balances. Do not confuse with clocks, gauges, meters, or cash registers that may also have dials or displays; a weighing scale always has a weighing surface, pan, tray, hook, or paired balance pans. Distinguish from laboratory instruments or other measuring devices by the clear presence of a weight-measuring mechanism and load-bearing platform or pans.

name: school bus
779.description: A school bus is a bus built for transporting students, typically painted bright yellow or yellow-orange and marked with the words “SCHOOL BUS.” It usually has a tall, boxy body, large rectangular side windows, black trim or horizontal rub rails, and red and amber warning lights at the front and rear; many also have a stop sign arm.
779.guidelines: Classify as a school bus when the vehicle is specifically designed or marked for student transport, especially with the characteristic yellow color and “SCHOOL BUS” signage. Do not confuse it with city transit buses, which are usually not yellow and often have route displays and larger passenger doors; coach buses, which are longer, smoother, and luggage-oriented; or ordinary minibuses/vans, which lack the standard school-bus markings and warning lights. Double-decker buses are not school buses unless they are clearly marked and used as such.

name: schooner
780.description: A schooner is a sailing vessel with at least two masts, typically with the foremast shorter than or about equal in height to the mainmast. Its sails are predominantly fore-and-aft rigged, running lengthwise along the hull, giving it a long, streamlined sail plan; some schooners may also carry square topsails on one or more masts.
780.guidelines: Classify as a schooner when the vessel has two or more masts and the principal sails are fore-and-aft rigged rather than mainly square-rigged. Common look-alikes include ketches and yawls, which usually have a much smaller rear mizzen mast behind the mainmast, unlike a schooner’s two substantial masts; brigs, brigantines, and barques, which emphasize square sails across the masts; and sloops or cutters, which usually have only one mast. Use the multi-mast layout plus the lengthwise sail arrangement as the key cue.

name: scoreboard
781.description: A scoreboard is a large, usually rectangular display panel used at sports venues or competitions to show scores, time, team names, innings/periods, counts, and other game information. It is typically divided into labeled sections and features bold numbers, letters, lights, or electronic screens that can be read from a distance.
781.guidelines: Classify as scoreboard when the main subject is a dedicated display for game or match information such as score, clock, teams, innings, balls/strikes/outs, downs, or player stats. It may be mechanical, painted, LED, or video-based, and is often mounted in a stadium, gym, or arena. Do not confuse with a general digital sign, billboard, jumbotron used mainly for ads or video, or a timing/results board not tied to a sporting event. The key cue is a structured layout for live game information with labeled scoring fields.

name: cathode-ray tube display
CRT display
782.description: A bulky old-style electronic display that uses a cathode-ray tube, with a deep boxy cabinet and a curved glass screen. The front face is usually nearly square or slightly rectangular, often surrounded by a thick plastic bezel, and the unit extends far backward compared with flat-panel screens. Examples may appear as computer monitors or television sets, but the defining feature is the protruding CRT form rather than a thin flat display.
782.guidelines: Classify as this category only when the display is clearly a CRT: look for a thick, heavy body, deep rear housing, and a curved or recessed glass screen. Include both CRT computer monitors and CRT televisions when the CRT display itself is the target. Do not confuse with LCD or other flat-panel monitors, which are thin and flat, or with generic televisions where the screen technology is not visibly CRT. If a TV is shown, the CRT display should still be identifiable by its bulky tube-based shape.

name: screw
783.description: A screw is a metal fastener with a long cylindrical shank and an արտաքին helical thread, typically with a pointed or blunt tip and a shaped head for driving by a screwdriver, hex driver, or similar tool. Common head forms include flat, pan, round, countersunk, and hex heads, and screws may be fully or partially threaded.
783.guidelines: Classify as a screw when the object is a threaded fastener designed to be driven by turning its head or body into material or into a threaded hole. Include common varieties such as wood screws, machine screws, self-tapping screws, and sheet-metal screws. Do not confuse with nails, which are smooth-shanked and hammered rather than threaded; bolts, which are usually blunter, more uniformly machine-threaded fasteners intended to be used with a nut; studs, which are headless threaded rods; or rivets, which lack helical threads.

name: screwdriver
784.description: A hand tool with a straight metal shaft ending in a shaped tip for turning screws, attached to a handle made of plastic, wood, or rubber. Common forms include flat-head and Phillips screwdrivers; they are typically slender, rod-like tools designed to be gripped in one hand.
784.guidelines: Classify as screwdriver when the object is a handheld screw-turning tool with a distinct handle, metal shank, and screw-driving tip. Include common variants such as flat-head, Phillips, stubby, precision, and insulated screwdrivers. Do not confuse with awls, picks, chisels, or punches, which may have pointed or blade-like ends but are not meant to engage screw heads; or with drill bits and powered drivers, which are attachments or machines rather than standalone hand tools. The key cue is a manual tool whose tip matches screw slots or recesses.

name: seat belt
785.description: A vehicle safety restraint consisting of a wide woven fabric strap anchored to the car interior, typically running diagonally across a passenger’s chest and lap or shown with its buckle, latch plate, or retractor hardware. It is usually dark gray, black, or tan and appears attached to a car seat or pillar.
785.guidelines: Classify as seat belt when the main object is the built-in passenger restraint strap or its buckle hardware inside a vehicle. Include images showing the belt worn across a person, hanging beside a seat, or buckled across a car seat. Do not confuse with a harness or racing harness, which uses multiple straps and specialized anchor points; a child car seat, which is the whole seat rather than the vehicle belt; or a strap/bandolier/bag strap, which is not mounted as a car restraint. The key cues are the automotive setting, single broad webbing strap, and metal latch plate or buckle receiver.

name: sewing machine
786.description: A sewing machine is a device for stitching fabric and other flexible materials with thread. It typically has a flat base or work surface, a vertical arm with a needle mechanism, a presser foot, thread guides and tension controls, and often a handwheel, motor housing, or foot treadle. Examples include both antique cast-iron treadle machines and modern electric tabletop models.
786.guidelines: Classify as sewing machine when the image shows a machine specifically built to sew using a needle-and-thread mechanism, usually with a needle area above a small platform for fabric. Common look-alikes include sergers/overlock machines, embroidery machines, and toy sewing machines; true sewing machines usually have a single main needle area and a conventional flat sewing bed rather than multiple cone threads or large computerized embroidery attachments. Do not confuse with typewriters, looms, or other tabletop machines that lack the characteristic needle, presser foot, and fabric feed area.

name: shield
787.description: A shield is a handheld protective panel for defense, typically rigid and broad enough to cover part of the body. It is usually round, oval, kite-shaped, heater-shaped, or rectangular, and often made of wood or metal with a central boss, rim, straps, or a rear handle. Many examples bear painted heraldic designs, crosses, emblems, or other decorative motifs, but the object still has the recognizable size, form, and construction of a shield.
787.guidelines: Classify as shield when the object is a portable defensive panel with clear shield-like proportions and a handle, arm straps, or obvious mounting for holding. Include ceremonial or decorative shields if they retain the standard shield form. Do not confuse with coats of arms or heraldic plaques, which are flat symbols or signs shaped like shields but not actual defensive objects; with armor plates, which are worn on the body; or with round wall plaques, trays, or signs that lack functional grip or shield construction. Bucklers are small round shields and still belong here.

name: shoe store
788.description: A retail shop primarily devoted to selling footwear. Typical images show store interiors or storefronts with many shoes displayed on shelves, walls, racks, or tables, often organized by style or size; customers may be trying on shoes or sitting in fitting areas.
788.guidelines: Classify as shoe store when the scene is clearly a retail environment centered on footwear sales, with shoes as the dominant merchandise. Include both interior aisles and exterior storefront views. Do not confuse with a general clothing store or department store unless the image is specifically focused on the shoe-selling section. Exclude single shoes, shoe closets, factory storage, repair shops, or market stalls where the setting is not clearly a dedicated retail shoe shop.

name: shoji
789.description: Traditional Japanese sliding doors, windows, or room screens made from a thin wooden lattice frame covered with translucent paper or similar translucent panels. They appear as light rectangular grids, often in natural wood or dark frames, and are used as partitions, doors, or freestanding folding screens.
789.guidelines: Classify as shoji when the defining feature is a Japanese-style grid frame with translucent paper-like infill, usually softening light rather than allowing a clear view. Distinguish from glass-paned doors and windows, which have transparent glass and heavier Western-style muntins; from blinds or curtains, which are fabric or slatted coverings without a paper lattice panel; and from plain room dividers, which may fold but lack the characteristic Japanese wooden grid and translucent surface.

name: basket
790.description: A basket is an open container used for carrying or holding items, typically with a wide opening and often one or two handles. It may be woven from wicker, cane, reeds, or plastic strips, or made from wire mesh or molded plastic. Common forms include rounded, oval, or rectangular bodies with low to medium-height sides.
790.guidelines: Classify any portable open basket here, including wicker hand baskets, woven market baskets, plastic shopping baskets, and wire carry baskets. The key cue is an open-top carrying container with a basket-like body. Do not confuse it with a hamper, which is usually larger, deeper, and intended for laundry or storage rather than hand-carrying; if it is specifically a wicker basket, keep it here rather than labeling it as a hamper. Also exclude shopping carts/trolleys, bins, buckets, and suitcases: carts have wheels and a push frame, bins are usually not meant to be carried by hand, and buckets are deeper cylindrical containers.

name: shopping cart
791.description: A wheeled retail cart with a large open wire or metal basket, a push handle at the rear, and usually four swivel or caster wheels beneath a metal frame. Common forms include nested supermarket trolleys and smaller basket-style carts, typically made of metal with plastic handle or child-seat details.
791.guidelines: Classify as shopping cart when the image shows a push cart used for carrying goods in a store or parking lot. Key cues are the large basket mounted on a wheeled base and a rear handle for pushing. Do not confuse with a shopping basket, which is hand-carried and has no full cart frame; a utility wagon or garden cart, which usually has solid sides or a different load bed; or a luggage trolley/hand truck, which is built for transporting baggage rather than store items and lacks the typical supermarket basket design.

name: shovel
792.description: A shovel is a hand tool with a long handle and a broad scooping blade, usually metal or rigid plastic, used to lift and move loose material. The blade may be rounded, pointed, square, or wide and deep depending on use, including digging earth or scooping snow.
792.guidelines: Classify as shovel when the object’s main feature is a scoop-like blade for lifting or moving material. This includes digging shovels, square shovels, and snow shovels. Do not confuse with a spade, which is often flatter and straighter-edged for cutting soil, or with a trowel, which is much smaller and hand-sized. Exclude rakes, hoes, pitchforks, and other long-handled garden tools that lack a scooping blade.

name: shower cap
793.description: A shower cap is a lightweight waterproof or water-resistant cap worn over the hair. It typically has a loose, rounded dome made of thin plastic, vinyl, or fabric-lined material, with an elastic edge that gathers around the head. Common appearances include plain translucent caps, solid colors, and patterned or decorative versions with ruffled edges.
793.guidelines: Classify as shower cap when the item is a loose protective cap designed to cover hair during bathing or similar use, usually with a gathered elastic rim and puffed dome. Do not confuse it with a surgical cap or bouffant cap, which are usually plainer and associated with medical or industrial settings; a swim cap, which fits tightly and smoothly to the head; or a chef's hat, which is taller and structured. Decorative novelty bath caps still count if they keep the same elasticized hair-covering form.

name: shower curtain
794.description: A shower curtain is a hanging waterproof or water-resistant panel used to enclose a bathtub or shower area. It is typically a rectangular sheet of plastic, vinyl, polyester, or fabric suspended from rings or hooks on a rod, and may be plain, translucent, opaque, or decorated with printed patterns, pictures, or textured designs.
794.guidelines: Classify as shower curtain when the image shows a curtain hung on a shower or bathtub rod, usually draping vertically and spanning the bathing area. It may be inside the tub as a liner or be a decorative outer curtain. Do not confuse it with window curtains or drapes, which hang over windows; door curtains or room dividers, which are not associated with a tub or shower; or ordinary sheets/tarps being held up without shower hardware. Bathroom context, curtain rings/hooks, and placement around a tub or shower stall are the strongest cues.

name: ski
795.description: A ski is a long, narrow board worn on the foot for traveling or gliding over snow. It is typically elongated and slightly upturned at the front, with a smooth running surface underneath and a binding mounted near the middle for attaching a boot. Skis may appear singly or as a pair and include cross-country skis and touring skis, which are generally slimmer and lighter than many downhill skis.
795.guidelines: Classify as ski when the object is an individual snow-travel board with a long narrow shape, pointed or rounded tip, and a boot binding. Include cross-country, touring, and similar snow skis. Do not confuse with snowboards, which are much wider single boards without a separated left/right pair; ski poles, which are thin sticks with handles and baskets; or water skis, which are used on water rather than snow. If a person is shown, the target object is the long board attached to each foot, not the boots or poles.

name: balaclava
796.description: A close-fitting knit face covering that covers most or all of the head, neck, and face, with openings for the eyes and sometimes the nose or mouth. It is typically made of wool or synthetic knit fabric and may appear as a full-face or half-face style, often worn alone or with ski goggles in cold weather.
796.guidelines: Classify as balaclava when the item is a tight hood-like face covering integrated over the head and neck, with built-in facial openings. Do not confuse it with a beanie or watch cap (covers the head but not the face), a scarf or neck gaiter pulled up over the mouth (not a full hood), or a generic ski mask/goggle setup where the face covering is not visible as a separate knit hood. Includes both full and partial balaclavas, even when paired with helmets or goggles.

name: sleeping bag
797.description: A sleeping bag is an insulated portable bed covering, usually a long padded sack sized for one person, with a zipper opening and often a hooded top. It is typically quilted or puffy, rectangular or mummy-shaped, and made of fabric filled for warmth.
797.guidelines: Classify as sleeping bag when the main object is a padded enclosed sack for sleeping, designed to wrap around a person lying down. Common variations include rectangular and mummy bags, with or without a hood. Do not confuse it with a blanket or quilt, which is flat and open on all sides; a bed comforter or duvet, which is household bedding rather than a portable enclosed sack; or a bivy sack/tent, which forms an outer shelter rather than the insulated inner sleeping covering itself.

name: slide rule
798.description: A slide rule is a long calculating instrument, usually straight and ruler-like, with one or more logarithmic scales printed on a fixed body and a movable central strip, often used with a transparent sliding cursor. Common versions are rectangular and made of wood, plastic, or metal, though circular and other specialized forms also exist.
798.guidelines: Classify as slide rule when the object is a manual analog calculator with printed numerical scales and a sliding strip or rotating scale arrangement. Include standard linear slide rules, circular slide rules, and large demonstration versions. Do not confuse with an ordinary ruler or measuring stick, which has simple linear units only and no calculator scales; with a caliper, which measures dimensions with jaws; or with a straightedge or drafting scale, which lacks the movable slide/cursor and dense logarithmic markings.

name: sliding door
799.description: A door made of one or more panels that open by sliding sideways along a track rather than swinging on hinges. It is often large and rectangular, commonly built with glass, wood, metal, or composite panels, and may appear as patio doors, closet doors, room dividers, vehicle side doors, or automatic entrance doors.
799.guidelines: Classify as sliding door when the door panel clearly moves laterally along rails or tracks. Include framed glass patio doors, bypass closet doors, shoji-style sliding panels, automatic storefront doors, and sliding vehicle doors. Do not confuse with hinged doors that swing outward or inward, folding doors with multiple hinged sections, revolving doors, or fixed windows. Key cues are parallel sliding panels, track-guided motion, and overlap or side-pocketing rather than a visible hinge side and swing arc.

name: snorkeler
801.description: A person in the water wearing snorkeling gear, typically a swim mask and a curved breathing tube that rises above the face. Often shown floating face-down at the surface or just below it, sometimes with fins, swimwear, or a flotation aid. The key visual cue is the visible snorkel tube attached to or beside the mask.
801.guidelines: Classify as snorkeler when the main subject is a person using a snorkel mask-and-tube setup in or at the water. Do not confuse with scuba diver: scuba images usually show an air tank, regulator, and heavier dive gear. Do not confuse with swimmer or goggled swimmer: those lack the external snorkel tube and full snorkeling mask. If the image mainly shows the tube or equipment alone rather than a person using it, it is not this category.

name: snowmobile
802.description: A motorized winter vehicle designed to travel over snow, typically with two narrow steering skis at the front, a single wide continuous track at the rear, a saddle-style seat, handlebars, and broad footrests or running boards along the sides. It usually has an enclosed front cowl and windshield and is ridden by one or more people seated astride.
802.guidelines: Classify as snowmobile when the vehicle clearly has the snow-going layout of two front skis plus a rear track. Do not confuse it with an ATV or motorcycle, which use wheels instead of skis and track; a sled or toboggan, which is not motorized; or tracked snow groomers and snowcats, which are much larger utility vehicles with cabin-like bodies. Small racing, touring, utility, and vintage models all count as snowmobiles as long as the basic ski-and-track configuration is present.

name: snowplow
803.description: A snowplow is a vehicle or vehicle-mounted machine used to remove snow and ice from roads, railways, parking lots, and other paved or cleared surfaces. It is typically identified by a large front-mounted plow blade, wedge, or angled shovel that pushes snow aside; some examples are trucks, tractors, loaders, trains, or small utility vehicles fitted with this equipment.
803.guidelines: Classify as snowplow when the defining feature is a vehicle equipped with a prominent snow-clearing blade or plow attachment intended to push snow. Include road plows, rail snowplows, tractor-mounted plows, and small utility plows. Do not confuse with snow blowers or snow throwers, which use an auger and chute to lift and discharge snow, or with ordinary trucks, tractors, bulldozers, or loaders that lack a dedicated snowplow blade. The key cue is the broad plow implement mounted at the front (sometimes also side or rear) for pushing snow aside rather than scooping or blowing it.

name: soap dispenser
804.description: A container or wall-mounted unit that holds liquid soap and dispenses it in measured amounts through a pump, push lever, sensor, or nozzle. It may be a refillable bottle, a decorative countertop vessel, or a fixed bathroom dispenser, but the defining feature is a soap reservoir with a dispensing mechanism.
804.guidelines: Classify as soap dispenser when the object is specifically designed to store and dispense soap, usually liquid soap. Include countertop pump bottles, wall-mounted bathroom units, and automatic soap dispensers. Do not confuse with lotion dispensers, shampoo bottles, sanitizer dispensers, or generic pump bottles unless they are clearly intended for soap. A soap dispenser is identified by its pump/nozzle and soap container form, often placed by sinks or labeled for soap.

name: soccer ball
association football
805.description: A round football used for soccer, typically made of stitched or molded polygon panels, most often a pattern of pentagons and hexagons. It is usually white with black or colored panels, though many modern designs use varied colors and graphics.
805.guidelines: Classify as this category when the object is a standard soccer/association-football ball: a spherical ball with the familiar paneled construction used in soccer. Do not confuse with volleyballs (fewer curved panels, smoother look), basketballs (orange with black channel lines), baseballs/softballs (much smaller with visible seam stitching), or American footballs/rugby balls (oval, not spherical). Futsal balls look very similar and are generally acceptable only if they are clearly soccer-style balls rather than another sport's ball.

name: sock
806.description: A soft foot covering made of knit or woven fabric that fits over the foot and usually extends to the ankle, calf, or knee. Socks are typically close-fitting and tubular, with a shaped heel and toe; they may be plain or patterned, thick or thin, and can appear alone or worn on a person.
806.guidelines: Classify any single sock, regardless of length, color, pattern, or whether it is being worn or laid flat. Annotate each sock separately rather than labeling a matching pair as one item. Do not confuse socks with stockings or tights, which are thinner and extend much higher up the leg, or with slippers/shoes, which have thicker structured soles. Leg warmers are open-ended tubes without a defined foot section, unlike socks.

name: solar collector
807.description: Devices designed to capture sunlight for energy use, including flat photovoltaic panel arrays, evacuated-tube solar water heaters, and reflective parabolic dishes or mirror assemblies. They typically appear as dark blue or black rectangular panels, rows of glass vacuum tubes connected to a storage tank, or shiny concave circular mirrors aimed toward the sun or a focal point.
807.guidelines: Classify images here when the main subject is equipment for collecting solar energy, whether photovoltaic, solar-thermal, or concentrating solar devices. Include solar panel installations, evacuated-tube collectors, and parabolic solar dishes. Do not confuse with satellite dishes or radio telescopes, which are communication equipment rather than solar devices; those usually lack photovoltaic cells, absorber tubes, or obvious solar-heating/concentrating context. Also exclude ordinary skylights, windows, or generic roof glass panels that are not clearly solar-energy hardware.

name: sombrero
808.description: A broad-brimmed hat with a high, usually pointed or rounded conical crown and an extra-wide circular brim. Commonly made of woven straw or felt, often light tan, but also seen in brightly colored or embroidered decorative versions.
808.guidelines: Classify as sombrero when the hat has the characteristic very wide brim and tall conical crown associated with Mexican-style sombreros. Do not confuse it with other wide-brim hats such as sun hats, cowboy hats, or straw hats: sun hats usually have a softer, flatter crown; cowboy hats have upturned side brims and a creased crown; ordinary straw hats typically have a much narrower brim and lower crown.

name: soup bowl
809.description: A soup bowl is a deep, round bowl-shaped dish with a broad open top and curved sides, designed to hold liquid foods such as soup or broth. It is typically deeper than a plate or pasta dish and may be plain or decorated, with ceramic, porcelain, glass, or similar materials common.
809.guidelines: Classify as a soup bowl when the main object is a deep round bowl intended for serving soup or other liquid dishes, whether empty or filled. Do not confuse it with a plate or shallow soup plate, which has a much flatter profile, or with a mug, cup, or ramekin, which are smaller and usually have handles or straighter sides. If the image mainly depicts the food rather than the vessel, use this class only when the bowl itself is still clearly the central object.

name: space bar
810.description: The long horizontal key on a keyboard or typewriter, usually positioned along the bottom row and noticeably wider than the surrounding keys. It is typically rectangular, plain, and unmarked or minimally marked, spanning a substantial portion of the keyboard's width.
810.guidelines: Classify this as a space bar only when the image focuses on the long bottom-row key itself, not just any keyboard. Distinguish it from other large keys such as the Enter key, Shift key, Tab key, or laptop palm rest: the space bar is characteristically the longest horizontal key and sits centrally along the bottom edge of the key layout. Do not use this label for entire keyboards, typewriters, or touchpads unless the space bar is the clear target.

name: space heater
811.description: A portable room-heating appliance designed to warm a small indoor area. It is typically a compact freestanding unit with a metal or plastic body, vents or a protective grille, and visible heating elements, radiator fins, ceramic panels, quartz tubes, or fan outlets. Common forms include tower heaters, box heaters, oil-filled radiators, and small radiant heaters.
811.guidelines: Classify as space heater when the main object is a portable appliance meant to heat a room or personal area. It may have glowing heating elements, radiator-style fins, a front mesh grille, or heater controls on top or front. Do not confuse with electric fans or air purifiers, which have airflow grilles but no heating elements or radiator body; radiators built into a building, which are fixed installations; fireplaces or stoves, which are larger permanent heating fixtures; or air conditioners/dehumidifiers, which are room-climate appliances but not dedicated portable heaters.

name: Space Shuttle orbiter
812.description: A reusable crewed spacecraft with a blunt rounded nose, black heat-shield underside, delta wings, and a tall vertical tail, typically white above with black cockpit windows and black leading-edge panels. It is often shown attached to a large orange external tank and two white solid rocket boosters during launch, or mounted on a carrier aircraft, displayed in museums, or landing like an unpowered glider.
812.guidelines: Classify as a space shuttle when the image shows the NASA Space Shuttle-style orbiter itself, whether flying alone, landing, on display, or attached to its tank and boosters. Distinguish it from generic rockets or launch vehicles, which lack airplane-like wings and tail; from the Soviet Buran, which is very similar but is a different named spacecraft; and from ordinary airplanes, which have jet engines and do not have the shuttle's black thermal-protection pattern, payload-bay fuselage, or launch stack with external tank and twin boosters.

name: spatula
813.description: A handheld kitchen utensil with a long handle and a broad flat working end, usually metal, wood, silicone, or plastic. The head may be solid, flexible, or slotted, and is used for lifting, turning, scraping, or spreading food.
813.guidelines: Classify as spatula when the utensil has a handle and a flat blade or paddle-like head for flipping or scraping food. Include turners, rubber/silicone spatulas, and similar kitchen spatulas shown in common usage. Do not confuse with a spoon or ladle (bowl-shaped head), whisk (wire loops), tongs (two gripping arms), or scraper/squeegee tools without the typical kitchen spatula form.

name: speedboat
814.description: A small, fast motorboat with a long pointed bow, a narrow low-profile hull, and a powerful engine mounted at the stern or enclosed in the rear. It is typically designed to plane across the water at high speed, often throwing spray or a wake. This category includes both classic recreational speedboats and low-slung racing speedboats.
814.guidelines: Classify as speedboat when the boat is clearly a compact high-speed powerboat with a sleek streamlined hull built for speed. Include both open and covered cockpit designs, and both leisure and racing types. Do not confuse with sailboats or catamarans, which have masts or sails; yachts and cabin cruisers, which are bulkier and more accommodation-focused; or rigid inflatable boats, which have obvious inflatable side tubes. Exclude larger ships and ordinary fishing or utility boats that lack the slim high-performance shape.

name: spider web
815.description: A spider web is a silken structure spun by a spider, typically appearing as fine, threadlike strands suspended between plants, branches, buildings, or other supports. In these images it is most often seen as a delicate circular or spiral orb web, sometimes with radial lines, sticky spiral threads, dew droplets, or a spider resting at the center or edge.
815.guidelines: Classify images here when the main subject is the silk web itself: visible strands forming a suspended web, especially orb-shaped or otherwise clearly woven spider silk. Include cases with or without the spider present. Do not confuse with a spider alone when no web is visible, insect nests, caterpillar tents, random silk threads, or man-made netting/string. Orb webs are the most common look-alike pattern here; distinguish from cobwebs or tangle webs by the organized radial-and-spiral structure, but any genuine spider-spun web belongs in this category.

name: drop spindle
816.description: A hand-spinning tool consisting of a long slender shaft with pointed ends and a circular or rounded whorl mounted near one end or the center. It is usually made of wood, sometimes decorated or painted, and often appears with yarn or wool fiber wound around the shaft below the whorl.
816.guidelines: Classify as a drop spindle when the object is a handheld yarn-spinning spindle with a pointed shaft and a distinct whorl for rotational balance. Do not confuse it with a distaff, which holds unspun fiber but lacks the weighted spinning whorl, or with a bobbin/spool, which is mainly for storing thread on a simple cylinder. Also distinguish it from machine spindles or axles: a drop spindle is a small manual textile tool, typically wooden and shaped for twisting fiber into yarn.

name: sports car
817.description: A sports car is a low-slung road-going automobile designed for high performance rather than racing. It typically has a sleek, aerodynamic body, a long hood or compact mid-engine proportions, wide tires, and a coupe, roadster, or convertible form with an emphasis on speed, handling, and styling.
817.guidelines: Classify as sports car when the vehicle is a street-legal performance-oriented car with a low profile, sporty proportions, and a design focused on speed and handling. Include coupes, convertibles, and roadsters made for road use rather than competition. Do not confuse with race cars, which usually have visible racing modifications such as large wings, sponsor decals, roll cages, or track-only features. Also distinguish from supercars and hypercars, which are more exotic and extreme but may overlap visually; if the category is broader road-performance cars in general, sports car is appropriate. Exclude ordinary sedans, hatchbacks, SUVs, and muscle cars unless the car clearly has classic sports-car proportions and styling.

name: spotlight
818.description: A spotlight is a directional lamp or lighting fixture that emits a concentrated, intense beam of light toward a specific target. It is typically housed in a round or cylindrical metal body, often mounted on a yoke, stand, wall bracket, ceiling track, or stage rig, and may have a visible lens, reflector, or protective grill at the front.
818.guidelines: Classify as spotlight when the image shows the lighting fixture itself whose purpose is to project a focused beam onto a person, object, or area. Include stage spotlights, searchlight-style fixtures, mounted directional lamps, and theatrical moving-head spotlights. Do not confuse with floodlights, which cast a broad unfocused wash; ceiling lights or downlights, which illuminate general indoor space; lampshades or decorative lamps, which are not beam-projecting fixtures; or cameras/projectors, which may have a similar body shape but include obvious imaging optics or screens. Mark the light fixture only, not the illuminated subject or beam alone.

name: stage
819.description: A raised or clearly designated performance area used for concerts, plays, dance, or other live presentations. It is typically a platform or open fronted area facing an audience, often equipped with curtains, rigging, spotlights, speakers, microphones, backdrops, or side wings.
819.guidelines: Classify as stage when the image centers on the performance platform or presentation area itself, whether occupied or empty, indoors or outdoors. Common look-alikes include auditorium or theater interiors, which emphasize seating and the room rather than the platform; dance floors or platforms, which lack clear performance equipment or audience orientation; and concert crowds, where the audience dominates and the stage is only incidental. Use cues such as a raised platform, proscenium, curtains, lighting trusses, sound equipment, and an arrangement facing spectators.

name: steam locomotive
820.description: A railway locomotive powered by a steam engine, typically with a large cylindrical boiler, tall smokestack, round front smokebox door, external running gear and driving wheels, and often a separate coal-and-water tender or side tanks. It is usually black or dark-colored metal and may be shown emitting steam or smoke.
820.guidelines: Classify as steam locomotive when the train engine has clear steam-era features such as a boiler, chimney/smokestack, exposed rods, and a steam tender or tank-engine body. Do not confuse it with diesel or electric locomotives, which have boxier bodies, no smokestack, and no exposed steam running gear. Exclude train cars, passenger coaches, and railroad scenes unless the steam-powered engine itself is the main subject.

name: steel arch bridge
821.description: A steel arch bridge is a bridge with one or more prominent curved steel arches that carry the roadway or railway deck. The arch may sit below the deck, rise above it with the deck suspended from hangers, or pass through at deck level. Typical examples show large steel ribs, trussed or solid arch members, and a long span over water or a valley.
821.guidelines: Classify as steel arch bridge when the defining load-bearing structure is a steel arch. Look for a clearly curved steel rib spanning between supports and carrying the deck directly or through vertical hangers. Do not confuse with truss bridges, which are supported mainly by a web of straight members without a dominant arch shape; suspension bridges, which use main cables draped between towers; or tied-arch bridges, where the deck acts as a tie between arch ends. If the visible primary structure is the steel arch, it belongs here.

name: steelpan
822.description: A percussion instrument made from a concave metal drum top or other metal shell, usually circular and bowl- or pan-shaped, mounted on a stand or worn for playing. It has a smooth metallic playing surface with hammered note areas and no stretched skin membrane, lugs, or tension rods like a conventional drum.
822.guidelines: Classify as steelpan when the instrument is a tuned metal pan or drum struck with mallets, typically shiny steel and deeply dished or barrel-based. Include tenor, double, and other steelband pans. Do not confuse with snare, tom, bass, or hand drums, which use a stretched membrane with rims and hardware. Also avoid confusing it with gongs or singing bowls: steelpans are mounted as tuned percussion instruments and usually have a circular concave playing face rather than a flat hanging disc or small bowl.

name: stethoscope
823.description: A stethoscope is a medical listening instrument with flexible rubber or plastic tubing connecting a round chestpiece to a metal binaural headset with two earpieces. The chestpiece usually has a flat circular diaphragm, often with a smaller bell on the reverse side, and the tubing forms a loop when worn around the neck or laid flat.
823.guidelines: Classify as a stethoscope only when the image shows the characteristic chestpiece plus tubing and two earpieces for auscultation. It may be worn by doctors, patients, or children, or shown alone. Do not confuse it with headphones, which lack a chestpiece; blood-pressure cuffs or sphygmomanometers, which include an inflatable cuff and gauge; or otoscopes and other handheld medical tools, which do not have the twin earpiece-and-tubing design.

name: stole
824.description: A soft fabric wrap wider than a typical scarf, usually rectangular or slightly tapered, designed to drape around the neck or over the shoulders. It is often made of knit, crochet, lace, or woven material and may appear plain, patterned, openwork, fringed, or textured.
824.guidelines: Classify as stole when the item is a separate shoulder wrap broader than a scarf and meant to be draped loosely around the shoulders or neck. Do not confuse with a scarf, which is usually narrower and longer; a shawl, which is often larger and may be square or triangular; or a poncho/cape, which is more garment-like and structured to cover the body. The key cue is a broad, draped wrap without sleeves or a tailored shape.

name: stone wall
825.description: A wall made of visible individual stones, usually gray, tan, or brown, with a rough, irregular surface. The stones may be stacked, fitted, or mortared, but the separate rocks or stone blocks are clearly seen rather than hidden behind a smooth finish.
825.guidelines: Classify as stone wall when the main structure is a wall built from clearly visible stones or rock blocks. Include dry-stacked, rubble, fieldstone, and cut-stone walls. Do not confuse with brick walls, which are made of small uniform rectangular bricks; concrete or stucco walls, which have smooth continuous surfaces; or natural rock faces and cliffs, which are not constructed walls.

name: stopwatch
826.description: A small handheld timer used to measure elapsed time, typically with a round or rectangular body, a prominent display or dial, and start/stop controls on the top or front. It may be analog with a circular face and sweep hand or digital with an LCD screen, often including buttons, a lanyard, or a pocket-watch-style case.
826.guidelines: Classify as stopwatch only when the device’s main purpose is timing an interval on demand. Common examples are handheld sports timers, pocket stopwatch models, and digital elapsed-time timers with start/stop and reset buttons. Do not confuse with wristwatches or smartwatches worn on the wrist for general timekeeping, countdown kitchen timers, wall clocks, or other measuring instruments; the key cue is a dedicated elapsed-time timing device meant to be operated by hand.

name: stove
827.description: A stove is a heat-producing appliance or structure used for cooking or heating. In this category it includes household kitchen ranges and cooktops, portable camping stoves, wood-burning stoves, and similar enclosed heating units or fireplace-like stove structures. Common visual cues are burners or a heated top surface, oven compartments or fireboxes, metal bodies, control knobs, and in some cases visible flames or a chimney/flue.
827.guidelines: Classify as stove when the main subject is a cooking or heating unit with burners, a hotplate, or an enclosed firebox used to generate heat. This includes kitchen stoves/ranges, portable camp stoves, and wood-burning stove heaters. Do not confuse with ovens when only the baking chamber is emphasized without stovetop burners, fireplaces that are fixed open hearths without a stove body, grills or barbecues meant for outdoor cooking over an open grate, or furnaces/boilers that are utility heating equipment rather than recognizable stoves. The key cue is a self-contained appliance or heater designed to cook on top and/or produce heat from an enclosed unit.

name: strainer
828.description: A strainer is a perforated or mesh utensil used to separate solids from liquids. It is typically made of metal or plastic and appears as a bowl, cup, cone, or shallow basket with many small holes or a fine wire mesh, often with a handle, rim, or supporting frame.
828.guidelines: Classify as strainer when the object’s main feature is a perforated or mesh surface for draining or filtering. This includes handheld kitchen strainers, tea strainers, sink strainers, and colander-like draining inserts. Do not confuse with a sieve, which usually has a flatter fine-mesh screen for sifting dry ingredients, or with a colander when the object is a larger bowl specifically for draining food; if the item is broadly any perforated draining/filtering utensil, strainer is appropriate.

name: tram
829.description: A tram is a rail vehicle that runs on tracks laid in city streets or other urban rights-of-way. It is typically a single car or short articulated set, powered electrically from overhead wires by a pantograph or trolley pole, with a boxy passenger cabin, large side windows, and doors along the sides. Trams may be vintage or modern low-floor designs, but they are consistently street-running rail vehicles rather than rubber-tired buses.
829.guidelines: Classify as tram when the vehicle is clearly running on rails and is a street-level urban passenger car, usually drawing power from overhead wires. Do not confuse with a trolleybus: trolleybuses have rubber tires and no rails, even though they also use overhead wires. Also distinguish from trains or light-rail metro vehicles by the typical street-running setting, shorter car body, and direct integration with city roads and tram tracks.

name: stretcher
830.description: A stretcher is a narrow portable bed or litter used to carry injured or ill people. It typically has a long rectangular fabric or padded surface with handles, poles, or a wheeled metal frame; some examples are folding canvas litters, while others are hospital gurneys with rails and casters.
830.guidelines: Classify as stretcher when the object is specifically made for transporting a person lying down, either by hand or on wheels. Common look-alikes include hospital beds, examination tables, and cots: stretchers are narrower, more portable, and often have carrying handles, collapsible frames, or ambulance-style wheeled undercarriages. Do not confuse with wheelchairs, which are designed for seated transport.

name: sofa
831.description: An upholstered indoor seating piece for two or more people, with a long padded seat, a backrest, and usually armrests. It may be straight, sectional, or futon-like, and is commonly covered in fabric or leather in solid colors or patterns.
831.guidelines: Classify as sofa when the main object is a padded multi-person couch-like seat with a continuous back and seat. Include loveseats, sectionals, and simple futon sofas if they are clearly used as couches. Do not confuse with an armchair or recliner (single seat), a bench (usually unupholstered or without full sofa arms/back), a bed/daybed used primarily for sleeping, or an ottoman/chaise lounge without the typical sofa form.

name: stupa
832.description: A stupa is a Buddhist religious monument, typically built as a rounded dome or mound on a pedestal or tiered base and often topped with a spire, finial, or umbrella-like pinnacle. Across examples, forms range from smooth white hemispherical domes to tall bell-shaped or conical towers, but the defining look is a solid reliquary mass with a prominent vertical crowning element and often a symmetrical, shrine-like setting.
832.guidelines: Classify as stupa when the main subject is a Buddhist reliquary monument with a dome, bell-shaped body, or mound-like mass set on a base and usually crowned by a spire or finial. Include regional variants such as white domed stupas, golden pagoda-like stupas, and small votive stupas. Do not confuse with pagodas, which are taller multi-story buildings with clearly separated roof tiers and occupiable interiors, or with temple halls/monasteries, which are building-like structures with doors, large rooflines, and usable internal space. Also distinguish from obelisks, memorial columns, and minarets, which lack the characteristic domed or mound-based Buddhist shrine form.

name: submarine
833.description: A submarine is a long, cylindrical watercraft with a rounded or tapered bow, a smooth dark hull, and a low profile that sits mostly below the waterline. It typically has a raised sail or conning tower with periscopes, masts, or antennas, and may show hatches, deck plates, or ballast openings along the top and sides.
833.guidelines: Classify as submarine when the vessel has a mostly submerged cigar-shaped hull and a distinct sail/conning tower. Do not confuse it with surface warships or patrol boats, which ride fully above the water with open decks and superstructures, or with torpedoes and small submersibles, which lack the full-sized naval vessel form. 'U-boat' is a historical subtype of submarine, but use submarine for the broader category shown here.

name: suit
834.description: A matching set of tailored formal or business clothing, typically consisting of a suit jacket and trousers made from the same fabric and color; in women’s versions, the matching lower garment may be a skirt. Suits are usually worn over a dress shirt or blouse and are often paired with a tie, bow tie, or formal shoes.
834.guidelines: Classify as suit when the person is wearing coordinated tailored pieces made from the same material as a set. The key cue is the matching jacket with matching trousers or skirt. Do not confuse with a blazer or sport coat worn with unmatched pants, a tuxedo/dinner suit with satin lapels and more formal styling, or a dress/coat that is not a two- or three-piece tailored set.

name: sundial
835.description: A sundial is a timekeeping device with a flat, angled, or curved dial marked with hour lines and a raised pointer or edge that casts a shadow. It is commonly made of stone, metal, or painted masonry, and may be mounted horizontally, vertically, or as a freestanding garden object.
835.guidelines: Classify as sundial only when the object tells time by the shadow cast from a gnomon, style, or raised edge onto marked hour lines. Common look-alikes include clocks, compasses, plaques, and decorative reliefs. Unlike clocks, sundials have no hands or internal mechanism; unlike compasses, they are organized around hour markings rather than cardinal directions; unlike decorative sun motifs or inscriptions, they include a shadow-casting element and a dial laid out for reading time.

name: sunglasses
836.description: Protective eyeglasses with dark or tinted lenses, usually set in a lightweight frame and worn over the eyes to reduce bright sunlight and glare. They appear in many shapes, including wraparound sport styles, aviator-like metal frames, oversized fashion frames, and shield-style single-lens designs.
836.guidelines: Classify as sunglasses when the defining object is eyewear with visibly tinted or darkened lenses intended for sun protection. Include varied frame styles and lens shapes. Do not confuse with clear eyeglasses or reading glasses, which have transparent lenses; safety glasses or goggles, which are usually designed for impact protection and often have clear lenses or sealed sides; and visors or face shields, which cover more of the face and are not standard eyeglasses.

name: sunscreen
838.description: A skin-protection product sold as a lotion, cream, spray, stick, or squeeze tube, usually in small handheld containers labeled with SPF or sun protection claims. It is often white or pastel and may be shown being applied to exposed skin as a white cream or lotion layer.
838.guidelines: Classify as sunscreen when the product is specifically for protecting skin from sunlight/UV exposure, typically indicated by SPF labeling or visible application to skin before sun exposure. Do not confuse with ordinary lotion, moisturizer, or cosmetic cream unless sun protection is explicit. Exclude tanning oil or after-sun products unless they are clearly labeled as sunscreen or sunblock.

name: suspension bridge
839.description: A bridge whose deck or walkway is hung from main cables draped between tall towers, usually with many vertical suspenders supporting the span. It typically has a long, lightly curved profile, prominent towers, taut cable lines, and an open span crossing water, roads, or forested ravines; some examples are pedestrian bridges and others carry vehicle traffic.
839.guidelines: Classify as a suspension bridge when the roadway or footbridge is suspended from one or more main cables that pass over towers and continue to anchorages. Distinguish it from cable-stayed bridges, where straight cables run directly from the towers to the deck in a fan or harp pattern and there is no draped main cable. Also avoid confusion with arch bridges, truss bridges, and simple rope footbridges: this class is defined by the hanging deck, tall support towers, and the characteristic sagging main cables with vertical hangers.

name: mop
840.description: A floor-cleaning tool with a long handle and an absorbent cleaning head made of hanging cotton or synthetic strings, yarn loops, cloth strips, or a flat fabric pad. The head is usually soft, thick, and flexible, often bundled or spread wide for wiping wet floors.
840.guidelines: Classify as a mop when the tool has a handle attached to an absorbent fibrous or fabric head meant for washing or wiping floors. Includes string mops, loop mops, sponge-strip mops, and flat dust/wet mops. Do not confuse with a broom, which has stiff bristles for sweeping; a duster, which is smaller and used for furniture; or a squeegee/floor wiper, which has a rubber blade rather than a soft absorbent head.

name: sweatshirt
841.description: A casual pullover or zip-front knit top made from soft, medium-to-heavy fabric, usually with long sleeves and ribbed cuffs and hem. It may be plain or printed, and can be hooded or unhooded, with some examples including a front kangaroo pocket or zipper.
841.guidelines: Classify as sweatshirt when the garment is a soft, long-sleeved casual top in sweatshirt fleece or similar knit fabric, including hoodies and crewneck sweatshirts. Do not confuse with sweaters, which are usually visibly knitted rather than fleece-like; jackets or coats, which are more structured or outerwear-focused; and track jackets, which are typically lighter, sportier, and more fitted. If a hood is present, it can still be a sweatshirt as long as it has the typical hoodie/sweatshirt construction.

name: swim trunks
842.description: Men’s or boys’ swimwear worn on the lower body, typically covering the waist, hips, groin, and upper thighs. It appears in several common forms, including loose shorts, square-cut trunks, and tight swim briefs, usually made from smooth quick-drying fabric and often seen at pools, beaches, or docks.
842.guidelines: Classify as swim trunks when the item is lower-body swimwear intended for swimming or beach use, whether loose or close-fitting. Include swim briefs and short bathing trunks if they serve the same role. Do not confuse with underwear or boxer briefs, which are usually cotton-like and not styled for swimming; bikinis, which are women’s two-piece swimwear; wetsuits or swim jammers, which extend farther down the legs; or board shorts if the image specifically emphasizes very long, knee-length surf shorts rather than general bathing trunks.

name: swing
843.description: A swing is a suspended seat—such as a flat board, molded seat, or tire—hung by two ropes or chains from an overhead support so it can move back and forth. The defining visible parts are the seat itself and its hanging connections; the full playground frame may or may not be shown.
843.guidelines: Classify as a swing when the image shows a hanging seat or tire attached by ropes or chains for swinging. Include tire swings and baby swings. Do not require the supporting frame to be visible. Exclude slides, seesaws, hammocks, benches, hanging chairs, or full playground scenes where no actual suspended swing seat is visible.
