Broccolini has much longer, thinner stems and smaller loose florets. Kale and cabbage show leafy heads rather than a dense bud crown.

name: cauliflower
Brassica oleracea var. botrytis
938.description: A compact head of densely packed, bumpy flower buds forming a rounded curd, usually white to cream but also seen in green, purple, or orange varieties, surrounded by thick pale stems and broad green leaves. It may appear whole in the field, trimmed as a single head, broken into florets, or cooked in pieces.
938.guidelines: Classify as cauliflower when the edible part is a tight curd made of many small undeveloped florets, typically with a chunky white or colored head and cabbage-like leaves. Do not confuse with broccoli, which has distinct branching green stems and separated flower clusters; Romanesco broccoli, which has sharper conical spiral florets; or cabbage, which forms smooth layered leaves rather than a granular curd.

name: zucchini
Cucurbita pepo
939.description: A zucchini is a smooth-skinned summer squash, usually cylindrical and slightly tapered, with dark green, medium green, pale green, yellow, or striped skin. It is typically harvested immature, so the flesh is firm and pale, and the fruit appears elongated rather than bulbous. Many images also show the large yellow-orange squash blossoms and broad, lobed leaves of the plant.
939.guidelines: Classify as zucchini when the fruit is an elongated summer squash with smooth skin and a cylindrical to gently club-shaped form, whether dark green, light green, yellow, or striped. Do not confuse it with cucumber, which is usually slimmer, more uniformly cylindrical, and lacks the typical squash blossom and thick squash stem; or with other summer squashes such as yellow crookneck/pattypan, which have more distinct curved necks or flattened shapes. Exclude round pumpkins, winter squashes, and bottle gourds with much harder-looking rinds or very different shapes.

name: spaghetti squash
Cucurbita pepo
940.description: An oblong to oval winter squash with smooth, hard skin that is pale yellow, cream, or ivory, sometimes deepening to golden yellow when mature. When cut open, it has a central seed cavity and yellow to orange flesh that, after cooking, separates into many thin, spaghetti-like strands.
940.guidelines: Classify as spaghetti squash when the fruit is oval and smooth-skinned, usually pale yellow, and especially when the cooked interior forms long noodle-like strands. Do not confuse it with butternut squash, which has a tan skin and a bulbous neck-and-base shape, or with other yellow summer squashes, which are usually smaller, softer-skinned, and not strand-forming inside. It can also resemble other oval winter squashes, but spaghetti squash is distinguished by its smooth elongated shape and its characteristic stringy cooked flesh.

name: acorn squash
Cucurbita pepo
941.description: A small winter squash with a squat, rounded to slightly elongated shape and pronounced deep vertical ribs, giving it an acorn-like form. The rind is most often very dark green, but can also be mottled, striped, white, or golden, often with orange or yellow patches. The flesh inside is yellow to deep orange, with a hollow seed cavity in the center.
941.guidelines: Classify as acorn squash when the fruit is small, strongly ribbed, and acorn-shaped with a thick dark rind and yellow-orange flesh. Do not confuse it with pumpkin, which is usually larger and less deeply ribbed; butternut squash, which has a long neck and bulbous end; delicata squash, which is more elongated with cream-and-green striping and shallower ribs; or carnival squash, which is more variegated and typically broader and flatter. The deep lobes and compact acorn form are the key cues.

name: butternut squash
Cucurbita moschata
942.description: A winter squash with a characteristic pear-shaped form: a long, narrow neck widening into a bulbous seed cavity at the bottom. The rind is smooth and matte, usually pale tan to beige, while the flesh is deep yellow to orange. When cut open, seeds are clustered in the rounded base.
942.guidelines: Classify as butternut squash when the fruit has a smooth buff-colored skin and the classic narrow-necked, bulb-bottom shape. Do not confuse it with pumpkins or kabocha squash, which are rounder and ribbed; acorn squash, which is dark green and deeply ridged; or spaghetti squash, which is more oval and uniformly cylindrical. The elongated neck with most seeds confined to the swollen base is the key cue.

name: cucumber
Cucumis sativus
943.description: A cucumber is a smooth to slightly bumpy, elongated green fruit with a cylindrical to mildly tapered shape. It is usually medium to dark green, sometimes striped or mottled, with pale watery flesh and small seeds when cut. It may appear fresh on the vine, harvested whole, sliced, or pickled.
943.guidelines: Classify as cucumber when the item is the familiar long or short green cucumber fruit, whether whole, growing on the plant, sliced, or prepared as pickles. Distinguish it from zucchini by its typically cooler green color, more watery pale interior, and less ridged shape; from gourds and squashes by its thinner skin and classic salad/pickling form; and from similar cucurbits such as Armenian cucumber by using the broader standard cucumber appearance shown here.

name: artichoke
Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus
944.description: A globe-shaped edible flower bud with many thick, tightly overlapping green to gray-green bracts, often tinged purple at the tips. When allowed to open, it produces a large tufted purple thistle-like flower emerging from the center. Buds are borne on stout stems with lobed, silvery green leaves.
944.guidelines: Classify as artichoke when the image shows the rounded immature bud or opened purple-flowering head of the cultivated globe artichoke. Do not confuse it with cardoon: cardoon is usually identified by its thick edible leaf stalks/ribs and a more spiny, less globular flower head. Also distinguish from other thistles by the artichoke's large, compact, layered bud with broad fleshy bracts rather than narrow sharp spines.

name: bell pepper
Capsicum annuum
945.description: A smooth, glossy sweet pepper with a blocky bell-like shape, thick fleshy walls, and 3–4 rounded lobes. It is typically green when unripe and may ripen to red, yellow, orange, purple, brown, or nearly black. Fruits are broad-shouldered, blunt-ended, and usually hang downward from the plant.
945.guidelines: Classify as bell pepper when the fruit is a large, squat, blocky sweet pepper with thick walls and distinct lobes. Include green and fully ripened color forms. Do not confuse with chili peppers or jalapeños, which are narrower, longer, more tapered, and usually less lobed; or with habanero/scotch bonnet types, which are smaller, wrinklier, and lantern-shaped. Exclude elongated sweet peppers such as banana or cubanelle peppers, which are more conical and less boxy.

name: cardoon
Cynara cardunculus
946.description: A tall, spiny thistle-like plant with large ribbed gray-green leaves and rounded flower heads made of overlapping prickly bracts, topped by dense tufted purple to pinkish-purple florets. The heads are usually narrower and more thistle-like than globe artichokes, and the plant often looks wilder, with sharper spines and a more open, branched habit.
946.guidelines: Classify as cardoon when the plant shows thistle-like purple flower heads with prominent spiny bracts and a coarse, silvery or gray-green, deeply lobed foliage typical of Cynara cardunculus. Do not confuse it with globe artichoke: artichoke has a larger, rounder, more compact edible bud with thicker, less aggressively spiny bracts. Also distinguish it from other thistles by the large Cynara-type heads and broad, robust leaves rather than smaller heads or finer stems.

name: mushroom
947.description: A fungal fruiting body, typically with a cap or other distinct spore-bearing structure growing from soil, wood, moss, or leaf litter. Members of this category vary widely in shape, color, and texture: they may be umbrella-shaped with a stalk and gills, pore-bearing or tooth-bearing, shelf-like on wood, clustered, rounded, or irregular. Common appearances include smooth, scaly, slimy, or matte caps in white, tan, brown, red, orange, yellow, or purple.
947.guidelines: Use this label for fungi that are clearly mushrooms but do not fit the excluded fine-grained classes such as coral fungus, agaric, Gyromitra, stinkhorn, earthstar, hen-of-the-woods, or bolete. Distinguish from agarics by avoiding the classic generic supermarket-style gilled mushroom look when a more specific excluded class applies; from boletes by checking that the underside is not dominated by pores; from coral fungi by ruling out upright branched coral-like forms; from stinkhorns by ruling out phallic or cage-like fruiting bodies with slimy spore mass; from earthstars by ruling out star-splitting outer layers; from hen-of-the-woods by ruling out large ruffled multilayer rosettes; and from Gyromitra by ruling out saddle-shaped or brain-like caps. If it is a recognizable mushroom-form fungus outside those excluded groups, classify it as mushroom.

name: Granny Smith
Malus domestica 'Granny Smith'
948.description: A round to slightly conical apple cultivar with smooth, glossy skin that is a vivid bright green, sometimes with small pale lenticels and occasional yellowish blush. The flesh is white to pale cream and crisp, with the typical apple core and brown seeds visible when cut.
948.guidelines: Classify as Granny Smith when the apple is distinctly bright green and has the typical smooth, shiny, round apple form. Do not confuse it with generic red or yellow apples, which differ mainly in skin color, or with pears, which usually have a more elongated neck and different stem-end shape. Use this label for the well-known green apple cultivar rather than for just any immature or unripe apple.

name: strawberry
Fragaria × ananassa
949.description: A strawberry is a small, soft, juicy fruit with a rounded conical to heart-like shape, usually bright red when ripe but sometimes white or green when unripe. Its surface is dotted with many tiny pale seeds, and it typically has a green leafy calyx attached at the top.
949.guidelines: Classify both ripe red strawberries and unripe pale green or white strawberries here. The key cues are the fleshy red-to-green fruit body, many small surface seeds, and the green leafy cap. Do not confuse with raspberries or blackberries, which are made of many distinct drupelets; cherries or small tomatoes, which have smooth skins without external seeds; or strawberry-flavored foods and decorations unless an actual strawberry fruit or plant is visibly present.

name: sweet orange
Citrus × sinensis
950.description: A round to slightly oval citrus fruit with a bright orange, finely dimpled rind and orange flesh divided into radial segments. It may be shown whole, cut in half, sliced, or peeled, often with juicy translucent pulp and a pale central pith visible.
950.guidelines: Classify as sweet orange when the fruit is the familiar larger orange with a fairly spherical shape and orange peel/flesh. Do not confuse with tangerines or mandarins, which are usually smaller, flatter, deeper reddish-orange, and often have a looser, easier-to-peel skin. Grapefruit is typically larger and paler yellow to pink inside; lemons are more elongated and yellow.

name: lemon
Citrus limon
951.description: A lemon is a bright yellow citrus fruit, usually oval to ellipsoidal with a pointed nipple at one or both ends. It has a thick, slightly bumpy rind and pale yellow, segmented, juicy flesh inside. Lemons may appear singly, in piles, cut open, or growing on a tree among glossy green leaves.
951.guidelines: Classify as lemon when the fruit is the familiar yellow, oval citrus with tapered ends and a textured rind. Do not confuse it with lime, which is usually smaller and green; orange or grapefruit, which are rounder and deeper orange or larger; or citron, which is often much larger, more irregular, and thicker-rinded. Very rough-skinned or unusually large lemons can still belong here if they retain the typical lemon color and overall form.

name: fig
Ficus carica
952.description: A fig is a soft, rounded to pear-shaped fruit with smooth skin, often green when unripe and turning purple, brown, or dark violet as it matures. It has a short neck and a small opening at the blossom end, and when cut open shows a dense, fleshy interior filled with many tiny seeds, usually pink, red, or amber.
952.guidelines: Classify as fig when the fruit is bulbous or pear-shaped with a short stem, smooth skin, and the characteristic seed-filled interior or small ostiole at the tip. Include both green unripe and dark ripe fruits. Do not confuse with pears or avocados, which lack the fig’s ostiole and seed-packed interior, or with plums, which usually have a single pit rather than many tiny internal seeds.

name: pineapple
Ananas comosus
953.description: A pineapple is a tropical fruit with a short, stout oval to cylindrical body covered in tough, overlapping diamond-shaped scales with spiny points, usually green, yellow, or brownish as it ripens. It is topped by a dense crown of long, narrow, stiff, sword-like leaves. The fruit may appear attached low to a rosette-form plant with long strap-shaped leaves, or shown cut into rings, chunks, or halves with yellow flesh.
953.guidelines: Classify as pineapple when the image shows the distinctive rough segmented fruit with a leafy crown, or the pineapple plant bearing this fruit. Do not confuse it with pine cones, artichokes, or other bromeliads: pineapple fruit is larger, fleshy, and has regular polygonal 'eyes' plus a crown. Bromeliad plants without the characteristic pineapple fruit should not be included. Cut pineapple should show the typical yellow fibrous flesh and association with the whole fruit form.

name: banana
954.description: An elongated, slightly curved fruit with a smooth peel, usually green when unripe and yellow when ripe, often developing brown speckles or patches with age. It typically has a thicker stem end, a tapered tip, and grows singly or in clustered hands on large bunches.
954.guidelines: Classify as banana when the image shows the characteristic curved, smooth-skinned fruit or bunches of such fruits, whether ripe, unripe, peeled, or still hanging on the plant. Do not confuse it with plantain: plantains are usually thicker, more angular, and commonly remain green longer or turn dull yellow with a starchier look. Also avoid confusing bananas with other elongated yellow fruits; the key cues are the familiar crescent shape, peel texture, and clustered growth in hands.

name: jackfruit
Artocarpus heterophyllus
955.description: Large tropical multiple fruit borne directly on the trunk or major branches, usually oblong to oval and very bulky, with a thick green to yellow-green rind covered in dense blunt conical bumps. When cut open, it shows many yellow fleshy bulbs surrounding large seeds within sticky fibrous pale pith.
955.guidelines: Classify as jackfruit when the fruit is very large, green to yellowish, rough with many small blunt knobs, and commonly grows from the trunk or older branches. Do not confuse with breadfruit, which is usually smaller, rounder, and more evenly surfaced with a tighter polygonal pattern; durian, which has much sharper dangerous spines; or cempedak, which is typically smaller, narrower, and often more orange-brown with softer flesh. Interior views of jackfruit should show multiple yellow pods and fibrous white latex-rich tissue rather than a few large segments.

name: sugar apple
Annona squamosa
956.description: A small to medium tropical fruit, usually round, heart-shaped, or slightly conical, with a thick green rind divided into many rounded, knobby segments that look like overlapping scales. The fruit may ripen from bright green to pale green, yellow-green, or slightly purplish. When opened, it has soft white to cream-colored custard-like flesh divided into segments, typically containing several glossy black or dark brown seeds.
956.guidelines: Classify as sugar apple when the fruit shows a clearly segmented, scaly surface with distinct rounded knobs and white segmented flesh with black seeds inside. Do not confuse it with cherimoya, which is usually smoother with less separated surface patterning; atemoya, which is often larger and more irregularly conical with more fused bumps; or soursop, which has longer soft spines rather than rounded scales. Avoid using this label for generic 'custard apple' images unless the fruit specifically matches the classic Annona squamosa look.

name: pomegranate
Punica granatum
957.description: A pomegranate is a round to slightly squat fruit with a thick, leathery skin that is usually red, pink-red, or yellow-red, often topped by a prominent crown-like calyx. When cut open, it shows many tightly packed, glossy, translucent red to pink arils separated by pale cream-colored membranes.
957.guidelines: Classify as pomegranate when the image shows the whole fruit with its crown-like calyx, a cut fruit revealing many jewel-like arils, or the loose arils themselves. Do not confuse it with apples or persimmons, which may be similarly round and red but lack the thick rind, crown, and densely packed arils. Loose arils can resemble berries or fish eggs, but pomegranate arils are smooth, ruby-like seed coverings typically shown in clusters or inside the fruit's pale segmented interior.

name: hay bale
958.description: A compact bundle of dried grass or straw, usually formed into a large cylindrical roll and tan to golden-brown in color. It has a rough, fibrous texture with visible layered or spiral-packed strands, and may appear as a single bale or in stacked groups in fields, barns, or farm settings.
958.guidelines: Classify as hay bale when the image shows compressed hay or straw formed into a distinct bale, especially the common large round type seen in harvested fields. Do not confuse it with loose hay, straw piles, or animal bedding, which lack a clear bale shape; with rectangular straw bales, which are block-shaped rather than cylindrical; or with rocks, logs, or barrels, which may have a similar silhouette but do not show dry fibrous plant material.

name: pasta alla carbonara
959.description: An Italian pasta dish made with long or ribbon pasta coated in a glossy creamy-looking pale yellow sauce, typically speckled with black pepper and mixed with small pieces of bacon, pancetta, or guanciale. It is usually served as a mound of noodles with cheese grated over the top.
959.guidelines: Classify as pasta alla carbonara when the image shows pasta in a smooth egg-and-cheese-based sauce with visible cured pork pieces and often black pepper. Include variations in pasta shape such as spaghetti, bucatini, fettuccine, or rigatoni. Do not confuse with Alfredo or other cream-sauce pastas, which are usually plain white and lack bacon/pancetta pieces; cacio e pepe, which has cheese and pepper but no pork; or tomato-based bacon pasta dishes, which are red or orange rather than pale yellow or cream-colored.

name: chocolate syrup
960.description: A dark brown, glossy, pourable chocolate topping or sauce, usually seen drizzled, swirled, or pooled over desserts such as ice cream, cakes, pastries, donuts, and plated sweets. It appears smooth and shiny, often in thin streams or thicker ribbons.
960.guidelines: Classify as chocolate syrup when the defining visible element is a liquid or semi-liquid chocolate topping used as a drizzle, coating, or sauce. It may appear on many different foods, but the shared category is the chocolate syrup itself. Do not confuse with chocolate frosting or icing, which is thicker and spread as a solid topping; chocolate ganache, which is usually denser and less syrup-like; melted chocolate pieces or bars; or non-chocolate dessert sauces such as caramel, fudge-colored fruit syrups, or balsamic reductions. The key cue is a glossy dark chocolate sauce in pourable drips, swirls, or pools.

name: dough
961.description: A soft, uncooked mixture of flour and liquid, often with yeast or fat, seen as a smooth to shaggy mass that can be sticky, elastic, kneaded, rolled, stretched, braided, or shaped. It is typically pale white, cream, or light tan, sometimes dusted with flour, and may appear as a ball, sheet, rope, or formed piece before baking.
961.guidelines: Classify as dough when the image shows raw, unbaked paste used for bread, pastry, pizza, noodles, or similar foods. Include kneaded balls, rolled sheets, proofing dough, and shaped raw pieces. Do not confuse with baked bread or pastries, which have browned crusts and finished structure; batter, which is much looser and pourable; fondant or modeling clay/playdough, which are smoother, more uniform, and often brightly colored; or masa/paste fillings, which are usually denser and less elastic.

name: meatloaf
962.description: A baked loaf-shaped dish made from ground meat mixed with herbs, seasonings, and often breadcrumbs, vegetables, or egg. It is typically rectangular or oval, browned on the outside, and served in thick slices; many examples are topped with a glossy ketchup or tomato glaze, and some are stuffed or wrapped with ingredients such as boiled egg or bacon.
962.guidelines: Classify as meatloaf when the food is a cohesive baked loaf of ground meat, usually shown whole or sliced, with a firm sliceable interior rather than a loose mince or a flat patty. Do not confuse with pâté or terrine, which are smoother and more finely textured; hamburger steak or Salisbury steak, which are individual patties rather than a loaf; or bread loaf/cake, which lack the meaty crumb and savory appearance. Meatballs are smaller separate portions, and roast cuts are whole-muscle meat rather than ground meat formed into a loaf.

name: pizza
963.description: A pizza is a baked flatbread dish, usually round but sometimes rectangular or sold by the slice, with a crust topped with sauce and melted cheese and often additional toppings such as pepperoni, vegetables, herbs, or other meats. It may appear thin-crust, thick-crust, pan-baked, wood-fired, or highly varied in style; toy or miniature depictions can mimic the same characteristic pizza appearance.
963.guidelines: Classify as pizza when the image shows the characteristic baked dough base with visible pizza-style toppings spread over the surface, typically including cheese and often tomato sauce. Include whole pies, slices, personal pizzas, unusual topping combinations, and realistic miniatures or representations if they clearly depict pizza. Do not confuse with savory tarts, quiche, focaccia, pide, flatbread sandwiches, or casseroles: pizza has an exposed crust with toppings baked on top rather than enclosed filling or custard. Distinguish from plain bread by the presence of a topping layer, and from calzones or stuffed crust items by the open-faced pie structure.

name: pie
964.description: A pie is a baked dish with a pastry crust or other covering enclosing or topping a filling. It is usually round and served whole or in individual portions, with a browned top crust, bottom crust, or both. Fillings vary widely and may be sweet or savory, including meat, vegetables, custard, fruit, or cream.
964.guidelines: Classify as pie when the food is a crust-based baked dish with an enclosed filling or a clearly defined pie shell and top. This includes double-crust pies, pot pies, and single-crust filled pies. Do not confuse it with quiche or tart, which usually have an open top with exposed filling; shepherd's pie, which is topped with mashed potatoes rather than pastry; or cake and casserole, which lack a true pie crust.

name: burrito
965.description: A burrito is a flour tortilla wrapped tightly around a savory filling and rolled into a compact cylinder, usually with the ends folded or tucked. It commonly appears as a handheld wrap, often partially covered in foil, with fillings such as rice, beans, meat, cheese, and salsa visible at a cut or open end.
965.guidelines: Classify as burrito when the food is a rolled flour tortilla enclosing the filling in a cylindrical package. Burritos are usually thicker and more fully wrapped than tacos, and unlike enchiladas they are typically served as a handheld wrap rather than covered in sauce on a plate. Do not confuse with wraps or sandwiches: burritos have a Mexican-style tortilla form and dense enclosed filling, often with foil wrapping. Also distinguish from chimichangas, which are deep-fried, and from fajitas, where the tortilla and fillings are usually served separately or loosely folded.

name: red wine
966.description: A dark red to purplish alcoholic drink, usually shown in a stemmed wine glass or in a wine bottle. It appears translucent but deep-colored, ranging from ruby red to nearly opaque burgundy, often with a smooth reflective surface or small bubbles along the rim.
966.guidelines: Classify as red wine when the beverage is visibly red, maroon, or purple-red and is presented in a typical wine context such as a wine glass, bottle, pouring scene, or dining table. Do not confuse it with white wine, rosé, grape juice, sangria, or other red beverages: red wine is generally darker and less bright than juice or cocktails, and is typically served in standard wine glasses or bottles rather than tumblers or mixed-drink glasses.

name: espresso
967.description: A small serving of concentrated coffee, usually very dark brown to nearly black, in a small cup or glass. It often has a thin layer of golden-brown crema on top and little to no visible milk, though some examples may show slight foam or mixing while being poured.
967.guidelines: Classify as espresso when the image shows a small shot of concentrated coffee, typically in a demitasse cup or small glass, with a dark liquid body and often a crema layer. Do not confuse it with drip coffee or Americano, which are usually larger servings with a thinner, more transparent appearance, or with cappuccino and latte, which have substantial milk and thicker foam. Exclude coffee makers or cups where the espresso itself is not the clear subject.

name: cup
968.description: A small open drinking vessel, usually rounded and deeper than wide, with a handle on the side. It is commonly made of ceramic, porcelain, glass, plastic, or metal, and may appear plain or decorated; many examples are shown with matching saucers and are sized for tea or coffee.
968.guidelines: Classify as cup when the object is a small handheld vessel meant for drinking individual servings. Typical cues are a single handle, an open top, and proportions suited for sipping rather than storage. Do not confuse with a mug, which is usually larger, taller, thicker, and less delicate; a bowl, which is wider and usually handleless; or a glass/tumbler, which lacks a handle. If a saucer is present, classify the drinking vessel itself as cup.

name: mountain
970.description: A mountain is a large natural landform that rises prominently above the surrounding terrain, usually with a distinct summit or ridgeline. It may appear as a single peak or as part of a mountain range, with rocky or vegetated slopes and, at higher elevations or colder climates, snow or ice cover.
970.guidelines: Classify as mountain when the main subject is a prominent elevated landform with a clear peak, massif, or high ridge. This can include isolated peaks and mountains within a range. Do not confuse with hills, which are lower and more rounded with less dramatic relief, or with cliffs/rock faces, which are steep exposures rather than whole mountains. If the annotated landform is primarily a piece of land projecting into water, classify it as promontory instead of mountain.

name: soap bubble
971.description: A soap bubble is a thin, transparent, nearly spherical film of साबुन solution, usually seen floating in air. It appears as a clear or lightly tinted round shell with bright reflective highlights and characteristic iridescent rainbow colors that shift across the surface; bubbles may occur singly, in clusters, or as large elongated bubbles made with a wand.
971.guidelines: Classify images as soap bubble when the main subject is a floating or freshly formed thin film bubble with a transparent surface and iridescent reflections. Include both small blown bubbles and large wand-made bubbles. Do not confuse with water droplets, glass marbles, balloons, or foam: water droplets are usually attached to a surface and lack the hollow film look; marbles are solid glass spheres with stronger internal refraction; balloons are opaque or rubbery with tied ends; foam shows many packed bubbles together rather than distinct floating bubbles.

name: cliff
972.description: A cliff is a very steep or nearly vertical exposed face of rock, soil, or sand, often forming a sharp drop in elevation. It may occur along coasts, canyons, river gorges, mountainsides, quarries, or eroded badlands, and typically appears as a tall wall-like escarpment with bare exposed material and little level surface.
972.guidelines: Classify as cliff when the defining feature is the steep exposed face and abrupt drop. Include rocky, sandy, or earthen vertical walls inland or by water. Do not label as promontory when the main feature is a projecting headland or cape extending into water, or as alp/mountain peak when the image is primarily of a high summit or pointed mountain mass rather than the sheer face. Also distinguish from canyon/valley scenes where the broad ravine is primary and from caves/arches where an opening is the main subject.

name: coral reef
973.description: A coral reef is an underwater marine habitat built by colonies of corals and other reef organisms. It typically appears as a dense, irregular rocky or branching structure covered with hard corals, soft corals, sea fans, sponges, and reef-associated fish and invertebrates. Reefs range from shallow, brightly lit tropical scenes to close underwater views of coral heads, plates, boulders, and branching formations in clear blue or turquoise water.
973.guidelines: Classify images as coral reef when the scene shows a reef habitat: substantial coral growth forming the visible underwater structure, often with multiple corals or other reef life integrated into the seafloor. Do not use this class for single isolated reef animals, plain sandy or rocky seabeds, open water with fish but no clear reef structure, kelp forests, oyster or mussel beds, or artificial reefs. If the image is a close-up, the coral colony or reef-building structure should still be the main subject rather than just a fish, turtle, diver, crab, or sponge.

name: geyser
974.description: A geyser is a geothermal hot spring that periodically or occasionally erupts, sending a vertical jet or plume of hot water and steam into the air. It is typically seen as a vent, mound, or pool in a mineral-stained basin, either actively erupting or sitting quiet between eruptions.
974.guidelines: Classify as geyser when the scene shows a natural eruptive hot spring or its recognizable vent/mound, whether currently erupting or inactive. Include tall water-and-steam columns as well as dormant geyser cones and pools. Do not confuse with fumaroles or steam vents, which emit mostly steam without a forceful water eruption; hot springs, which are calm pools without eruptive jets; mud pots, which bubble thick mud; or man-made fountains, which have artificial structures and regular engineered spray.

name: shore
975.description: The boundary between a body of water and the land, usually shown as a broad strip of sand, pebbles, mud, rocks, or wet flats beside calm or wavy water. Shores may appear on lakes, rivers, lagoons, or the sea, and often include shallow water, exposed sediment, driftwood, or a gently curving waterline stretching across much of the image.
975.guidelines: Classify images as shore when the main subject is the land-water edge itself. The shoreline or beach should dominate the scene, not just appear as background behind another object. Include sandy beaches, rocky shores, muddy banks, tidal flats, and similar waterside margins. Do not confuse with open water scenes where little or no land edge is visible, or with generic landscapes in which the shore is minor. Also exclude images focused mainly on animals, boats, or structures unless the shore itself remains the primary visual subject.

name: headland
976.description: A headland is a prominent mass of high land that projects out into the sea or a large lake. It is typically seen as a rocky or steep-sided point jutting into open water, often with cliffs, bluffs, or sloping coastal hills along its edges.
976.guidelines: Classify as headland when the main subject is a landform that clearly extends outward into surrounding water on multiple sides. Water should be visible, and the projecting shape is the key cue. Do not confuse it with a cliff, where the image focuses mainly on a vertical rock face rather than the outward-pointing landform; with an island, which is fully surrounded by water and not connected to the mainland; with a peninsula, which is usually broader and larger-scale than the pointed coastal projection shown here; or with a mountain/alp, where elevation is emphasized without the defining projection into water.

name: sandbar
977.description: A sandbar is a long, narrow ridge or strip of sand forming a shallow, exposed or barely submerged area surrounded by water, often along coasts, beaches, lagoons, or tidal flats. It is typically pale tan or white, low and flat, and created or reshaped by waves, currents, and sea tides.
977.guidelines: Classify images as sandbar when the main subject is a distinct sandy shoal, spit, or exposed bar separated from the main shore by water or extending as a shallow sandy strip into water. It may appear as a narrow island-like strip, a curved shoal, or a broad shallow sand flat at low tide. Do not confuse with a beach, where the sand forms the regular shoreline attached to land; a dune, which is elevated wind-shaped sand often with vegetation; or a mudflat/tidal flat, which is usually darker, muddier, and less clearly sandy. Ignore people, birds, boats, or beach objects if the defining landform is the exposed sandy bar itself.

name: shore
978.description: The narrow margin where land meets a body of water, typically shown as a broad horizontal scene with water on one side and exposed sand, mud, pebbles, rocks, or tidal flats on the other. It may appear as a beach, coastline, lake edge, or riverbank, and often includes shallow water, wet ground, wave wash, or a visible waterline.
978.guidelines: Classify images as shore when the main subject is the water’s edge itself—the boundary between land and water. Include sandy beaches, rocky shorelines, mudflats, and quiet banks of seas, lakes, or rivers. Do not require ocean waves or saltwater. Distinguish from open water/sea scenes by the presence of substantial visible land at the edge, and from beaches used as leisure scenes when the shoreline rather than people or activities is the main subject. Exclude marshes, harbors, boats, or coastal animals unless the shore remains the primary visual category.

name: valley
979.description: A valley is a low-lying stretch of land between mountains, hills, ridges, or cliffs, often elongated and sloping along its length. It typically appears as a broad or narrow depression with higher ground on both sides, and many examples include a river, stream, lake, or dry channel running along the valley floor.
979.guidelines: Classify as valley when the image shows a distinct low area enclosed or bordered by higher terrain on both sides. A visible river or stream is common but not required if the landform clearly forms a trough between slopes. Do not confuse it with a canyon or gorge, which is usually much narrower, deeper, and bounded by steep rock walls; a ravine, which is smaller and tighter; or a plain or basin, which may be low and open but lacks the clear between-higher-ground structure. If the image mainly shows a mountain, cliff, river, or lake without the surrounding enclosing landform, do not label it as valley.

name: volcano
980.description: A volcano is a broad mountain or cone built around a vent or crater, often with a rounded, truncated, or sharply conical summit rather than an ordinary pointed mountain peak. It may be snow-covered or bare, and may appear active with glowing lava, ash, smoke, or steam, or dormant with a quiet crater and volcanic slopes.
980.guidelines: Classify as volcano when the landform clearly shows a volcanic cone, crater, caldera, or eruptive activity such as lava or ash. Include both active and dormant volcanoes. Do not confuse with ordinary mountains or peaks: non-volcanic mountains usually lack a summit crater, central vent, lava flows, or the characteristic symmetric cone shape. Exclude toy models or artwork unless the real volcano itself is depicted.

name: baseball player
981.description: A baseball player is a person in a baseball uniform, typically wearing a jersey, long pants, cleats, and either a baseball cap or batting helmet. Players often carry or wear baseball equipment such as a bat, glove, or protective gear, and they are usually shown on a baseball field, near the dugout, or in a stadium setting.
981.guidelines: Classify as baseball player when the person is clearly participating in baseball and is identifiable by a baseball uniform, field context, or baseball equipment. This category includes batters, fielders, pitchers, baserunners, and players off the field in uniform. Do not confuse with softball players, who often appear on similar fields but may have different uniforms and equipment; use the broader baseball context and professional-style uniforms when visible. Also avoid confusion with cricket players, who use flat bats, wickets, and different uniforms, or with other athletes wearing numbered jerseys outside a baseball setting.

name: groom
982.description: A man in formal wedding attire, typically a dark suit, tuxedo, or light-colored ceremonial suit, often wearing a boutonniere, ribbon, or corsage on his lapel or chest. He is commonly shown beside the bride or participating in a wedding ceremony or reception.
982.guidelines: Classify as groom when the image centers on the male participant in a wedding, identified by wedding formalwear and context such as standing with the bride, receiving guests, or taking part in wedding rituals. Do not confuse with a generic man in a suit, best man, or other wedding guest: a groom is specifically the man being married, usually marked by pairing with the bride, prominent wedding staging, or distinctive boutonniere and ceremonial dress.

name: scuba diver
983.description: A person underwater or at the surface wearing self-contained scuba equipment, typically including a mask, regulator, air tank, buoyancy vest, wetsuit or drysuit, and often fins. The figure is usually submerged in open water, near reefs, wrecks, or pools, with hoses and breathing gear clearly visible.
983.guidelines: Classify as scuba diver only when the person is using scuba apparatus, especially a tank and regulator. Do not confuse with snorkelers or swimmers, who lack tanks and usually breathe through a surface snorkel, or with freedivers, who may wear fins and masks but no scuba tank. Also exclude surface-supplied divers if the setup is dominated by an umbilical air line rather than self-contained gear.

name: rapeseed
Brassica napus
984.description: Bright yellow flowering rapeseed growing in dense fields or stands, often forming broad carpets of yellow across farmland. Individual plants have slender green stems topped with clusters of small four-petaled yellow flowers and elongated buds or seed pods.
984.guidelines: Classify as rapeseed when the image shows yellow Brassica flowers or large agricultural fields blooming bright yellow. Key cues are the massed yellow flower heads, upright green stems, and typical crop-field appearance. Do not confuse with mustard or other yellow wildflowers: rapeseed is usually shown as a dense cultivated crop with uniform fields and small cruciform flowers, not isolated daisy-like blooms or irregular meadow flowers.

name: daisy
985.description: A daisy is a composite flower of the aster family, typically with a round central disk surrounded by many narrow ray petals. The flower head is usually white, pink, purple, yellow, or orange, often with a yellow or dark center, and has the simple radial 'classic daisy' look seen across many garden and wild species.
985.guidelines: Classify as daisy when the flower has the characteristic aster-family head: a single round center with a ring of petal-like rays, giving a clean, open, daisy-like form. This category includes common daisy-like ornamentals in several colors. Do not confuse with sunflower, which usually has a much larger, heavier central disk and broader rays; gerbera, which often has denser, more layered petals and a thicker cultivated look; or asters/chrysanthemums, which are often bushier or have many more, finer, or more crowded petals. Use the overall simple radiating flower head as the key cue.

name: yellow lady's slipper
Cypripedium parviflorum
986.description: A woodland orchid with a large inflated slipper-shaped pouch that is bright yellow, surrounded by long narrow twisted petals and sepals that are usually brownish, olive, or purplish with darker striping. The plant has several strongly pleated oval leaves along an upright stem, and flowers singly or in small clusters close to the top.
986.guidelines: Classify this as yellow lady's slipper when the flower has a prominent yellow pouch and thin elongated twisted lateral petals, with pleated orchid leaves on the stem. Distinguish it from pink lady's slipper, which has a pink pouch, and from other Cypripedium species such as showy lady's slipper or queen's lady's slipper, which have white and pink flowers rather than a solid yellow slipper. Avoid confusing it with non-orchid yellow wildflowers that lack the inflated pouch and twisted sepals.

name: corn
Zea mays
987.description: The category shows corn: ears or cobs covered with tightly packed rows of rounded kernels, usually yellow, white, orange, red, blue, or multicolored, often partly wrapped in green or dried tan husks with visible silk. Images may show whole ears on the plant, harvested cobs, loose kernels, dried decorative ears, or corn as a prominent ingredient in food.
987.guidelines: Classify as corn when the defining subject is maize ears/cobs or kernels, whether fresh, dried, ornamental, or prepared as visible corn pieces. Distinguish it from wheat, rice, barley, and oats by its large cob with kernels in regular rows rather than many tiny grains on a seed head. Distinguish it from baby corn by the much larger mature ears shown here. Do not confuse it with popcorn only when it is fully popped; unpopped popcorn kernels still count as corn.

name: acorn
988.description: The nut of an oak tree, typically smooth and oval to elongated, with a rounded or pointed tip and a rough, scaly cup (cap) attached at the base. Acorns are usually green when immature and turn tan, brown, or dark brown as they ripen; they may appear singly, in pairs, or in clusters on branches or on the ground.
988.guidelines: Classify as acorn when the image shows an oak nut with its characteristic cup-shaped cap and smooth nut body. Include both immature green acorns and mature brown ones, whether attached to the tree or fallen. Do not confuse with hazelnuts, chestnuts, beechnuts, or other tree nuts, which lack the distinct scaly oak cup; also avoid oak leaves or catkins shown without a clearly visible acorn.

name: rose hip
989.description: The fruit of a rose, typically a small red to orange, oval to round fleshy pod borne on thin stems. It often has a dried, star-like tuft of persistent sepals at the tip and may appear smooth, glossy, or slightly wrinkled as it matures.
989.guidelines: Classify as rose hip when the image shows the red/orange fruiting body of a rose with the characteristic dried sepal crown at one end. Do not confuse it with hawthorn berries, crabapples, or cherries: those usually lack the prominent star-like sepal tuft and often have different stem attachment and surface shape. Also exclude chestnuts or other nuts in husks, which are larger, harder-shelled, and not borne as fleshy rose fruits.

name: conker
Aesculus hippocastanum
990.description: Glossy, rounded dark reddish-brown seeds of the horse chestnut, each with a large pale tan circular or oval scar on one side. They are often shown partly enclosed in or beside a thick green to brown husk covered with short, widely spaced blunt spines; the husk typically splits into sections to reveal one or more shiny seeds.
990.guidelines: Classify as conker when the image shows the characteristic horse chestnut seed or its spiny capsule: a smooth polished brown seed with a broad pale patch, usually larger and rounder than a true chestnut. Do not confuse with edible chestnut, which usually sits in a much denser, hairier burr and has a pointed tip with a small tuft rather than a large pale scar. Also distinguish from other buckeyes: buckeye seeds are similar, but the classic conker of Aesculus hippocastanum is especially glossy and commonly paired with a thick husk bearing sparse blunt spines rather than a nearly smooth or warty husk.

name: coral fungus
991.description: A branching mushroom with an upright, coral-like form made of many slender clubs or forked tips arising from a short base. It may be dense or loosely branched, and is commonly white, cream, yellow, orange, pink, lavender, or purple.
991.guidelines: Classify as coral fungus when the fruiting body forms a tuft or cluster of erect, repeatedly branched fingers resembling marine coral. Include both finely branched and thicker club-like forms. Do not confuse it with antler fungi, which are usually simpler and less densely coral-like; with jelly fungi, which look translucent or gelatinous; or with cauliflower fungus, which has broad ruffled folds rather than cylindrical branches.

name: fly agaric
Amanita muscaria
992.description: A large, stout mushroom with a bright red to orange-red cap covered in scattered white to cream wart-like patches, a white stem, white gills, and often a skirt-like ring on the stem. Young specimens may be round or egg-shaped; mature caps become convex to nearly flat. It commonly grows on the ground in woodland, moss, grass, or leaf litter.
992.guidelines: Classify as fly agaric when the mushroom has the classic red or orange-red cap with distinct white warty veil remnants and a white stalk with white gills, often plus a ring. Do not confuse it with other agarics or red-capped mushrooms that lack white warts, have brown gills, darker stems, or different cap textures. Distinguish it from other Amanita species by the vivid scarlet-to-orange cap with white spots; avoid using this label for plain brown, tan, or unspotted mushrooms.

name: false morel
Gyromitra
993.description: A mushroom with a wrinkled, lobed, brain-like or saddle-shaped cap, usually reddish-brown to dark brown, sometimes tan, mounted on a thick pale stem. The cap surface is folded and convoluted rather than pitted, and the fruiting body often grows on the ground or near decaying wood, commonly in coniferous forest habitats.
993.guidelines: Classify as false morel when the mushroom has an irregularly folded, brain-like or saddle-like cap with broad wrinkles and a stout stem. Do not confuse it with true morels (Morchella), which have a honeycomb of deep pits and ridges, or with cup fungi such as Peziza, which form open cups without a thick stem. The key cue is the fleshy, convoluted cap rather than a neatly pitted or smoothly cup-shaped fruiting body.

name: stinkhorn
Phallaceae
994.description: Fungi in the stinkhorn family, typically emerging from a round whitish 'egg' and developing into foul-smelling fruiting bodies. Mature forms vary widely: many are upright and phallus-shaped with a white or orange stalk and a dark olive-brown slimy spore mass on the tip, while others are bright red or orange and form starfish-, anemone-, finger-, or lattice-like structures.
994.guidelines: Classify as stinkhorn when the fungus shows the characteristic egg stage or an adult form with a spongy stalk or bizarre red/orange arms, often bearing dark slimy gleba and growing from mulch, leaf litter, or wood debris. Do not confuse with morels or other cap-and-stem mushrooms: stinkhorns often have foul-smelling slime instead of gills or pores. Separate from inkcaps by the lack of a normal mushroom cap with dissolving black gills, and from puffballs/earthballs by the emergence of a distinct stalked or star-like fruiting body from an egg.

name: earthstar
Geastrum
995.description: A small round spore sac sits in the center of a star-shaped outer layer that has split open into several thick pointed segments. The rays spread flat or curl back around the ball, and are usually tan, brown, gray, or whitish, on leaf litter or soil.
995.guidelines: Classify as earthstar when a puffball-like central spore case is surrounded by a distinctly split outer skin forming star-like rays. Do not confuse it with puffballs, which lack the opened star base, or bird's nest fungi, which are cup-shaped and contain multiple egg-like peridioles rather than one central spore ball. Also distinguish from flowers or seed pods by the dry, leathery fungal texture and the central pore on the spore sac.

name: hen of the woods
Grifola frondosa
996.description: A large, dense, bush-like bracket fungus made of many overlapping fronds arising from a single branched white base. The caps are thin, flat, spoon-, fan-, or tongue-shaped with wavy edges, typically gray-brown, tan, or buff above and pale to white beneath, forming a ruffled leafy mass.
996.guidelines: Classify as hen of the woods when the fungus forms one big clustered rosette of many small overlapping fronds from a shared base, usually at the base of hardwood trees. Distinguish it from cauliflower mushroom, which has curled ribbon-like folds rather than distinct caps; Berkeley's polypore, which has fewer, broader lobes; and oyster mushrooms, which grow in shelf-like layers with clearer individual caps and gills instead of pores.

name: bolete
997.description: A fleshy mushroom with a thick stem and a rounded to cushion-shaped cap, usually brown, tan, reddish, yellowish, or orange. Instead of gills, the underside has a sponge-like layer of tiny pores or tubes, often white, cream, yellow, olive, or reddish. Many have stout proportions and a dry, velvety, or slightly sticky cap surface.
997.guidelines: Classify as bolete when the mushroom has pores rather than gills beneath the cap. This separates it from typical gilled mushrooms such as Agaricus, Russula, and Lactarius. Do not rely on one cap color: boletes vary widely in color and stem patterning. Distinguish from polypores/bracket fungi by the bolete’s cap-and-stem form, and from earthballs or puffballs by the visible stem and pore surface under the cap.
